_note: Short summaries of the entities (who or what, the part in the Eddas, key relations), written by an AI model (Claude) from the aligned texts and general knowledge, not copied from Wikipedia. status draft = not reviewed: the page shows them as 'AI draft · not reviewed' until a person checks them (status reviewed, reviewed_by user:<id>). First pass 2026-11-07: every entity with at least 5 Old Norse mentions; second pass the same day: those with 1-4 (one short paragraph each), except 11 whose index entry mixes figures or is a false match. English only; an Icelandic text goes in 'is' (with 'by' as {lang: author} when the authors differ). CC BY 4.0 like the rest of the edition.

odin.en:
Óðinn is the chief of the Æsir, god of wisdom, poetry, magic, war and the dead. Husband of Frigg and father of Þórr, Baldr, Váli and Víðarr, he lives in Ásgarðr, gathers fallen warriors in Valhöll and rides the eight-legged Sleipnir. He bears scores of names, many listed in Grímnismál and Gylfaginning (chapter 20).

He runs through both Eddas. In Gylfaginning he appears as the triple Hárr, Jafnhárr and Þriði (chapter 2), while Snorri's Prologue (chapter 3) makes him a human king descended from the kings of Troy. Völuspá is addressed to him, and at Ragnarök he is swallowed by Fenrir (Gylfaginning chapter 51; Völuspá in skamma 15). He seeks wisdom by contest or disguise in Vafþrúðnismál, Grímnismál (as Grímnir, tormented by King Geirröðr), Hárbarðsljóð (as the ferryman Hárbarðr mocking Þórr) and Baldrs draumar; Hávamál gathers his counsels and tells how he won the runes and the mead of poetry, a story Snorri retells in Skáldskaparmál (from chapter 5). In the heroic poems he shapes human fates: he gives Dagr the spear that kills Helgi (Helgakviða Hundingsbana II, prose) and puts Sigrdrífa to sleep (Sigrdrífumál 2).

thor.en:
Þórr is the god of thunder and the strongest of the Æsir, son of Óðinn and Jörð (Earth), husband of Sif, father of Magni, Móði and Þrúðr and stepfather of Ullr. His hall is Bilskirnir in Þrúðvangar (Þrúðheimr in Grímnismál 4); he owns Mjöllnir (his hammer), a belt of strength, iron gloves and a goat-drawn chariot (Gylfaginning chapter 21). The Prologue (chapter 3) turns him into Trór, a grandson of King Priam of Troy.

He is the giants' great enemy. In Gylfaginning he kills the builder of Ásgarðr's wall (chapter 42), visits Útgarða-Loki (chapters 44-47), fishes for Jörmungandr (the Midgard serpent) with Hymir (chapter 48) and kills the serpent at Ragnarök, dying of its venom (chapter 51); Skáldskaparmál tells of his duels with Hrungnir (chapters 24-25) and Geirröðr (chapter 26). Hárbarðsljóð, Hymiskviða, Lokasenna, Þrymskviða (the stolen hammer recovered with Þórr disguised as Freyja) and Alvíssmál are built around him. Snorri says the serpent survived the fishing trip, whereas Hymiskviða has Þórr strike its head.

sigurdr.en:
Sigurðr Fáfnisbani ("Fáfnir's slayer") is the central hero of the Völsung-Niflung cycle, son of Sigmundr and Hjördís, raised at King Hjálprekr's court and fostered by the smith Reginn. He married Guðrún, daughter of Gjúki, and was the father of Svanhildr; his tragedy turns on his entanglement with Brynhildr.

A sequence of Eddic poems follows his life: Grípisspá, where his uncle Grípir foretells it; Reginsmál (the otter's ransom, the horse Grani, vengeance on Hundingr's sons); Fáfnismál (he kills the dragon Fáfnir on Gnitaheiðr, tastes the heart, understands the birds and kills Reginn); Sigrdrífumál (he wakes the sleeping valkyrie). At Gjúki's court he swears brotherhood with Gunnarr and Högni and, in Gunnarr's shape, rides through the flames to win Brynhildr for him (Sigurðarkviða in meiri 2-3). When the deception comes out, Brynhildr has him killed; Guðrúnarkviða I and II, Sigurðarkviða in skamma and Helreið Brynhildar deal with the aftermath. Snorri retells the story in Skáldskaparmál chapters 47-50. The sources disagree about his death: slain in bed by Gotthormr (Sigurðarkviða in skamma, Snorri) or out of doors, as the prose note to the Brot reports from "German men". He is the Siegfried of the Nibelungenlied.

loki.en:
Loki (also Loptr) is the shape-changing trickster counted among the Æsir though born of giants: Gylfaginning (chapter 33) and Skáldskaparmál (chapter 23) name his father Fárbauti, his mother Laufey or Nál, and his brothers Býleistr and Helblindi. With the giantess Angrboða he fathers Fenrir, Jörmungandr and Hel (Gylfaginning 34); as a mare he bears Sleipnir to the stallion Svaðilfari (Gylfaginning 42); Sigyn is his wife.

He is both helper and enemy of the gods. Snorri has him travel with Þórr to Útgarða-Loki (Gylfaginning 44-46), lose and then recover Iðunn from Þjazi (Skáldskaparmál 2-3), have Sif's hair cut and the gods' treasures made (Skáldskaparmál 43), extort the dwarf Andvari's gold for Otter's ransom (Skáldskaparmál 46; Reginsmál), and lead Þórr to Geirröðr (Skáldskaparmál 26). In Þrymskviða he recovers Mjöllnir. He guides Höðr's mistletoe shaft at Baldr, refuses to weep as the giantess Þökk, and is bound with venom dripping on him (Gylfaginning 49-50; Völuspá 35; Lokasenna, where he insults every god at Ægir's feast). At Ragnarök he steers the ship of the dead and he and Heimdallr kill each other (Völuspá 51; Gylfaginning 51).

gudrun.en:
Guðrún Gjúkadóttir is the daughter of King Gjúki and Grímhildr, sister of Gunnarr and Högni, and the central woman of the Niflung cycle. She is married first to Sigurðr (their children are Sigmundr and Svanhildr), then to Atli, and finally to King Jónakr, whose sons by her are named in the prose of Guðrúnarhvöt as Sörli, Erpr and Hamðir.

Skáldskaparmál chapters 48-49 tell her story in prose, including the quarrel with Brynhildr while washing their hair in the river that leads to Sigurðr's murder. In the poems she grieves silently over Sigurðr (Guðrúnarkviða I), recalls her sorrows to Þjóðrekr (Guðrúnarkviða II) and clears herself of adultery by ordeal (Guðrúnarkviða III). After Atli kills her brothers she kills their sons, then Atli, and burns his hall (Atlakviða, Atlamál). When Svanhildr is trodden to death by Jörmunrekkr's order she urges her sons to vengeance (Guðrúnarhvöt, Hamðismál 2). The two Atli poems differ in tone and detail; in the German Nibelungenlied the corresponding figure, Kriemhild, instead avenges her husband on her own brothers.

etzel.en:
Atli Buðlason, the Norse counterpart of the Hunnic king Attila (German Etzel), is the son of Buðli and brother of Brynhildr and Oddrún. After Sigurðr's death the Gjúkungar give him Guðrún as wife; Brynhildr blames him for her fate in Guðrúnarkviða I (25) and Sigurðarkviða in skamma.

He invites Gunnarr and Högni to his court and has them killed for the Niflung gold. Guðrún avenges her brothers by killing their two sons, serving them to Atli, and then killing him and burning his hall: so in Atlakviða, the longer Atlamál and Skáldskaparmál chapter 50. In Guðrúnarkviða III he suspects Guðrún of adultery with Þjóðrekr, and in Oddrúnargrátr he refuses Gunnarr his sister Oddrún. In the Nibelungenlied, by contrast, Etzel is not the killer of the Burgundians. The name is also borne by others (a giantess Atla among Heimdallr's mothers in Völuspá in skamma 8, a warrior in Helgakviða Hundingsbana I 52); the index may mix them.

gunnar.en:
Gunnarr Gjúkason is king of the Gjúkungar or Niflungar, son of Gjúki and Grímhildr, brother of Högni, Guðrún and Guðný, with Gotthormr as Gjúki's stepson (Skáldskaparmál chapter 48; Hyndluljóð 27). He corresponds to Gunther of the Nibelungenlied and ultimately to the Burgundian king Gundaharius, destroyed by Hunnish forces in the 430s.

Unable to ride through the fire around Brynhildr, he wins her when Sigurðr takes his shape (Skáldskaparmál chapter 48; Grípisspá 39). Driven by Brynhildr, he plots Sigurðr's death, carried out by Gotthormr (Skáldskaparmál chapter 49; Sigurðarkviða in skamma; Brot af Sigurðarkviðu). Invited by Atli, he goes despite warnings (Atlakviða 1-3; Atlamál 7), and the gold of Fáfnir is hidden in the Rhine, never to be revealed. Captured, he is thrown into a snake pit and plays the harp until an adder kills him. Atlakviða (31) has him strike the harp with his hand, whereas Atlamál (66) and Snorri (Skáldskaparmál chapter 50) say he played with his toes, his hands being bound. Oddrúnargrátr tells of his love for Atli's sister Oddrún; in Atlamál his wife is Glaumvör (6).

gestumblindi.en:
Gestumblindi is a powerful man of Reiðgotaland who has fallen out of favour with King Heiðrekr, and also the name under which Óðinn disguises himself to take his place. Facing judgement, the real Gestumblindi sacrifices to Óðinn for help, and a guest who looks exactly like him goes to the king's court in his stead.

In the riddle contest of Heiðreks gátur (Gestumblindi's riddles) the disguised god poses some three dozen riddles, many opening "What is that wonder which I saw outside before Dellingr's doors?", and Heiðrekr solves each one (ale, a bridge, dew, an anchor, a leek, a sow with piglets). The last question (stanza 36), what Óðinn whispered into Baldr's ear before he was laid on the pyre, can be answered only by Óðinn himself. Heiðrekr then strikes at him with the sword Tyrfingr; the god escapes as a falcon, its tail cut short, and that same night the king is killed.

hogni.en:
Högni is a son of Gjúki and Grímhildr, brother of Gunnarr and Guðrún, and one of the Niflungar; Atlamál names his wife Kostbera. With Gunnarr he swore blood-brotherhood with Sigurðr (Skáldskaparmál chapter 48; Grípisspá 37).

When Brynhildr demands Sigurðr's death, Högni is the voice of caution: in Sigurðarkviða in skamma 17 he refuses to break the oaths, and in the Brot (stanzas 5, 7) he blames Brynhildr's jealousy; the deed is left to Gotthormr, though Högni tells Guðrún the news (Guðrúnarkviða II 7). Invited by Atli, he reads the warning in Guðrún's ring wound with a wolf's hair (Atlakviða 8) but rides with Gunnarr; at Atli's court his heart is cut out, and Gunnarr dies in the snake-pit (Atlakviða, Atlamál, Oddrúnargrátr 28, Skáldskaparmál chapter 50). In the Nibelungenlied his counterpart Hagen is a vassal rather than a brother, and is Siegfried's killer. The name is also borne by Sigrún's father in the Helgi poems and by Hildr's father in the tale of the Hjaðningar (Háttatal); the index may mix them.

baldur.en:
Baldr is the son of Óðinn and Frigg, husband of Nanna and father of Forseti; his hall is Breiðablik (Grímnismál 12; Gylfaginning chapter 22, where Snorri describes him as so fair that light shines from him). Skáldskaparmál (chapter 12) lists his kennings, among them owner of the ship Hringhorni and the ring Draupnir.

His death is the central tragedy of the myths. Baldrs draumar tells of his ominous dreams and Óðinn's ride to a dead seeress, who foretells that Höðr will kill him; Völuspá 31-33 has the mistletoe, Höðr's shot and the vengeance of Baldr's newborn brother (Váli). Snorri's fuller account (Gylfaginning 49) adds Frigg's oath from all things, Loki's trick, the funeral on Hringhorni, Hermóðr's ride to Hel and the failed weeping. In Lokasenna 27-28 Loki boasts of his part. Baldr returns after Ragnarök with Höðr (Völuspá 62). The final question of Gestumblindi in Heiðreksgátur (36), what Óðinn whispered into Baldr's ear on the pyre, is also the question that ends Vafþrúðnismál. Saxo tells a quite different, euhemerised story of Balderus and Høtherus.

fafnir.en:
Fáfnir is the son of Hreiðmarr and brother of Reginn and Otr. When the Æsir pay Hreiðmarr gold as compensation for killing Otr, Fáfnir murders his father for it, refuses Reginn a share, takes the helm of terror (ægishjálmr) and the sword Hrotti, and lies on the hoard on Gnitaheiðr in the shape of a serpent.

The story is told in Skáldskaparmál chapters 46-47 and in the prose and verse of Reginsmál. Urged by Reginn, Sigurðr digs a pit in the dragon's path and stabs him from below. In Fáfnismál the dying Fáfnir questions Sigurðr, who at first conceals his name, warns him that the gold will be his death and answers his questions about the gods; Sigurðr then roasts the heart, comes to understand the speech of birds and kills Reginn. Gold is accordingly called "Fáfnir's lair" or "metal of Gnitaheiðr" (Skáldskaparmál chapter 47), and Sigurðr is known as Fáfnisbani, "Fáfnir's slayer".

gylfi.en:
Gylfi is a legendary king of Sweden who frames Snorri's Gylfaginning. In chapter 1 he grants the wandering woman Gefjun as much land as four oxen can plough in a day and a night; she, of the race of the Æsir, ploughs out a piece of his realm and draws it to Denmark (Bragi's verse is quoted). In the Prologue (chapter 5) he meets the Æsir arriving from Asia and offers Óðinn power in his realm.

Troubled by the Æsir's cunning, Gylfi travels to Ásgarðr in disguise under the name Gangleri (chapter 2) and questions three figures, Hárr, Jafnhárr and Þriði, about the creation, the gods and Ragnarök; nearly all his mentions are these questions. At the end the hall vanishes and he returns to tell what he has heard. In Skáldskaparmál (chapter 64) the sea is called "Gylfi's land", where Gylfi is used as a sea-king name.

freyja.en:
Freyja is the foremost goddess of the Vanir, daughter of Njörðr and sister of Freyr (Gylfaginning chapter 24). She is married to Óðr, for whom she weeps tears of red gold; their daughter is Hnoss. She owns the necklace Brísingamen and is also called Mardöll, Hörn, Gefn and Sýr (Gylfaginning chapter 35). Her hall is Fólkvangr, and she takes half of the slain, Óðinn the other half (Grímnismál 14; Gylfaginning chapter 24); she drives a chariot drawn by cats (Gylfaginning chapter 49).

Giants covet her: the master builder of Ásgarðr's wall asks for her as his wages (Gylfaginning chapter 42), and in Þrymskviða the giant Þrymr will return Þórr's hammer only if she becomes his bride. She lends Loki her feather-dress but angrily refuses the marriage, so Þórr goes to Jötunheimar disguised as her. In Lokasenna (29-32) Loki accuses her of having lain with all the gods and elves, her brother included. In Hyndluljóð she rides with her favourite Óttarr, in the form of a boar, to the giantess Hyndla to learn his ancestry.

freyr.en:
Freyr is a god of the Vanir, son of Njörðr and brother of Freyja, who lives among the Æsir. Gylfaginning (chapter 24) says he rules rain, sunshine and the fruits of the earth and is invoked for good seasons and peace. He was given Álfheimr as a tooth-gift (Grímnismál 5) and owns the ship Skíðblaðnir, made by the sons of Ívaldi (Grímnismál 43; Skáldskaparmál chapter 14). Skáldskaparmál chapter 14 lists his kennings, among them "Adversary of Beli".

His central myth is told in Skírnismál and Gylfaginning (chapter 37): sitting in Hliðskjálf he sees the giantess Gerðr, falls sick with love, and gives his sword to his servant Skírnir, who wins her for him. Without the sword he kills Beli with a hart's antler, and at Ragnarök he falls to Surtr (chapter 51). In Lokasenna Týr praises him and Loki taunts him with the sold sword. Snorri calls him "most renowned of the Æsir" although he is by origin one of the Vanir.

helgi-hundingsbani.en:
Helgi Hundingsbani ("Hundingr's slayer") is a Völsung hero, son of Sigmundr and Borghildr, born at Brálundr and named after the earlier hero Helgi Hjörvarðsson. His beloved is the valkyrie Sigrún, daughter of King Högni.

His story is told in Helgakviða Hundingsbana I and II (the latter called Völsungakviða in forna in the manuscript). As a youth he spies on King Hundingr, escapes disguised as a bondwoman at the mill, and then kills Hundingr. Sigrún, promised against her will to Höðbroddr son of Granmarr, rides to him for help; he defeats Granmarr's sons in battle at Frekasteinn, in which Sigrún's father Högni also falls. Her brother Dagr, lent Óðinn's spear, later kills Helgi. In the second poem the dead Helgi returns from his burial mound and Sigrún spends a night with him there; the prose says that he went to Valhöll, where Óðinn bade him rule with him, and that the lovers were believed to have been born again as Helgi Haddingjaskati and Kára. The flyting between Helgi's half-brother Sinfjötli and Granmarr's son Guðmundr appears in both poems in different forms.

heidrekr.en:
Heiðrekr is a legendary king of the Goths in the cycle preserved in Hervarar saga ok Heiðreks: son of Höfundr and the shield-maiden Hervör, and owner of the cursed sword Tyrfingr. In Hervararkviða (18) the dead Angantýr foretells his birth to Hervör.

In Heiðreksgátur he has vowed that an offender may go free by setting him a riddle he cannot solve. Gestumblindi, who is Óðinn in disguise, poses riddle after riddle (each ending "King Heiðrekr, think on the riddle"), and Heiðrekr solves them until the last (36): what Óðinn said into Baldr's ear. Recognising his guest, the king strikes at him with Tyrfingr; Óðinn escapes as a falcon, and that night Heiðrekr is killed. In Hlöðskviða his sons Angantýr and Hlöðr quarrel over his inheritance, which leads to the battle of Goths and Huns.

The Heiðrekr of Oddrúnargrátr, father of Borgný, is a different king; the index may mix them.

bragi.en:
Bragi is the god of poetry and eloquence among the Æsir, husband of Iðunn. Gylfaginning (chapter 26) says he is renowned for wisdom and skill with words, and that poetry (bragr) is named after him.

In Skáldskaparmál (chapters 1-7) Bragi sits beside Ægir at the gods' feast and tells him the myths of Iðunn and Þjazi and of the mead of poetry, which frame the book. In Lokasenna (stanzas 8-18) he tries to buy Loki off with a horse, a sword and a ring and is mocked as the least brave of the gods. Grímnismál 44 names him the best of skalds, Sigrdrífumál 16 speaks of runes on "Bragi's tongue", and in a verse quoted in Skáldskaparmál chapter 9 Óðinn sends Hermóðr and Bragi to welcome a dead king to Valhöll.

Many mentions in this index refer instead to the ninth-century skald Bragi Boddason (Bragi the Old), whose verses Snorri often quotes, and one to Bragi son of Högni in Helgakviða Hundingsbana II; the index may mix them. Whether the god is a deified form of the skald is debated.

gjuki.en:
Gjúki is the king of the Gjúkungar (Niflungar), the Norse counterpart of the Burgundian king Gibica. According to Skáldskaparmál chapter 48 his wife is Grímhildr and his children are Gunnarr, Högni, Guðrún and Guðný, with Gotthormr as his stepson; Hyndluljóð 27 likewise says Gotthormr was not of Gjúki's race. Guðrúnarkviða I adds a daughter Gollrönd (12) and a sister Gjaflaug (4).

Gjúki himself barely acts: he is chiefly a point of reference. Sigurðr comes to his court after killing Fáfnir (foretold in Grípisspá and Fáfnismál 41; Sigurðarkviða in skamma 1-2) and marries Guðrún, whom Gjúki dowers with gold (Guðrúnarkviða II 1). Throughout the heroic poems his sons and daughter are called "Gjúki's heirs" and "Gjúki's daughter", down to the end of the line with Hamðir and Sörli (Skáldskaparmál chapter 50).

regin.en:
Reginn is a son of Hreiðmarr and brother of Fáfnir and Otr, a smith of dwarfish stature, wise, fierce and skilled in magic, who becomes the foster-father of Sigurðr at King Hjálprekr's court (Reginsmál prose). When Fáfnir kills their father and keeps all the gold paid as compensation for Otr, Reginn is left without his share (Reginsmál; Skáldskaparmál chapter 47).

He forges the sword Gramr for Sigurðr and urges him to kill Fáfnir on Gnitaheiðr. After the killing he cuts out the dragon's heart, drinks the blood and asks Sigurðr to roast the heart for him; tasting it, Sigurðr understands the birds, who warn that Reginn means to betray him and avenge his brother, and Sigurðr kills him (Fáfnismál 25-37 and prose; Skáldskaparmál chapter 47). A dwarf named Reginn also appears in the dwarf list of Völuspá (12).

frigg.en:
Frigg is Óðinn's wife and the foremost of the goddesses, the mother of Baldr; Snorri names her father as Fjörgvinn. Her hall is Fensalir and her attendants include Fulla and Gná (Gylfaginning chapter 35). She knows all fates though she does not speak of them (Gylfaginning chapter 20; Lokasenna). The Prologue (chapter 3) makes her the wife of Vóden, the Trojan-descended Óðinn.

Her largest role is in the death of Baldr (Gylfaginning chapter 49): she takes oaths from all things not to harm him, leaves out the young mistletoe and reveals this to the disguised Loki, then asks for a rider to Hel to ransom her son. Völuspá 33 has her weeping in Fensalir, and Völuspá 53 speaks of her second grief when Óðinn falls to the wolf. In Vafþrúðnismál (1-4) she counsels Óðinn before his contest with the giant; in the prose of Grímnismál she wagers with Óðinn over their foster-sons Agnarr and Geirröðr; in Lokasenna (25-29) Loki accuses her of sleeping with Vili and Vé.

gripir.en:
Grípir is a wise, far-seeing king, son of Eylimi and brother of Hjördís, and so the maternal uncle of Sigurðr. He is known only from Grípisspá ("Grípir's prophecy").

In the poem the young Sigurðr rides to his hall, is announced by the servant Geitir, and asks his uncle to foretell his life. Grípir predicts in order the vengeance for Sigmundr, the slaying of Fáfnir and Reginn, and the waking of the valkyrie; then, at first reluctantly (Grípisspá 19-21), the darker part: Sigurðr's love for Brynhildr, the forgetfulness brought on by Grímhildr's wiles (33, 35), the exchange of shapes with Gunnarr (37-39) and his death at the hands of his brothers-in-law. He assures Sigurðr that he will bear no shame and that his name will be famous for ever (23). The poem works as a summary of the Sigurðr story told in the poems that follow it in the Codex Regius.

brynhild.en:
Brynhildr is the daughter of Buðli and sister of Atli, a warrior maiden at the centre of the Sigurðr tragedy. Grípisspá (27) has her fostered by Heimir; in Oddrúnargrátr (16-17) Buðli makes her a helmeted "wish-maid".

In Snorri's summary (Skáldskaparmál 48-49) Sigurðr wakes a sleeping valkyrie who calls herself Hildr and is Brynhildr; later, in Gunnarr's shape, he rides through the flames around her hall and wins her for Gunnarr. When she learns of the deception in a quarrel with Guðrún, she presses Gunnarr and Högni to have Sigurðr killed (Sigurðarkviða in skamma; Brot af Sigurðarkviðu, where she laughs once at the news, 14). She then kills herself and is burned beside Sigurðr; in Helreið Brynhildar she justifies herself to a giantess on her way to Hel. Guðrúnarkviða I (25) has her blame Atli, and in Dráp Niflunga Atli blames the Gjúkungar for her death.

The poems call the awakened valkyrie Sigrdrífa, while Snorri, Helreið Brynhildar and the Völsunga saga identify her with Brynhildr; the German Nibelungenlied's Brünhild is a queen of Iceland.

sigmund.en:
Sigmundr is the son of Völsungr and father of Sigurðr. In the Eddic prose he is a king in the land of the Franks; his eldest son is Sinfjötli, with Borghildr he has Helgi (Hundingsbani) and Hámundr, and with Hjördís, daughter of Eylimi, he fathers Sigurðr.

The prose of Grípisspá (Frá dauða Sinfjötla) tells how he carried the poisoned Sinfjötli's body to a mysterious ferryman and later fell in battle against the sons of Hundingr; Reginsmál 26 celebrates Sigurðr's vengeance on his killer. Hyndluljóð 2 says Óðinn gave him a sword, and Skáldskaparmál chapter 51 that he could drink poison unharmed. Elsewhere he is mostly named in the formula "son of Sigmundr" for Sigurðr or Helgi. A fragment among the Eddubrot shows him and Sinfjötli sawing through a stone slab, a scene from the Völsunga saga, which tells his story in full; the Old English Beowulf already knows a Sigemund as a dragon-slayer.

The same name is borne by Sigurðr's young son, killed with his father (Skáldskaparmál chapter 49; Guðrúnarkviða II 28); the index may mix them.

vafthrudnir.en:
Vafþrúðnir is a giant famed for ancient lore, Óðinn's opponent in the eddic poem Vafþrúðnismál. Frigg warns Óðinn against visiting him (stanzas 1-2), but Óðinn goes to his hall under the name Gagnráðr.

The poem is a wisdom contest. Vafþrúðnir first tests his guest (11-17), then they wager their heads (19), and Óðinn questions the giant about the making of the world from Ymir (21), the origin of sun and moon (23), day and night (25), winter and summer (27), the oldest giants Bergelmir and Aurgelmir (29-35), and Ragnarök and what comes after (51, 53). Óðinn wins with a question only he can answer, what he whispered to his dead son Baldr, and the giant recognises him. Snorri draws on the poem repeatedly in Gylfaginning and quotes Vafþrúðnir by name in chapter 5.

fjolsvidr.en:
Fjölsviðr ('very wise') is the watchman at the gate of Menglöð's hall in Fjölsvinnsmál. The hero Svipdagr, arriving under the false name Vindkaldr (6), addresses him as a giant, and he answers churlishly that the stranger will not be let in. The same name is one of Óðinn's names in Grímnismál 47.

Most of the poem is a question-and-answer exchange in which Fjölsviðr names what Svipdagr sees: the mistress of the hall, Menglöð (8); the gate Þrymgjöll (10); the house Gastropnir, which he says he built himself from the limbs of Leirbrimir (12); the tree Mímameiðr (14); the golden cock Víðófnir (18); the hounds Gífr and Geri (20); and the sword Lævateinn, kept by Sinmara (26). When the stranger reveals himself as Svipdagr, Fjölsviðr announces him to Menglöð and the gates open (44).

angantyr.en:
Angantýr is the name of several legendary figures, chiefly in the poems of Hervarar saga. The best known is the berserk son of Arngrímr and Eyfura, father of Hervör and owner of the cursed sword Tyrfingr. He and his brothers fell on Sámsey fighting Hjálmarr, who died of the wounds Tyrfingr gave him (Hjálmarskviða 2). In Hervararkviða Hervör goes to his burial mound, wakes him and forces him to hand over the sword, despite his warning that it will destroy her kin.

His grandson, also Angantýr, son of Heiðrekr, is king of the Goths in Hlöðskviða. He refuses to divide the inheritance equally with his half-brother Hlöðr, defeats the Huns and kills Hlöðr, lamenting over him (stanzas 31-32). Hyndluljóð names Angantýr as Óttarr's opponent in a wager (stanza 9) and among the sons of Arngrímr (stanza 22). The index mixes these figures.

njordr.en:
Njörðr is a god of the Vanir who lives at Nóatún, father of Freyr and Freyja. Snorri describes him as ruling the course of the wind and calming sea and fire, the god to call on for seafaring and fishing, and so rich that he can grant wealth (Gylfaginning chapter 23).

He came to the Æsir as a hostage from the Vanir, in exchange for Hœnir (Gylfaginning chapter 23; Vafþrúðnismál 38; Lokasenna 34-35). Grímnismál 16 names Nóatún as his hall. His marriage to the giantess Skaði, who chose him by his feet, failed because she could not bear the sea nor he the mountains (Gylfaginning chapter 23; Skáldskaparmál chapter 3). In Lokasenna Loki mocks him as a hostage and says that he had Freyr by his own sister (36). In Gylfaginning chapter 37 it is Njörðr who sends Skírnir to speak with the lovesick Freyr, whereas the prose of Skírnismál gives that role to Skaði. Skáldskaparmál chapter 13 lists his kennings. His name is also a common base word in skaldic kennings for a warrior (Háttatal).

einarr.en:
Einarr Skúlason is a twelfth-century Icelandic skald and priest who served the Norwegian kings of his day; his best-known work is Geisli, a poem on St Óláfr. He is one of the poets Snorri quotes most often in Skáldskaparmál, chiefly to illustrate kennings and poetic names: for the sea (chapter 33), Freyja as mother of Hnoss (44), Christ (65), the names of Ægir's daughters (76), weapons, ships and other heiti.

Several of the quotations are introduced only as "Einarr sang", and some of these may belong to the tenth-century Einarr skálaglamm, author of Vellekla; the index may mix the two.

hrungnir.en:
Hrungnir is a giant, said in Skáldskaparmál to be the strongest of them, with a heart and head of stone; he owns the horse Gullfaxi. His duel with Þórr is the main myth told of him.

In Skáldskaparmál chapter 24 Hrungnir races Óðinn on Sleipnir into Ásgarðr, gets drunk in Valhöll and threatens to carry off Freyja and Sif. Þórr challenges him to single combat at Grjótúnagarðar. Þjálfi tricks him into standing on his stone shield, Mjöllnir shatters his skull, and his hone breaks, one piece lodging in Þórr's head; the giant falls with his foot across Þórr's neck, and only the infant Magni can lift it, receiving Gullfaxi as reward. Chapter 25 continues with the seeress Gróa trying to charm out the hone. Hence the shield is called "Hrungnir's foot-soles" (chapter 61, quoting Bragi). The poems allude to the fight: Hárbarðsljóð 14-15, Lokasenna 61 and 63 ("Hrungnir's slayer"), Sigrdrífumál 15, and Gróttasöngr 9, where the giantesses Fenja and Menja count him among their kin.

frodi.en:
Fróði is the name of several legendary Danish kings; the main one here is Fróði son of Friðleifr, grandson of Skjöldr, whose reign is the proverbial "Fróði's peace" (Fróðafriðr). Skáldskaparmál chapter 52 and the prose before Gróttasöngr date it to the time of Augustus and say no one harmed even his father's slayer.

He buys the giant maids Fenja and Menja in Sweden and sets them to grind gold, peace and happiness on the mill Grotti, refusing them rest. In Gróttasöngr they grind instead an army against him: the sea-king Mýsingr kills Fróði and the peace ends. Hence gold is called "Fróði's meal". Gróttasöngr 22 also foretells vengeance by Yrsa's son (Hrólfr kraki). The name also belongs to other figures, such as Frjóðigar "whom we call Fróði" in the Prologue's genealogy (chapter 4) and a Fróði in Hyndluljóð 19; the index may mix them.

helgi-hjorvardsson.en:
Helgi Hjörvarðsson is the hero of Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar, son of King Hjörvarðr and Sigrlinn, daughter of King Sváfnir. A silent youth without a name, he is named by the valkyrie Sváva, daughter of King Eylimi, who tells him of a sword, protects him in battle and later becomes his betrothed (6-7 and prose).

With his companion Atli Iðmundarson he avenges his mother's father by killing Hróðmarr and kills the giant Hati; Hati's daughter Hrímgerðr then threatens his fleet and is kept talking until daybreak turns her to stone (13-30). His half-brother Heðinn rashly vows to take Sváva (32-34). Helgi, foreseeing his death, falls fighting Álfr, son of Hróðmarr, at Sigarsvöllr, and asks Sváva to give her love to Heðinn (40-41). A closing prose note says that Helgi and Sváva were born again, which links him to Helgi Hundingsbani, whose Sigrún is called Sváva reborn.

sigrun.en:
Sigrún is a valkyrie, daughter of King Högni, and the beloved of Helgi Hundingsbani. In Helgakviða Hundingsbana I she rides to Helgi after his first victories, shields his fleet in a storm (stanza 30) and greets him after his victory over Granmarr's sons (stanza 54).

Helgakviða Hundingsbana II tells the fuller story. Her father has promised her to Höðbroddr, son of Granmarr, but she chooses Helgi; in the war that follows Helgi kills Höðbroddr and also her father, and they marry. Her brother Dagr, who was spared, later kills Helgi with Óðinn's spear, and she curses him. When the dead Helgi rides back to his burial mound she spends a night with him there, and she soon dies of grief. The closing prose says the two were believed to have been born again, she as Kára, daughter of Hálfdan. The prose at the end of Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar likewise makes her a rebirth of the valkyrie Sváva.

aegir.en:
Ægir, also called Hlér and, according to the Lokasenna prose and Skáldskaparmál chapter 33, Gymir, is a giant who personifies the sea. His wife is Rán and their nine daughters are the waves (Skáldskaparmál chapter 76).

At the start of Skáldskaparmál (chapter 1) he is a man from Hlésey, skilled in magic, who visits Ásgarðr; his questions to Bragi frame the first part of the treatise (Þjazi and Iðunn, the mead of poetry, the terms of poetry). He is also the gods' host: in Hymiskviða the gods ask him to brew ale for them, and Þórr fetches the giant Hymir's great kettle for the purpose (stanzas 1, 39); Lokasenna is set at the feast in his hall, and Loki curses him at the end (65). Skáldskaparmál chapter 41 explains the kenning "Ægir's fire" for gold by the glowing gold that lit his hall at a feast for the Æsir. His name is common in kennings for the sea, and in Heiðreks gátur "Ægir's maidens" is the answer to one of Gestumblindi's riddles (the waves).

alviss.en:
Alvíss ("all-wise") is a dwarf who lives beneath the rocks (Alvíssmál 3) and comes to claim Þórr's daughter as his bride. Þórr, who had not consented, says the dwarf may have her only if he can answer every question put to him.

In Alvíssmál Þórr asks what earth, heaven, moon, sun, clouds, wind, calm, sea, fire, wood, night, seed and ale are called among men, gods, Vanir, giants, elves, dwarfs and the dead (stanzas 9-34), and Alvíss answers each with a list of synonyms. The contest is a trick: Þórr keeps him talking until daybreak, and the dwarf is caught by the sunlight and turned to stone. The poem is essentially a versified list of poetic names of the kind Snorri collects in Skáldskaparmál.

hymir.en:
Hymir is a giant living in the east, beyond Élivágar at the edge of heaven; he owns a huge kettle and herds of oxen. In Hymiskviða he is Týr's father, whereas Snorri makes Týr a son of Óðinn.

In Gylfaginning (chapter 48) Þórr, disguised as a youth, stays with Hymir, uses the head of the ox Himinbrjótr as bait and hooks Jörmungandr (the Midgard serpent); the terrified Hymir cuts the line before Þórr can strike. Hymiskviða tells a fuller version: Þórr and Týr go to fetch Hymir's kettle so that Ægir can brew ale for the gods (stanza 5). Þórr eats two of Hymir's oxen (15); Hymir hauls up two whales while Þórr catches the serpent (21); on the advice of Týr's mother Þórr breaks an unbreakable cup on the giant's skull (30), then carries off the kettle and fights off the pursuing giants (35, 39). In Lokasenna 34 Loki insults Njörðr with "the daughters of Hymir".

heimdall.en:
Heimdallr is the watchman of the gods, called the White God, born of nine mothers (Gylfaginning chapter 27; Skáldskaparmál chapters 15 and 23). He lives at Himinbjörg by Bifröst, needs less sleep than a bird, sees a hundred leagues and hears grass grow. His horse is Gulltoppr and he owns the Gjallarhorn; Snorri also gives him the names Hallinskíði and Gullintanni.

At Ragnarök he blows the Gjallarhorn to wake the gods (Völuspá 46; Gylfaginning chapter 51), and he and Loki kill each other. In Völuspá 1 humankind are called "Heimdallr's sons", and Völuspá 27 speaks of his horn (or hearing) hidden under the world tree. He advises dressing Þórr as a bride in Þrymskviða 15, rebukes Loki in Lokasenna 47-48, rides to Baldr's pyre (Úlfr Uggason's verse, Skáldskaparmál chapter 9), and is identified with Rígr in the prose of Rígsþula. Kennings call him Loki's foe and seeker of Freyja's necklace.

huns.en:
The Huns (Húnar) appear in the heroic poems as a remembered people of the migration period, echoing Attila and the historical destruction of the Burgundians by Hunnish forces in the 430s. In Atlakviða they are Atli's people: the poem speaks of slaves from Hunland, the wary Huns in the hall, Hunnish youths and the weeping of the Huns when Guðrún takes her revenge (4, 2, 34, 38). Guðrúnarkviða II (15) also names them.

In Hlöðskviða (the battle of the Goths and Huns, from the Hervarar saga tradition) Húnaland is ruled by King Humli (1). His kinsman Hlöðr, half-brother of the Gothic king Angantýr, is refused an equal share of their father Heiðrekr's inheritance and leads the Hunnish host through Myrkviðr against the Goths, who defeat it; the Huns kill Angantýr's sister Hervör in the opening fight (20).

jotunheim.en:
Jötunheimar (the giants' worlds) is the land of the giants, usually placed to the east or north of the world of gods and men and separated from it by rivers and wild country. Many giants of the myths live there: Þjazi, Þrymr, Gymir, Hrungnir and Angrboða, the mother of Loki's monstrous children (Gylfaginning chapter 34).

It is the destination of many journeys. Gefjun takes her four oxen from there (Gylfaginning chapter 1); Loki flies there in Freyja's falcon form to recover Iðunn from Þjazi (Skáldskaparmál chapter 3); Skírnir rides there to woo Gerðr for Freyr (Skírnismál); Þórr and Loki, dressed as bride and maid, go there to recover Mjöllnir from Þrymr (Þrymskviða); and Þórr goes there to Útgarða-Loki (Gylfaginning chapter 45). Völuspá 8 tells of three powerful giant-maids coming from Jötunheimar, and Völuspá 48 has all Jötunheimar groaning at the onset of Ragnarök.

utgarda-loki.en:
Útgarða-Loki ("Loki of the Outer Enclosures") is the giant king of the stronghold Útgarðr, a master of illusion, distinct from the god Loki. He appears only in Snorri's Gylfaginning (chapters 45-47).

Disguised as the huge Skrýmir, he joins Þórr, Loki, Þjálfi and Röskva on their journey, ties their food bag so that Þórr cannot open it, and shrugs off three hammer blows in his sleep. In his hall he sets the visitors contests which they all lose: Loki in eating against Logi, Þjálfi in running against Hugi, Þórr in draining a drinking horn, lifting a grey cat and wrestling an old woman, Elli. As they leave, he reveals the tricks: Logi was fire, Hugi his own thought, the horn's end lay in the sea, the cat was the Miðgarðr serpent, Elli was old age, and Þórr's blows had struck a mountain. When Þórr turns back in anger, hall and king have vanished. In chapter 48 Gangleri asks whether Þórr ever took revenge for this, which leads into the story of his fishing for the serpent.

wayland-the-smith.en:
Völundr is the master smith of Germanic legend, known in English as Wayland. In the prose and stanzas of Völundarkviða he is one of three brothers, with Slagfiðr and Egill, sons of a king of the Finns; the three live for some years with swan-maidens who then fly away (2-5). Alone in Úlfdalir, Völundr is captured by King Níðuðr of the Njárar (6-13), who takes his ring and sword; on the queen's advice he is hamstrung and set to work on an island.

He takes revenge by killing Níðuðr's two sons, making goblets of their skulls, gems of their eyes and a brooch of their teeth for their sister Böðvildr (25), and by seducing Böðvildr when she brings him a broken ring to mend (26-27). He then rises into the air and, once Níðuðr has sworn not to harm his wife and child, tells the king what he has done (29-38). The poem calls him a prince of the elves (32). The story is also known in the Old English poem Deor, on the Franks Casket and in Þiðreks saga.

grani.en:
Grani is Sigurðr's horse. In the prose of Reginsmál Sigurðr chooses him from King Hjálprekr's stud; the Völsunga saga adds that he was descended from Sleipnir.

Grani carries the hoard from Fáfnir's lair (Skáldskaparmál chapter 47, Fáfnismál prose, Grípisspá 13), so that gold is called "Grani's burden" (Skáldskaparmál chapters 47, 56, 57; Háttatal). Only he will carry Sigurðr through the fire around Brynhildr's hall when Sigurðr rides in Gunnarr's shape (Skáldskaparmál chapter 48; Sigurðarkviða in meiri 2). After the murder he comes back riderless and hangs his head in grief (Guðrúnarkviða II 4-5). He also appears in the lists of horse names ("Sigurðr rode Grani", Skáldskaparmál chapter 72). Two Skáldskaparmál mentions refer instead to a skald named Grani; the index may mix them.

tyr.en:
Týr is a god of war and courage among the Æsir, the boldest of them, whom men should call on in battle (Gylfaginning chapter 25). Snorri calls him a son of Óðinn (Skáldskaparmál chapter 16), whereas Hymiskviða makes the giant Hymir his father.

When the gods bind the wolf Fenrir, only Týr dares to feed him, and he places his right hand in the wolf's mouth as a pledge; the wolf bites it off, so he is the one-handed god (Gylfaginning chapter 34). At Ragnarök he and the hound Garmr kill each other (chapter 51). In Hymiskviða he guides Þórr to Hymir to fetch a great kettle (stanzas 4-6, 33). In Lokasenna he defends Freyr, and Loki taunts him with the lost hand and with having fathered a son on his wife (37-40). Sigrdrífumál 6 bids men call twice on Týr when carving victory runes, and in skaldic verse "Týr" serves as a base word for a warrior (Háttatal).

atli-idmundarson.en:
Atli Iðmundarson is the son of Iðmundr, jarl of King Hjörvarðr, and the loyal companion of Helgi Hjörvarðsson in Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar. He is not the same as Atli Buðlason of the Niflung poems.

Atli is sent to woo Sigrlinn, daughter of King Sváfnir, for Hjörvarðr; he is refused, and a talking bird promises him help in return for sacrifices (prose and 1-4). On a second journey Sigrlinn is won, and she becomes Helgi's mother. Later Atli sails with Helgi, helps him kill Hróðmarr, and keeps watch over the fleet in Hatafjörðr. There he trades insults with the giantess Hrímgerðr, refusing to come ashore to fight her (13-23), and holds her in talk until daybreak, when she is turned to stone and becomes a landmark for men to mock (30).

ulfr-uggason.en:
Úlfr Uggason was an Icelandic skald of the late tenth century. His Húsdrápa was composed for Óláfr pái of Hjarðarholt and described the mythological scenes carved on the panels of Óláfr's new hall.

Snorri quotes the poem in many chapters of Skáldskaparmál, and it is a main source for several myths: Baldr's funeral procession, with Óðinn and Freyr riding to the pyre (chapters 9, 12 and 14); Þórr's fishing for Jörmungandr (the Midgard serpent) (chapter 11); and the fight between Heimdallr and Loki over the Brísingamen (chapters 15 and 23). Other stanzas illustrate kennings and poetic terms for men, fire and the land (chapters 59, 61, 67 and 70).

valhalla.en:
Valhöll ("hall of the slain") is Óðinn's great hall in Ásgarðr, where warriors fallen in battle, the einherjar, live until Ragnarök. Grímnismál 8 places it in Glaðsheimr and says that Óðinn chooses the slain there every day; Grímnismál 23, also quoted in Gylfaginning chapter 40, counts five hundred and forty doors, through each of which eight hundred warriors will go out to fight the wolf.

Snorri describes life there in Gylfaginning chapters 20 and 36-41: Óðinn as Father of the Slain receives the fallen, valkyries serve the drink, the warriors eat boar's meat and drink mead, and every day they fight one another in the courtyard and then ride home to feast. The hart Eikþyrnir stands on the hall (chapter 39), and the grove Glasir with leaves of red gold stands before its doors (Skáldskaparmál chapter 42). Two poems quoted in Skáldskaparmál chapter 9, Hákonarmál and Eiríksmál, describe kings received there, and the prose of Helgakviða Hundingsbana II says that Óðinn invited Helgi to rule beside him in Valhöll. Völuspá 33 speaks of Frigg weeping for "Valhöll's woe" after Baldr's death.

goths.en:
The Goths (Gotar, also Goðþjóð) were the East Germanic people whose fourth-century kingdom under Ermanaric (Jörmunrekkr) and wars with the Huns survived in heroic legend. In the Eddic poems the name is used loosely and with heroic colour: Gunnarr is called lord of the Goths (Grípisspá 35; Brot af Sigurðarkviðu 13), and in Helreið Brynhildar (9) Hjálmgunnarr is the "leader of Goths".

They are Jörmunrekkr's people in Guðrúnarhvöt and Hamðismál, where Hamðir and Sörli fight their way into his hall (Hamðismál 22-30). In Hlöðskviða they are Angantýr's people at Árheimar, whose land is invaded by Hlöðr and the Huns.

Some indexed mentions are not the people at all: the horse name Goti in the þulur (Skáldskaparmál 72) and other "Gota-" forms are flagged uncertain; the index may mix them.

sif.en:
Sif is a goddess, the wife of Þórr and mother of Ullr, Þórr's stepson; Skáldskaparmál chapter 29 also calls her mother of Þrúðr. She is known chiefly for her hair.

Skáldskaparmál chapter 43 tells how Loki cut off her hair out of mischief and, threatened by Þórr, had the sons of Ívaldi make her new hair of gold that would grow like real hair; hence gold is called "Sif's hair" (chapters 40, 56). Poets often name Þórr "Sif's husband" (Hymiskviða 3, 15, 34; Þrymskviða 24). In Lokasenna 53 she offers Loki mead to keep the peace, but he claims to have been her lover, and Hárbarðsljóð 48 likewise taunts Þórr that she has a lover at home. In Skáldskaparmál chapter 24 Hrungnir boasts that he will carry her off. The Prologue (chapter 3) gives a euhemerised account in which she is the prophetess "Síbil", wife of Þórr of Troy.

asgard.en:
Ásgarðr is the stronghold of the Æsir. In Gylfaginning chapter 9 the gods build it in the middle of the world, and Snorri, following his euhemerist frame, says men call it Troy; Gylfi travels there to question the gods, and chapter 3 also names an "Old Ásgarðr".

Many myths begin or end at its walls. Loki lures Iðunn out of Ásgarðr to the giant Þjazi and must bring her back (Skáldskaparmál chapters 2-3); Skaði comes there armed to avenge her father (chapter 3); Óðinn flies back with the mead of poetry and spits it into vats (chapter 6); Hrungnir drinks there and threatens to carry Valhöll off (chapter 24); Ægir visits the gods there (chapters 1 and 41); and the grove Glasir stands before Valhöll's doors (chapter 42). In Þrymskviða 18 Loki warns that giants will settle in Ásgarðr if Mjöllnir is not recovered, and in Hymiskviða 7 Þórr and Týr set out from there.

hedin-hjarrandason.en:
Heðinn Hjarrandason is the king of the legend of the Hjaðningavíg, the endless battle of the Hjaðningar. In Skáldskaparmál (chapter 62) he carries off Hildr, daughter of King Högni, while her father is away. Högni pursues him to Hoy in Orkney, rejects the necklace and gold offered for peace, and draws his sword Dáinsleif. They fight all day, and each night Hildr wakes the dead by magic, so that the battle will go on until Ragnarök. Snorri quotes Bragi's Ragnarsdrápa on the tale, which underlies kennings for battle (Háttatal chapter 2).

The index also includes here a different Heðinn, son of King Hjörvarðr and Álfhildr and half-brother of Helgi in Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar. He vows to take Helgi's beloved Sváva, confesses this to Helgi (31-34), and as Helgi dies is asked to marry her; he swears first to avenge his brother (43).

hreidmarr.en:
Hreiðmarr is the father of Fáfnir, Reginn and Otr, and in the prose of Reginsmál also of daughters, Lyngheiðr and Lofnheiðr. The story of the otter's ransom, which begins the cursed treasure of the Völsung legend, turns on him.

When Loki kills Otr, who had taken the shape of an otter, the three travelling gods Óðinn, Loki and Hœnir lodge with Hreiðmarr and show him the skin. He seizes them and demands that the skin be filled and covered with red gold. Loki fetches the dwarf Andvari's hoard, and Óðinn has to give up the ring he had kept back to cover the last whisker (Skáldskaparmál chapter 46; Reginsmál prose and stanzas 7-9). Hreiðmarr refuses to share the wergild with his sons, and Fáfnir kills him (Skáldskaparmál chapter 47). Dying, he calls on his daughter to bear a child who will avenge him (Reginsmál 11).

skadi.en:
Skaði is a giantess, daughter of Þjazi, who became the wife of Njörðr and is counted among the goddesses. She hunts on skis with a bow and is called the ski-goddess (Gylfaginning chapter 23).

After the Æsir killed Þjazi, she came armed to Ásgarðr for vengeance and accepted a settlement instead: she might choose a husband from among the gods by looking only at their feet, and picked Njörðr, hoping for Baldr; Loki had to make her laugh, which he did with a goat; and Óðinn set Þjazi's eyes in the sky as stars (Skáldskaparmál chapters 3-4). The marriage failed because she would not live by the sea nor Njörðr in the mountains; Gylfaginning chapter 23 quotes their exchange of verses, and she returned to her father's home Þrymheimr (Grímnismál 11). In the Skírnismál prose she asks Skírnir to speak with Freyr. In Lokasenna (49, 51) she threatens Loki, who boasts of his part in Þjazi's death, and she later hangs a venomous snake over the bound Loki (Lokasenna prose; Gylfaginning chapter 50).

skirnir.en:
Skírnir is Freyr's servant and messenger. In Skírnismál, after Freyr has seen the giantess Gerðr from Hliðskjálf and fallen sick with longing, Skírnir agrees to woo her for him in return for Freyr's horse and the sword that fights by itself (8). He rides through the flickering fire to Gymir's dwelling, offers Gerðr gifts including a ring (21), and, when she refuses, threatens her with the sword (23, 25) and with a curse of runes until she agrees to meet Freyr in the grove Barri after nine nights (41).

Snorri retells the wooing in Gylfaginning (chapter 37), where Njörðr sends Skírnir; in the poem it is Skaði who speaks the opening lines. Snorri notes that Freyr's lack of the sword he gave away will cost him at Ragnarök (Gylfaginning 51). In Gylfaginning 34 Skírnir is also the messenger sent to the dwarfs for the fetter Gleipnir that binds Fenrir.

budli.en:
Buðli is a legendary king, father of Atli and of Brynhildr. Skáldskaparmál chapter 80 makes him the founder of the Buðlungar, the line from which Atli and Brynhildr descend, and buðlungr is used in poetry simply to mean "king".

He never acts in the Eddic poems; his name identifies his children, as in the recurring formula "Brynhildr, Buðli's daughter" (Grípisspá 27, Sigurðarkviða in meiri 12 and 18, Guðrúnarkviða I 23-27, Sigurðarkviða in skamma 15 and 30, Helreið Brynhildar 4) and "Buðli's son" for Atli (Guðrúnarkviða II 27, Guðrúnarkviða III 1). Sigurðarkviða in skamma 67 mentions servants Buðli gave Brynhildr, and Atlamál refers to the home and lands Buðli left (stanzas 38, 96) and to his death (55).

hrolfr-kraki.en:
Hrólfr kraki is a legendary Danish king of the Skjöldung line who ruled at Hleiðr (Lejre), praised in Skáldskaparmál chapter 54 as the most renowned of ancient kings for generosity, valour and graciousness. He gets his nickname "kraki" (pole) from the poor boy Vöggr, who swears to avenge him.

Snorri tells how Hrólfr and his berserks go to Uppsala to claim pay from King Aðils, the husband of his mother Yrsa, endure a fire heaped up before them by Aðils' men, and receive a horn full of gold from Yrsa. Pursued across the Fýrisvellir, Hrólfr scatters gold, and Aðils stoops for the ring Svíagríss; hence gold is "Kraki's seed" or "seed of the Fýrisvellir". Gróttasöngr (quoted in chapter 53) foresees "Yrsa's son and brother" avenging Fróði. Fuller accounts are in Hrólfs saga kraka, Saxo and, as Hrothulf, in Beowulf.

ymir.en:
Ymir, also called Aurgelmir, is the primeval giant from whom the frost giants descend and from whose body the world was made. In Gylfaginning (chapters 5-8) he forms from drops of rime where the cold of Niflheimr meets the heat of Múspellsheimr and is nourished by the cow Auðumla. The sons of Borr kill him; his blood drowns all the frost giants but one, and from his body they make the world: the earth from his flesh, the sea from his blood, rocks from his bones, the sky from his skull and Miðgarðr from his brows.

Vafþrúðnismál (21, 28-30) and Grímnismál (40) give the same cosmogony in verse; Vafþrúðnismál calls the first giant Aurgelmir, grandfather of Bergelmir, and Snorri identifies him with Ymir. Völuspá in skamma (5) derives all giants from Ymir, and skalds call the sky Ymir's skull and the sea Ymir's blood (Skáldskaparmál chapters 31-33).

hamdir.en:
Hamðir is a son of Guðrún and King Jónakr, brother of Sörli and Erpr, and so half-brother of Svanhildr, Sigurðr's daughter. Snorri makes all three brothers Guðrún's sons; in Hamðismál Erpr is born of another mother.

When King Jörmunrekkr has Svanhildr trampled to death, Guðrún goads Hamðir and Sörli into avenging her (Guðrúnarhvöt; Hamðismál). On the way they kill their brother Erpr, who had offered help. They cut off Jörmunrekkr's hands and feet, but no iron can bite them, and they are stoned to death; Hamðir's line "his head were now off if Erpr were living" (Hamðismál 28) admits their mistake. Snorri tells the story in Skáldskaparmál chapter 50 and quotes Bragi's verses on it from Ragnarsdrápa (chapter 51). "Hamðir's shirt" is a kenning for a mail-coat (Skáldskaparmál chapter 61; Háttatal).

hervor.en:
Hervör is the warrior maiden of Hervarar saga, daughter of the berserkr Angantýr and Sváfa (Hervararkviða 8), who in the saga dresses as a man and goes viking.

Hervararkviða ("The Waking of Angantýr") tells how she comes to the island where her father and his brothers lie buried, among burning grave-fires, and calls up the dead to demand the dwarf-forged sword Tyrfingr. Angantýr warns her that it will destroy her kin (stanza 17), but she persists, threatening the dead with curses, until he gives it to her (stanza 24); she declares she would rather have it than all Norway (stanza 25). In the saga she later becomes the mother of Heiðrekr. The index also includes mentions from Hlöðskviða, where the Hervör concerned is her granddaughter, Heiðrekr's daughter and sister of King Angantýr, who commands a border fortress against the invading Huns and falls in battle; the two women are mixed under this name.

jormungandr.en:
Jörmungandr, the Miðgarðsormr or Midgard serpent, is the second child of Loki and the giantess Angrboða (Gylfaginning chapter 34). Óðinn throws it into the sea, where it grows until it lies around all the earth biting its own tail.

It is Þórr's great enemy. At Útgarða-Loki's court the cat Þórr cannot lift turns out to be the serpent (Gylfaginning 47). Out fishing with the giant Hymir, Þórr baits a hook with an ox-head and draws the serpent up to the gunwale before Hymir cuts the line (Gylfaginning 48; the same tale in Hymiskviða and in skaldic verses quoted in Skáldskaparmál chapter 11). At Ragnarök it writhes in the sea (Völuspá 50) and blows venom; Þórr kills it but falls dead after nine steps from its poison (Gylfaginning 51). Skáldskaparmál (chapter 23) calls Loki its father, and lists Jörmungandr among the names for serpents (73).

loddfafnir.en:
Loddfáfnir is the man to whom a section of Hávamál, often called Loddfáfnismál, is addressed. Nothing is known of him beyond his name, and it is unclear whether he is meant as a real person, a pupil figure or the speaker's own persona.

Stanzas 112-137 each open with the refrain "I counsel you, Loddfáfnir, take my advice", followed by practical and moral precepts: do not rise at night without cause, beware of a witch's embrace and of another man's wife, visit friends often, never mock a guest or a grey-haired speaker, and use remedies such as earth against drink. He is named once more in Hávamál 162, at the end of the list of charms, where the speaker tells him he will long lack these songs.

nidudr.en:
Níðuðr is the cruel king of Völundarkviða, described in the prose introduction as a king in Sweden and in the poem as lord of the Njárar; he has two sons and a daughter, Böðvildr, and a wise but ill-advising queen. He corresponds to Niðungr of Þiðreks saga and Old English Nithhad.

His men seize Völundr asleep in Ulfdalir (6, 13); Níðuðr takes Völundr's sword and gives his ring to Böðvildr, and on the queen's advice Völundr is hamstrung and set to work on the island of Sævarstaðr. Völundr kills the king's two sons, sends their skulls as silver-mounted cups to Níðuðr, gems from their eyes to the queen and a brooch from their teeth to Böðvildr (24-25), then seduces Böðvildr and flies away. Níðuðr is left sleepless and grieving (31, 38) and learns the truth from his daughter (41).

geirrodr.en:
Geirröðr is a giant, enemy of Þórr and father of the giantesses Gjálp and Greip. In Skáldskaparmál (chapter 26) Snorri tells how Loki, caught by Geirröðr while flying in a falcon shape, buys his life by promising to bring Þórr to the giant's home without his hammer and belt of strength. On the way the giantess Gríðr lends Þórr her own belt, iron gloves and staff. Þórr survives the river swollen by Gjálp, and at Geirröðr's house breaks the backs of both daughters when they try to crush him against the roof. Geirröðr then hurls a glowing iron bar at him; Þórr catches it and throws it back through an iron pillar, through the giant and through the wall.

Snorri quotes Eilífr Goðrúnarson's Þórsdrápa on the episode, and kennings call Þórr Geirröðr's slayer (Skáldskaparmál chapter 11). The verses gathered as Eddubrot preserve another version of the tale. King Geirröðr of Grímnismál is a different figure.

hel.en:
Hel is both the realm of the dead and the giantess who rules it. She is the daughter of Loki and the giantess Angrboða, and sister of Fenrir and Jörmungandr. Gylfaginning chapter 34 tells how Óðinn cast her into Niflheimr and gave her power over those who die of sickness or old age. Snorri describes her as half dark and half flesh-coloured.

Her best-known part is in the death of Baldr (Gylfaginning chapter 49). Hermóðr rides to Hel to ransom him, and she agrees to release Baldr only if everything in the world, living and dead, weeps for him; the giantess Þökk refuses ("let Hel keep what she has"). As a place, Hel appears in Völuspá 43 (a cock crowing beneath the earth at Hel's halls), Fjölsvinnsmál 25, Atlamál 55 and Sólarljóð 39. Kennings make Baldr and Höðr "Hel's companions" (Skáldskaparmál chapters 12 and 20). The entry covers both the person and the place.

idunn.en:
Iðunn is a goddess, wife of Bragi, who keeps the apples the gods eat to stay young (Gylfaginning chapter 26).

Her abduction is told in Skáldskaparmál chapters 2-3: Loki, captured by the giant Þjazi in eagle form, promises to bring her out of Ásgarðr and lures her into a wood with talk of better apples, where Þjazi carries her off. As the gods grow grey and old, they force Loki to recover her; in a hawk's plumage he turns her into a nut and flies her home, and Þjazi, pursuing, is killed at the walls. Skáldskaparmál chapter 30 gives her kennings (Wife of Bragi, Keeper of the Apples, Spoil of Þjazi). In Lokasenna (16-18) she tries to calm Bragi and is accused by Loki of having embraced her brother's slayer, an allusion otherwise unknown. The late poem Forspjallsljóð (Hrafnagaldr Óðins 6) calls her of elf race, the youngest of Ívaldi's children.

jormunrekkr.en:
Jörmunrekkr is the legendary form of Ermanaric, the fourth-century king of the Goths whose death the historian Jordanes links with the killing of a woman, Sunilda, and the revenge of her brothers. In Norse legend he is the husband-to-be and slayer of Svanhildr, daughter of Sigurðr and Guðrún.

Snorri tells the story in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 50): Jörmunrekkr sends his son Randvér to woo Svanhildr; on Bikki's evil counsel he hangs Randvér and has Svanhildr trampled to death by horses. Guðrún urges her sons Hamðir and Sörli to vengeance (Guðrúnarhvöt 2-5); they kill their brother Erpr on the way (a half-brother in Hamðismál), then cut off Jörmunrekkr's hands and feet in his hall, but without Erpr cannot kill him, and he has them stoned (Hamðismál 19-24). Sigurðarkviða in skamma (64) foretells his wrath, and Snorri quotes Bragi's Ragnarsdrápa on the attack (Skáldskaparmál 51).

thjalfi.en:
Þjálfi is Þórr's servant, son of a peasant and brother of Röskva. Gylfaginning (chapter 44) explains how he entered Þórr's service: he split the thigh-bone of one of Þórr's goats for the marrow, the goat rose lame, and the peasant gave both children to Þórr in compensation.

He goes with Þórr and Loki to Útgarða-Loki (Gylfaginning chapters 45-47). The fastest runner among men, he races three times against Hugi and loses, and Útgarða-Loki later reveals that Hugi was his "thought". In Skáldskaparmál chapter 24 he helps Þórr against Hrungnir, tricking the giant into standing on his shield and felling the clay giant Mökkurkálfi. Þórr is called "master of Þjálfi and Röskva" (Skáldskaparmál chapter 11), and in Hárbarðsljóð 39 Þórr says berserk women drove Þjálfi off.

thjazi.en:
Þjazi is a giant, son of Ölvaldi and father of Skaði, who lived at Þrymheimr (Grímnismál 11; Gylfaginning chapter 23). Skáldskaparmál chapter 4 says he and his brothers Iði and Gangr divided their father's gold by mouthfuls, so gold is called the giants' "speech".

In eagle form he forces Loki to lure Iðunn and her apples out of Ásgarðr (Skáldskaparmál chapters 2-3). When the ageing gods compel Loki to fetch her back, Þjazi pursues him as an eagle, his feathers catch fire at the wall of Ásgarðr, and the Æsir kill him. Skaði comes to avenge him and is compensated; Óðinn throws his eyes into the sky as stars (chapter 4), while in Hárbarðsljóð 19 Þórr claims both the killing and the eyes. Loki boasts in Lokasenna 50 of having been first and last at the slaying, and Skaði answers in 51. Gróttasöngr 9 names him among the mill-maids' mighty kin.

thjodolfr.en:
Þjóðólfr of Hvinir, in southern Norway, was a skald of about the late ninth century, associated with the circle of Haraldr hárfagri and best known for Ynglingatal and Haustlöng. Haustlöng describes scenes painted on a shield: Þjazi's theft of Iðunn and Þórr's duel with the giant Hrungnir.

Snorri cites him in Gylfaginning (chapter 2) for the roof of shields on Valhöll, and in Skáldskaparmál quotes Haustlöng for the Hrungnir story (chapter 30) and Þjóðólfr's verses for many kennings and poetic terms (chapters 9, 31-32 and later). Many later citations say only 'as Þjóðólfr sang', and some of these, such as the verses on King Haraldr in chapter 66, probably belong to the eleventh-century Þjóðólfr Arnórsson, court poet of Haraldr harðráði; the index may mix the two.

arnorr.en:
Arnórr Þórðarson jarlaskáld (Earls' Skald) was an eleventh-century Icelandic skald. He took his nickname from his service with the earls of Orkney, Rögnvaldr Brúsason and Þorfinnr Sigurðarson, and he also composed for the Norwegian kings Magnús the Good and Haraldr harðráði.

Snorri quotes him often in Skáldskaparmál as one of the "chief skalds". He opens the examples of skaldic usage in chapter 9 and supplies verses for heaven-kennings (chapter 31), terms for men and rulers (chapters 59, 65, 66 and 79, including a stanza from his poem on Earl Rögnvaldr in chapter 66), and the name-lists for the sea, fire and the wolf (chapters 71, 76 and 77).

niflungar.en:
The Niflungar (Hniflungar) are the royal family of Gjúki, above all Gunnarr and Högni, and by extension their people and their treasure; the name corresponds to the German Nibelungen. Skáldskaparmál chapter 80 derives them from Nefir, one of the sons of Hálfdan the Old.

The term belongs chiefly to the story of their fall at Atli's court. In Atlakviða Gunnarr, the last who knows where "the Niflungs' hoard" lies, refuses to reveal it and declares that the Rhine shall keep the gold (stanzas 26-27); Snorri adds that the brothers sank Fáfnir's gold in the Rhine before setting out and that it has never been found, and that Guðrún held the funeral feast for the Niflungs before killing Atli (Skáldskaparmál chapter 50). Atlamál 52 praises their last fight. The poems also use the name loosely: Helgakviða Hundingsbana I 48 applies it to the sons of Granmarr, and Guðrúnarhvöt 12 to Guðrún's sons by Atli.

sinfjotli.en:
Sinfjötli is the eldest son of Sigmundr the Völsung and half-brother of Helgi Hundingsbani; according to the Völsunga saga he was born of Sigmundr's incest with his sister Signý. Snorri notes (Skáldskaparmál chapter 51) that Sigmundr could drink poison unharmed, while Sinfjötli could bear it only on his skin.

In Helgakviða Hundingsbana I (33-45) he trades insults with Granmarr's son Guðmundr before the battle at Frekasteinn, an exchange also recalled in Helgakviða Hundingsbana II. The prose Frá dauða Sinfjötla (placed with Grípisspá) tells how he killed the brother of his stepmother Borghildr, who poisoned him in revenge; Sigmundr carried the body to a mysterious ferryman. A fragment printed among the Eddubrot has him and Sigmundr sawing through a great stone slab. In Old English, Beowulf knows him as Fitela.

skrymir.en:
Skrýmir is the name used by a huge giant whom Þórr, Loki, Þjálfi and Röskva meet in the forest on their way to Útgarðr; at the end of the story Útgarða-Loki reveals that he himself was Skrýmir.

In Gylfaginning (chapter 45) the travellers spend the night in what turns out to be the thumb of Skrýmir's glove. He carries their food, but Þórr cannot undo the bag's knots, and three hammer blows to the sleeping giant's head only make him ask whether a leaf, an acorn or something from the birds above has fallen on him. Skrýmir then points them to Útgarðr and leaves. Útgarða-Loki later explains that the bag was tied with iron and that the blows struck a mountain, leaving three square valleys. Loki taunts Þórr with "the straps of Skrýmir's wallet" in Lokasenna 62, so the story was known to that poet.

surtr.en:
Surtr is the fire giant who guards Múspellsheimr: in Gylfaginning chapter 4 he sits at the land's end with a flaming sword, and at the end of the world will overcome the gods and burn the world.

At Ragnarök he comes from the south with fire and a blazing sword (Völuspá 52; Gylfaginning chapter 51). Freyr fights him and falls for lack of the sword he gave to Skírnir (Völuspá 53; Gylfaginning chapter 51), and Surtr then casts fire over the whole earth. The battlefield where he meets the gods is Vígríðr, a hundred leagues each way (Vafþrúðnismál 17-18), and the gods' sons survive "when Surtr's fire has sunk" (Vafþrúðnismál 50-51; Gylfaginning chapter 53). Fáfnismál 14 names the island where the gods and Surtr will fight, and in Skáldskaparmál chapter 9 his name stands for giants in general in a kenning for the mead of poetry.

yggdrasil.en:
Yggdrasill is the world ash, the great tree at the centre of the Norse cosmos, standing ever green over Urðr's well (Völuspá 19; Gylfaginning chapter 16). The gods hold court beneath it every day, and Þórr must wade rivers to reach it (Gylfaginning chapter 15; Grímnismál 29).

Grímnismál (31-35) gives it three roots, over Hel, the frost giants and mankind, and fills it with life: the squirrel Ratatoskr carries words between the eagle at the top and the dragon Níðhöggr below, harts bite its shoots and serpents gnaw its roots, so that it suffers more than men know. Snorri quotes these stanzas but places the three roots among the Æsir, the frost giants and over Niflheimr, each with its spring (Gylfaginning chapters 15-16). At Ragnarök the ancient tree shakes and groans (Völuspá 47; Gylfaginning chapter 51). Grímnismál 44 calls it the best of trees.

midgard.en:
Miðgarðr (the middle enclosure) is the world of humankind. In Völuspá 4 Burr's sons lift the land and make Miðgarðr. In Snorri and Grímnismál 41 the gods build it as a defensive wall made from the eyebrows of the giant Ymir, set around the inner earth to keep out the giants who live along the encircling sea (Gylfaginning chapter 8).

The name also lives on in Jörmungandr, the Miðgarðsormr (the Midgard serpent) that lies around the world in the ocean. Þórr is called "defender of Ásgarðr and Miðgarðr" (Skáldskaparmál chapter 11), and Völuspá 56 and Gylfaginning chapter 51 tell how, as Miðgarðr's warder, he fights the serpent at Ragnarök. Gylfaginning places Ironwood, home of the troll-women, east of Miðgarðr (chapter 12). Hyndluljóð 16 calls the noble families "the noblest of men in Miðgarðr".

mjolnir.en:
Mjöllnir is Þórr's hammer, the chief of his three treasures alongside the belt of strength and iron gloves (Gylfaginning chapter 21). Snorri tells in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 43) how the dwarf Brokkr and his brother forged it in a wager with Loki, its handle left short because a fly stung Brokkr on the eyelid as he worked the bellows.

With it Þórr kills giants: the builder of the gods' wall (Gylfaginning chapter 42) and Hrungnir, whose hone shatters against it in flight (Skáldskaparmál chapter 24). He uses it to hallow his goats' bones before raising them to life (Gylfaginning chapter 44) and Baldr's pyre (chapter 49). In Þrymskviða the giant Þrymr steals it and demands Freyja as ransom; Þórr comes disguised as the bride, and when the hammer is laid in her lap to hallow the marriage (stanza 30) he seizes it and kills the giants. In Lokasenna (57-63) his repeated threat of the hammer finally silences Loki. After Ragnarök his sons Móði and Magni will possess it (Vafþrúðnismál 51; Gylfaginning chapter 53).

sleipnir.en:
Sleipnir is Óðinn's grey eight-legged horse, the best of all steeds (Grímnismál 44; Gylfaginning chapters 15 and 41). Gylfaginning 42 tells his origin: a giant builder offered to wall Ásgarðr, helped by his stallion Svaðilfari; to stop the work being finished in time Loki took the shape of a mare and lured the stallion away, and later gave birth to Sleipnir. Völuspá in skamma (11) alludes to the same story.

Óðinn rides him to the underworld in Baldrs draumar (2), and Hermóðr borrows him to ride to Hel after Baldr's death (Gylfaginning 49). In Skáldskaparmál (chapter 24) Óðinn's ride on Sleipnir provokes Hrungnir's race to Ásgarðr. Sigrdrífumál (15) mentions runes cut on Sleipnir's teeth, and one of Gestumblindi's riddles in Heiðreksgátur turns on the horse's eight legs. In skaldic kennings a ship may be the "Sleipnir" of the sea.

svafa.en:
Sváfa is a valkyrie, daughter of King Eylimi, and the beloved of Helgi Hjörvarðsson in Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar. According to the prose she gives the silent youth his name, tells him where to find a sword and shields him in battle; later they exchange vows, though she remains a valkyrie.

When Helgi is mortally wounded by Álfr at Frekasteinn, Sigarr fetches her to his side (stanzas 37-39). The dying Helgi asks her to give her love to his brother Heðinn (41); she answers that she vowed never to take an unfamed man after Helgi (42), and Heðinn swears vengeance (43). The closing prose says the two were believed to be reborn, and the prose of Helgakviða Hundingsbana II calls Sigrún "Sváfa reborn".

The name also belongs to other women: Sváfa, mother of Hildigunnr (Hyndluljóð 17), and Sváfa, wife of Angantýr and mother of Hervör (Hervararkviða 8); the index may mix them.

svanhildr.en:
Svanhildr is the daughter of Sigurðr and Guðrún, the fairest of women. Brynhildr foretells her birth and fate in Sigurðarkviða in skamma (55, 63).

She is brought up at the court of King Jónakr, Guðrún's third husband. The Gothic king Jörmunrekkr sends his son Randvér to woo her for him; on the false counsel of Bikki that Randvér and Svanhildr are lovers, the king hangs his son and has Svanhildr trampled to death by horses (Skáldskaparmál chapter 50; Hamðismál 3). Guðrún then urges her sons Hamðir and Sörli to avenge her, which leads to their deaths at Jörmunrekkr's hall (Guðrúnarhvöt, with Guðrún's lament for her in stanzas 15-16; Hamðismál 2; Skáldskaparmál chapter 50). The story goes back to the Gothic legend of Ermanaric, where Jordanes names a woman Sunilda.

vali-2.en:
Váli, son of Loki and brother of Narfi (or Nari), is known almost only from his father's punishment. In Gylfaginning (chapter 50) the Æsir turn Váli into a wolf, he tears his brother Narfi apart, and Loki is bound with Narfi's entrails. The prose at the end of Lokasenna reverses the roles: Loki is bound with the entrails of his son Váli, and Narfi is changed into a wolf. The Hauksbók text of Völuspá (34) also has lines on Váli and Loki's bonds, and Skáldskaparmál (chapter 23) names Áli among Loki's children.

Most mentions of the name in the index refer instead to Váli son of Óðinn and Rindr, who avenges Baldr at one night old by killing Höðr (Baldrs draumar 11; Völuspá in skamma 1; Gylfaginning chapter 30; Skáldskaparmál chapter 19) and lives on after Ragnarök (Vafþrúðnismál 51; Gylfaginning chapter 53); others are a dwarf in the list of Gylfaginning (chapter 14) and the horse Valr. The index may mix them.

dvalinn.en:
Dvalinn is the name of a prominent dwarf and of one of the four harts that browse in the branches of Yggdrasill (Grímnismál 33; Gylfaginning chapter 16; the hart-names in Skáldskaparmál chapter 71). The index entry is labelled as the stag, but most mentions are of the dwarf.

The dwarf appears in the dwarf lists of Völuspá (11, 14) and Gylfaginning (chapter 14). In Hávamál 143 he carved runes for the dwarfs, as Óðinn did for the gods. Some norns are "Dvalinn's daughters" (Fáfnismál 13; Gylfaginning chapter 15). The sun is called "Dvalinn's deceiver" or "plaything" (Alvíssmál 16; Skáldskaparmál chapter 69), because dwarfs caught by daylight turn to stone, and poetry is "Dvalinn's drink" (Skáldskaparmál chapter 10). In Hervararkviða he is named as one of the makers of the sword Tyrfingr.

hjorvardr.en:
Hjörvarðr is a king of the Helgi poems, the father of Helgi Hjörvarðsson. According to the prose of Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar he had four wives and vowed to marry the fairest woman alive; Atli, son of his jarl Iðmundr, won him Sigrlinn, daughter of King Sváfnir, and she became Helgi's mother. His other sons included Heðinn.

He figures mainly in the opening prose and stanzas on the wooing of Sigrlinn (for example stanza 3). In stanza 10 the young Helgi reproaches him over his counsels, and in the following prose Hjörvarðr gives Helgi men to avenge his mother's father on King Hróðmarr. The name is common in heroic legend, and the index gathers several bearers under it, many flagged as uncertain: one of the sons of Arngrímr, uncle of Hervör, named in Hervararkviða 9 and 11 and in Hyndluljóð 22; a son of Hundingr killed by Helgi Hundingsbani (Helgakviða Hundingsbana I 14); and others in genealogical lists.

hundingr.en:
Hundingr is a king, enemy of the Völsungs, killed by the young Helgi, who is called Hundingsbani ("Hundingr's slayer") after the deed (Helgakviða Hundingsbana I 10; Helgakviða Hundingsbana II prose). Helgi then kills his sons as well when they demand compensation (Helgakviða Hundingsbana I 11-14).

Helgakviða Hundingsbana II opens with Helgi spying on Hundingr's court and then escaping Hundingr's men disguised as a bondwoman; in stanza 39, after his death, Helgi gives Hundingr menial tasks in Valhöll. The sons of Hundingr also killed Sigmundr and Eylimi, Sigurðr's grandfather, and Sigurðr's vengeance on them is foretold or urged in Grípisspá (9) and Reginsmál (15).

suttungr.en:
Suttungr is a giant, son of Gillingr and brother of Baugi, who holds the mead of poetry until Óðinn steals it. In Skáldskaparmál (chapter 5) the dwarves who killed Gillingr give Suttungr the mead, brewed from Kvasir's blood, to save their lives; he hides it in Hnitbjörg and sets his daughter Gunnlöð to guard it.

Chapter 6 tells how Óðinn, calling himself Bölverkr, works a summer for Baugi, bores into the mountain, sleeps three nights with Gunnlöð and drinks the mead, then flies to Ásgarðr in eagle form with Suttungr in pursuit. Poetry is therefore called "Suttungr's mead" and similar names (chapter 10). Hávamál tells the theft from Óðinn's side (104, 109-110), mentioning Suttungr's hall and his betrayal, without naming Baugi. "Suttungr's sons" is a general term for giants in Skírnismál 34 and Alvíssmál 34.

vidarr.en:
Víðarr is the silent god, son of Óðinn and the giantess Gríðr (Skáldskaparmál chapter 26), nearly as strong as Þórr, with a thick shoe (Gylfaginning chapter 29). His land is Viði, overgrown with brush and grass (Grímnismál 17).

His great deed comes at Ragnarök: when the wolf Fenrir swallows Óðinn, Víðarr avenges his father. Völuspá 55 has him thrust his sword into the wolf's heart, while Vafþrúðnismál 53 says he tears the jaws apart; Snorri combines the two, having him set his shod foot on the lower jaw and rend the wolf (Gylfaginning chapter 51; the shoe is made of the scraps of leather men cut from their shoes). He and Váli survive and dwell in the gods' home after Surtr's fire (Vafþrúðnismál 51; Gylfaginning chapter 53). In Lokasenna 10 Óðinn makes him give Loki a seat, and he pours Loki's drink.

eadgils.en:
Aðils (Old English Eadgils) is a legendary king of the Swedes at Uppsala, husband of Yrsa and so stepfather of the Danish king Hrólfr kraki. He is the Eadgils of Beowulf and also appears in Ynglinga saga and Hrólfs saga kraka.

In Skáldskaparmál (chapter 54) Snorri tells the tale behind the gold kenning 'Kraki's seed'. Aðils defeats King Áli on the ice of lake Vænir with the help of Hrólfr's twelve berserks, then refuses them their pay and the treasures promised to Hrólfr. Hrólfr comes to Uppsala, survives Aðils' fire, receives gold from Yrsa and rides off across the Fýrisvellir. When Aðils pursues, Hrólfr scatters the gold on the road and throws down the ring Svíagríss, which Aðils stoops to pick up with his spear. The battle on the ice and Aðils' horse Slöngvir also figure in the horse-name verses of Skáldskaparmál (chapter 72) and Eddubrot.

eyvindr.en:
Eyvindr Finnsson skáldaspillir (Plagiarist, or Spoiler of Skalds) was a tenth-century Norwegian skald in the service of King Hákon the Good. His best-known poems are Hákonarmál, on Hákon's death and reception in Valhöll, and Háleygjatal, a genealogy of Earl Hákon of Hlaðir's family.

Snorri quotes him about fifteen times in Skáldskaparmál. His verses illustrate kennings for Óðinn and for poetry (chapters 9 and 10), the earth as Óðinn's wife (chapters 9 and 32) and Freyr as "Adversary of Beli" (chapter 14). Gold is "Fulla's snood" (chapter 44) and "seed of Fýrisvellir" (chapter 54) in stanzas on King Hákon's generosity. Other verses illustrate battle, the gods as jólnar, and rulers (chapters 60, 61, 66, 68 and 80).

grimhildr.en:
Grímhildr is the wife of King Gjúki and mother of Gunnarr, Högni and Guðrún (Skáldskaparmál chapter 48), a queen versed in magic who works on the fates of her children and of Sigurðr.

In Grípisspá (33, 35, 51) Grípir foretells that Grímhildr's wiles will make Sigurðr forget Brynhildr, marry her daughter and woo Brynhildr for Gunnarr; Völsunga saga makes this explicit with a potion of forgetfulness. In Guðrúnarkviða II she gives the widowed Guðrún a drink of forgetfulness mixed with magic and pig's blood (21), offers her treasure and lands (25, 32), and presses her to marry Atli against her will (28-30), while foreseeing grief for her own sons. In Atlamál Guðrún calls herself "Grímhildr's daughter" as she confronts Atli (80, 91). In the German Nibelungenlied the name Kriemhild belongs not to the mother but to the daughter, Guðrún's counterpart.

hrimgerdr.en:
Hrímgerðr is a giantess, daughter of the giant Hati whom Helgi Hjörvarðsson has killed (Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar 17). She and her mother try to wreck Helgi's fleet in a fjord, but the ships are guarded.

Much of Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar (about stanzas 14-30) is a flyting between Hrímgerðr and Helgi's man Atli, who keeps watch on the ship, with Helgi joining in. She demands Helgi spend a night with her as compensation for her father (24) and reveals that the fleet was protected by a band of valkyries led by a white maiden (28). Atli holds her talking until sunrise, and she is turned to stone, to stand as a landmark that men will mock (29-30), the same fate that overtakes the dwarf Alvíss.

king-geirrod.en:
Geirröðr is the king of the frame story of Grímnismál, son of King Hrauðungr and younger brother of Agnarr; he is not to be confused with the giant Geirröðr whom Þórr visits.

The opening prose tells how the two boys were shipwrecked and fostered for a winter by a peasant couple, who were really Óðinn and Frigg. Óðinn's fosterling Geirröðr pushed his brother's boat out to sea and became king. Frigg, wagering with Óðinn, claims that Geirröðr is a stingy host, and sends her servant Fulla to warn him against a wizard. When Óðinn arrives as Grímnir, the king has him set between two fires for eight nights (stanza 2); only the king's son Agnarr gives him drink. Grímnir then reveals himself in a long monologue, rebuking the king as drunk and abandoned by Óðinn (51).
