In the closing prose Geirröðr stumbles, falls on his own sword and dies, and young Agnarr rules after him.

mimir.en:
Mímir (also Mímr, Mím) is a being of great wisdom who keeps a well of wisdom and understanding under the root of Yggdrasill that reaches towards the frost giants (Gylfaginning chapter 15). He drinks from the well out of the Gjallarhorn, and Óðinn had to pledge one of his eyes for a single drink (Völuspá 28, quoted there).

At the onset of Ragnarök Óðinn rides to Mímir's well and takes counsel of Mímir (Gylfaginning chapter 51) or consults "Mímir's head" (Völuspá 46-47, quoted in the same chapter); Sigrdrífumál 14 also speaks of Mímir's head uttering true words. In skaldic poetry Óðinn is called "Mímir's friend" (Skáldskaparmál chapter 9, in Egill Skallagrímsson's and Refr's verses; Háttatal). The story of how his head came to be severed by the Vanir and preserved by Óðinn is told only in Snorri's Ynglinga saga.

sorli.en:
Sörli is a son of Guðrún and King Jónakr, brother of Hamðir and Erpr and half-brother of Svanhildr. When King Jörmunrekkr has Svanhildr trampled to death by horses, Guðrún sends Sörli and Hamðir to avenge her, armed with mail and helmets that iron cannot bite (Guðrúnarhvöt prose; Skáldskaparmál chapter 50).

Hamðismál tells the expedition. Sörli, called wise, speaks calmly to his mother (9); on the way the brothers kill Erpr, regretting it later when one of them stumbles; they cut off Jörmunrekkr's hands and feet, but since weapons cannot harm them they are stoned to death, Sörli falling by the gable (31). Snorri, who retells the story and quotes Bragi's Ragnarsdrápa on it (chapter 51), makes Erpr Guðrún's son, while Hamðismál calls him a son of another mother. The 'upright' Sörli of Sólarljóð 20, betrayed by Vígúlfr, is a different figure.

dellingr.en:
Dellingr is a god connected with daybreak. Vafþrúðnismál 25 calls him the father of Dagr (Day). Gylfaginning chapter 10 makes him, "of the race of the Æsir", the third husband of Nótt (Night) and Dagr's father by her.

His name survives mostly in a formula: "before Dellingr's doors", that is, at dawn. In Hávamál 160 the dwarf Þjóðrerir sang a spell before Dellingr's doors, and in Heiðreks gátur Gestumblindi (Óðinn) opens many riddles with "What is that wonder which I saw outside before Dellingr's doors?". Dellingr is also named among the builders of Menglöð's hall in Fjölsvinnsmál 34, and Forspjallsljóð (Hrafnagaldr Óðins) 24 describes "Dellingr's son" (Day) riding his horse across the sky.

gerdr.en:
Gerðr is a giantess, daughter of Gymir and Aurboða, of the hill-giants' race, the most beautiful of women, who becomes the wife of Freyr and is counted among the goddesses (Gylfaginning chapter 37; Skáldskaparmál chapter 1; Völuspá in skamma 2).

Freyr sees her from Óðinn's seat Hliðskjálf and falls lovesick. In Gylfaginning chapter 37, and at length in Skírnismál, his servant Skírnir rides to Gymir's house to woo her for him, receiving Freyr's sword as reward. Gerðr refuses the eleven golden apples (Skírnismál 19-20) and a ring burned with Óðinn's son (22), and defies threats of force (24), but gives way when Skírnir lays a curse of misery and loveless longing on her; she then promises to meet Freyr in the grove Barri after nine nights (39, 41). In stanza 16 she fears that the visitor may be her brother's slayer, an allusion not explained elsewhere in the Eddas.

innsteinn.en:
Innsteinn is one of the leading warriors of the legendary King Hálfr, known from Hálfs saga ok Hálfsrekka. In Hálfsrekkaljóð he warns Hálfr not to trust his kinsman King Ásmundr (3, 5) and tells three ominous dreams of fire and water (7-11), but the king does not heed him (15). Ásmundr sets fire to the hall; Hálfr and his men break out but are overwhelmed, and Innsteinn speaks verses over his fallen lord before he too is killed at nightfall, saying men will tell that Hálfr died laughing (24).

In Hyndluljóð (12) Innsteinn is the father of Freyja's protégé Óttarr and son of Álfr the Old, the same descent the saga gives Hálfr's champion, so the two are usually taken to be the same figure.

ottar.en:
Óttarr, called "the foolish" (heimski) in Hyndluljóð, is Freyja's human protégé. Freyja says he made her a shrine of stones, reddened with sacrificial blood until the rock turned to glass (stanza 10), and that he has a wager with Angantýr about their ancestry and their father's inheritance (9).

To help him Freyja rides to the giantess Hyndla, with Óttarr apparently disguised as her boar, and asks her to recite his lineage. Hyndla names him son of Innsteinn, son of Álfr the Old (12), and goes on through famous families such as the Skjöldungar, Ynglingar, Völsungar and Gjúkungar, with the repeated refrain "all are your kinsmen, Óttarr, you fool" (16, 17, 20-28). The poem ends with Freyja demanding memory-ale so that he can recall it all at the meeting.

refr.en:
Hofgarða-Refr (Refr Gestsson) is an Icelandic skald of the eleventh century, one of the poets Snorri quotes most often in Skáldskaparmál, though only in fragments.

His lines illustrate kennings for Óðinn, who is called High God, friend of Mímir and adversary of the wolf (chapter 9); for poetry, in a verse offering the "drink of the rock-folk" to one Þorsteinn (chapter 10); and for the sea and ships, where the sea is "Ymir's blood" and the ship the "deer of the masthead" (chapter 33; chapters 61 and 64). He is also cited for heiti of trees and for names of waves and the sea in the lists of chapters 59 and 76. Snorri refers to him once more in the commentary of Háttatal.

rhine.en:
The Rhine (Rín) is the river of the Niflung legend. Before riding to Atli, Gunnarr and Högni sink Fáfnir's gold in it, and it has never been found (Skáldskaparmál chapter 50); in Atlakviða (27) Gunnarr declares that the swift Rhine shall keep the gold of the Niflungs. Brot af Sigurðarkviðu (9) places Sigurðr's death south of the Rhine, and the Rhine and its gold are mentioned in Sigurðarkviða in skamma (16), Völundarkviða (14) and Atlakviða (17).

From this, skalds call gold the Rhine's amber, the Rhine's red metal or the Rhine's pebbles, kennings Snorri quotes in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 56) and uses in his own Háttatal. Rín is also among the rivers named in Grímnismál 27.

rig.en:
Rígr is the name taken by a god, identified in the prose introduction of Rígsþula as Heimdallr, who walks the land and fathers the three social ranks of humankind.

In Rígsþula he visits three households in turn. At each he sits between the couple at table, sleeps between them for three nights and leaves a son behind. Ái and Edda bear Þræll, ancestor of the thralls; Afi and Amma bear Karl, ancestor of free farmers; Faðir and Móðir bear Jarl, ancestor of the nobility. Rígr later returns to the young Jarl, teaches him runes, gives him his own name and claims him as his son (stanza 36). Jarl's youngest son, Konr ungr, surpasses him in rune-lore and wins the right to be called Rígr himself (stanza 45). The poem breaks off unfinished. The identification with Heimdallr rests only on the prose, though Völuspá also calls humankind Heimdallr's offspring.

skuli.en:
Skúli Þorsteinsson was an Icelandic skald of around the year 1000, son of Þorsteinn Egilsson and grandson of Egill Skallagrímsson; he fought with Earl Eiríkr Hákonarson at the battle of Svöldr and composed verse about it.

Snorri quotes him several times in Skáldskaparmál as an authority for kennings and poetic terms: for the sun (chapter 34), for gold as Freyja's tears (chapter 44), in the account of Hölgi's mound in chapter 55, and in the lists of poetic words (chapter 75). The mentions from Háttatal belong to a different man: Earl Skúli Bárðarson, the Norwegian regent and Snorri's patron, who is praised together with King Hákon Hákonarson in that poem. The index mixes the two.

ull.en:
Ullr is a god, son of Sif and stepson of Þórr. Snorri (Gylfaginning chapter 31) describes him as a fine archer and skier, handsome and warlike, a god to invoke in single combat; he is also among the gods at Ægir's feast in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 1). His hall is Ýdalir (Grímnismál 5), and in Grímnismál 42 the captive Óðinn promises "the favour of Ullr" to whoever first frees him from the fire.

No myth about him survives, but his name is common in poetry: an oath sworn "by Ullr's ring" in Atlakviða (30); Þórr and Sif are periphrased as his stepfather and mother (Skáldskaparmál chapters 11 and 29); a shield is "Ullr's ship" (chapter 61), and "Ullr" serves as base word in kennings for warriors. Place-names in Norway and Sweden suggest he once had a larger place in cult than the literary sources show.

volsung.en:
Völsungr is the legendary ancestor of the Völsungar, father of Sigmundr and grandfather of Sigurðr. The Prologue (chapter 4) traces the house to Óðinn's son Sigi and his son Rerir, rulers in Frankland, and Skáldskaparmál chapter 80 likewise places Völsungr in the land of the Franks and names Siggeirr as his son-in-law.

In the Eddic poems he is mentioned mainly through his descendants. The prose of Helgakviða Hundingsbana II calls Sigmundr his son and says the family were called Völsungar and Ylfingar; Hyndluljóð 26 traces Sigurðr from "Völsungr's seed"; and Sigurðr himself is "the Völsungr" in Sigurðarkviða in skamma 13. His own story, in which Siggeirr betrays and kills him, is told in the Völsunga saga rather than in the Eddas.

erpr.en:
Erpr is the son of Jónakr and the youngest brother of Hamðir and Sörli. In Skáldskaparmál chapter 50 he is Guðrún's son by Jónakr, raven-haired like the Niflungs; in Hamðismál he is a half-brother born of another mother.

When the brothers ride to avenge Svanhildr on Jörmunrekkr, they ask Erpr what help he will give; he replies that he will help them as one foot helps the other (Hamðismál 13), or in Snorri's version as the hand helps the foot. Mocking him as a bastard, or in Snorri wishing to hurt their mother, who loved him most, they kill him (Hamðismál 14; Skáldskaparmál chapter 50). Later Sörli stumbles and steadies himself with his hand, they realise the meaning of his words, and at Jörmunrekkr's hall Hamðir says the king's head would be off if Erpr were living (Hamðismál 28). A different Erpr, Atli's son by Guðrún, killed by her with his brother Eitill, appears in Atlakviða 37 and Hamðismál 8; the index mixes the two.

gymir.en:
Gymir is a giant, husband of Aurboða and father of Gerðr, whom Freyr falls in love with after seeing her from Hliðskjálf as she walks to Gymir's house (Gylfaginning chapter 37; Skírnismál 6; Völuspá in skamma 2).

In Skírnismál Freyr's servant Skírnir rides past Gymir's hounds to woo Gerðr for him; Gerðr replies that there is no lack of gold in her father's house (22) and warns that Gymir would fight him (24). In Lokasenna (42) Loki taunts Freyr for having bought Gymir's daughter with gold and given away his sword. Separately, Gymir is also a name of the sea giant Ægir: the prose before Lokasenna and Skáldskaparmál (chapter 33) say that Ægir and Gymir are the same.

hlodr.en:
Hlöðr is a son of the Gothic king Heiðrekr, born and raised among the Huns, the grandson through his mother of the Hunnish king Humli. He is the claimant in Hlöðskviða, the poem on the battle of the Goths and Huns preserved in Hervarar saga.

After Heiðrekr's death Hlöðr rides from Húnaland to Árheimar, where his half-brother Angantýr is holding the funeral feast, and demands half of everything, including the sword Tyrfingr. Angantýr offers rich gifts but not an equal share, and old Gizurr insults Hlöðr as the son of a slave-woman. Hlöðr and Humli then lead a vast Hunnish army against the Goths. Hlöðr falls in the battle, and Angantýr, finding him among the dead, laments that he has become his brother's slayer (stanzas 31-32).

yngvi.en:
Yngvi is a name of several overlapping uses, chiefly that of the ancestor of the Swedish royal house of the Ynglingar, who is identified elsewhere (as Yngvi-Freyr) with the god Freyr. In Snorri's Prologue (chapter 5) Yngvi is a son of Óðinn who ruled Sweden after him, the founder of the Yngling line; in Skáldskaparmál chapter 80 he is instead one of the sons of Hálfdan the Old, from whom the Ynglingar descend, and the name is also listed as a poetic term for a king.

As a royal title it appears in skaldic verse ("Yngvi's kin" in Hákonarmál, Skáldskaparmál chapter 9), and heroic poems call princes his offspring: Helgi is "offspring of Yngvi" in Helgakviða Hundingsbana I 55, and Reginsmál 14 calls Sigurðr "Yngvi's heir". Quite separately, Yngvi is a dwarf in the dwarf list of Völuspá 16, repeated in Gylfaginning chapter 14, and a warrior summoned against the Völsungs in Helgakviða Hundingsbana I 52. All mentions are flagged as uncertain, and the index mixes these figures.

bodvildr.en:
Böðvildr is the only daughter of King Níðuðr in Völundarkviða. Níðuðr gives her the gold ring taken from the captive smith Völundr (prose), and Völundr laments seeing her wear it (19). After killing her two brothers, Völundr sends her a brooch made from their teeth (25).

When the ring breaks she brings it secretly to Völundr to mend (26-27); he plies her with beer and lies with her, then flies away, leaving her weeping (29). Völundr tells Níðuðr that she is pregnant (36), and she confirms to her father that she was with Völundr on the island and could not resist him (40-41). The Old English poem Deor also mentions her grief (as Beadohild), and in Þiðreks saga her son by the smith is the hero Viðga.

denmark.en:
Denmark (Danmörk) appears in Snorri's Edda and the poems as a real kingdom. The Prologue (chapter 5) lists it among the lands to which the Æsir brought their language, and the verse in Gylfaginning chapter 1 calls the island Gefjun ploughed out of Sweden "Denmark's increase".

Skáldskaparmál chapter 52 and the prose of Gróttasöngr say the realm was ruled by Óðinn's son Skjöldr, ancestor of the Skjöldungar, and was then called Gotland; his descendant Fróði owned the mill Grótti, whose stones were found in Denmark. In the heroic poems Sigmundr lives for a time in Borghildr's kingdom there (Grípisspá prose), and after Sigurðr's death Guðrún stays seven half-years in Denmark with Þóra, daughter of Hákon (Guðrúnarkviða I prose, Guðrúnarkviða II 14). Skáldskaparmál chapter 66 also notes Danish terms for a king's retainers.

egill-skallagrimsson.en:
Egill Skallagrímsson is the tenth-century Icelandic skald and Viking, hero of Egils saga, known for his feud with King Eiríkr blóðøx of Norway. Snorri quotes him several times in Skáldskaparmál.

From Sonatorrek, his lament for his sons, comes a stanza calling Óðinn "Víli's brother" and "Mímir's friend" (chapter 9); a couplet on carrying Óðinn's mead (poetry) to the English shore illustrates kennings for poetry (chapter 10), and a curse-like verse naming Freyr and Njörðr illustrates kennings for Freyr (chapter 14). He is also quoted for a kenning for summer (chapter 38) and in the heiti lists (chapters 71, 76 and 80).

einarr-skalaglamm.en:
Einarr skálaglamm Helgason was an Icelandic skald of the later tenth century and a court poet of Hákon jarl Sigurðarson, ruler of Norway. His main surviving work is Vellekla ('lack of gold'), a praise poem on Hákon's wars and rule.

Snorri quotes him (in Brodeur's translation 'Einarr Tinkling-Scale') about a dozen times in Skáldskaparmál, mostly from Vellekla: for kennings of poetry as the mead of the gods and dwarves (chapters 9-10), for terms for gold, rulers, weapons and arrows (chapters 56-61 and 66), and among the examples for terms for gods and for the raven (chapters 68 and 75).

einherjar.en:
The einherjar are the dead warriors whom Óðinn chooses on the battlefield and gathers in Valhöll as his host for Ragnarök. Gylfaginning chapter 20 explains that all who fall in battle are Óðinn's adopted sons.

Gylfaginning (chapters 38-41), largely drawing on Grímnismál and Vafþrúðnismál, describes their life. Every day they arm, go out and fight one another, then ride home and sit together in friendship. They eat the boar Sæhrímnir, which is cooked each day and whole again by evening, drink mead that flows from the goat Heiðrún, and are served by valkyries such as Hrist and Mist (Grímnismál 36). Valhöll has 540 doors, and 800 warriors will go out through each when they go to fight the wolf (Grímnismál 23). At Ragnarök they follow Óðinn into the last battle (Gylfaginning chapter 51).

fenrir.en:
Fenrir (Fenrisúlfr, "the Fenris wolf") is the monstrous wolf born to Loki and the giantess Angrboða, brother of Jörmungandr (the Midgard serpent) and Hel (Gylfaginning chapter 34; Skáldskaparmál chapter 23).

Gylfaginning chapter 34 tells how the gods raised him in Ásgarðr, where only Týr dared to feed him, and, fearing the prophecies, tried to bind him. He broke the fetters Læðingr and Drómi; the third, Gleipnir, made by dwarves from impossible things, held him, but only after Týr laid his hand in the wolf's mouth as a pledge and lost it (also Gylfaginning chapter 25 and the Lokasenna prose). The wolf was then left bound with a sword propping his jaws. At Ragnarök he breaks free, swallows Óðinn and is killed by Víðarr, who tears his jaws apart (Gylfaginning chapter 51; Skáldskaparmál chapter 18 calls Víðarr his slayer). The refrain of Völuspá ("the fetters will burst, and the wolf run free") is usually taken to refer to him, and Grímnismál 39 names Hati, the wolf who pursues the moon, as son of Hróðvitnir, a name commonly understood as Fenrir.

hermodr.en:
Hermóðr "the bold" is, in Snorri, a son of Óðinn and messenger of the gods. When Baldr dies, Hermóðr volunteers to ride to Hel to ransom him (Gylfaginning chapter 49): he rides Sleipnir nine nights through dark valleys to the river Gjöll and its gilded bridge, leaps the gate of Hel, and obtains Hel's terms that Baldr may return if all things weep for him. Baldr sends Draupnir back to Óðinn with him.

In poetry the name looks more like that of a hero received in Valhöll: in Hyndluljóð (2) Óðinn gave Hermóðr helmet and mail-coat, and in the verse from Eyvindr skáldaspillir's Hákonarmál quoted in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 9) Óðinn bids Hermóðr and Bragi go to greet the dead King Hákon. Whether these are the same figure is uncertain.

hildr.en:
Hildr ("battle") is a valkyrie. Her name appears in the valkyrie lists of Völuspá 30 and Grímnismál 36 (quoted in Gylfaginning chapter 36), and as a common noun for battle it underlies many kennings, such as "Hildr's wheel" for a shield (Skáldskaparmál chapter 61).

The name is also borne by Hildr, daughter of King Högni, whose abduction by Heðinn leads to the endless battle of the Hjaðningar told in Skáldskaparmál chapter 62: she offers her father a necklace for peace, and when he refuses she wakes the dead each night so that the fight goes on until Ragnarök. In Skáldskaparmál chapter 48 the sleeping valkyrie woken by Sigurðr gives her name as Hildr, "who is called Brynhildr". In Helgakviða Hundingsbana II 29 Helgi tells Sigrún "you have been a Hildr to us", meaning a cause of strife. The index may mix these figures.

hodbroddr.en:
Höðbroddr is a son of King Granmarr, with brothers Guðmundr and Starkaðr (prose of Helgakviða Hundingsbana II). Sigrún's father Högni betrothes her to him against her will; she calls him no better than a cat's son and seeks the help of Helgi Hundingsbani instead (Helgakviða Hundingsbana I 18; Helgakviða Hundingsbana II 16).

Helgi brings a fleet against the sons of Granmarr; Helgakviða Hundingsbana I gives the flyting of Sinfjötli and Guðmundr before the battle and shows Höðbroddr calling up his forces (35, 48, 51). In the battle all the sons of Granmarr fall; the prose of Helgakviða Hundingsbana II says Sigrún found Höðbroddr dying on the field, and Helgi tells her of the deaths (20-21). The first Helgi poem is introduced as a poem "about Helgi Hundingsbani and Höðbroddr".

hogni-sigrunar.en:
Högni is a king, father of the valkyrie Sigrún and of Bragi and Dagr, in the poems of Helgi Hundingsbani. He has promised Sigrún to Höðbroddr, son of King Granmarr, but she chooses Helgi (Helgakviða Hundingsbana I 17; Helgakviða Hundingsbana II 13-17 and prose).

Högni joins Granmarr's sons against Helgi at Frekasteinn and falls there, with his son Bragi; only Dagr is spared, after swearing oaths to the Völsungar (Helgakviða Hundingsbana II, prose). Dagr later sacrifices to Óðinn for vengeance for his father and kills Helgi. This Högni is distinct from Högni Gjúkason, Gunnarr's brother, and from Högni the father of Hildr in the Hjaðningavíg legend.

oddrun.en:
Oddrún is a sister of Atli (and so of Brynhildr) who loved Gunnarr, the Burgundian king. In Sigurðarkviða in skamma 58 Brynhildr prophesies to Gunnarr that Atli will refuse him Oddrún but that they will love each other in secret.

She speaks Oddrúnargrátr (Oddrún's lament). Hearing that Borgný, daughter of King Heiðrekr, is unable to give birth to her lover Vilmundr's children, Oddrún rides to her and delivers her with charms (stanza 7). Then she tells her story: Atli would not let her marry Gunnarr; their secret meetings were betrayed; Atli took his revenge on the Gjúkungs, and Gunnarr died in the snake-pit while she was away at Geirmundr's. The poem ends with her grief (stanza 34). The prose Dráp Niflunga also mentions her.

ormr-steinthorsson.en:
Ormr Steinþórsson is an Icelandic skald known almost only from the verses Snorri quotes from him; little is known of his life or date.

Snorri cites him in Skáldskaparmál as an authority on poetic diction: for terms for poetry (chapter 10), for kennings for winter (chapter 37), and for words for a woman, such as "prop" (chapter 58). Some further quotations ascribed simply to "Ormr" (chapter 58 and the lists in chapter 76) may also be his. The mentions in chapters 31 and 33 belong at least in part to a different poet, Ormr Barreyjarskáld; the index may mix them.

ottarr-svarti.en:
Óttarr svarti ("the Black") is an Icelandic skald of the early eleventh century, nephew of Sigvatr Þórðarson. He composed for several kings, among them Óláfr Haraldsson (St Óláfr) and Knútr the Great, for whom he made a Knútsdrápa.

Snorri quotes him about a dozen times in Skáldskaparmál, almost all in the later sections on poetic names (heiti): for a man as "breaker of gold" (chapter 57), for land and fields (70), for the sea and waves (76), and for rulers and royal titles such as "leader" and "Yngling" (79-80).

skidbladnir.en:
Skíðblaðnir is Freyr's ship, made for him by the dwarves called the sons of Ívaldi. Grímnismál 43-44 names it the best of ships, and Gylfaginning (chapters 41 and 43) repeats this, adding that although Naglfar is larger, Skíðblaðnir is the most skilfully made.

Gylfaginning chapter 43 says it can carry all the Æsir with their weapons, has a favourable wind as soon as the sail is raised, and can be folded up like a cloth and kept in a pouch. Skáldskaparmál chapter 43 places its making in the story of Sif's hair: Loki has Ívaldi's sons make the golden hair, the spear Gungnir and Skíðblaðnir, and gives the ship to Freyr when the gods judge the treasures. Freyr may be called "possessor of Skíðblaðnir" (chapter 14).

sweden.en:
Svíþjóð (Sweden) appears in the Eddas mainly as the land of legendary kings. In the Prologue (chapter 5) Óðinn comes north to Sweden, where King Gylfi rules and yields him power; Óðinn's son Yngvi becomes king there, ancestor of the Ynglings. Gylfaginning chapter 1 opens with Gylfi ruling "the land men now call Sweden".

In Skáldskaparmál chapter 52 and the prose of Gróttasöngr, King Fróði buys the giant maids Fenja and Menja at a feast of King Fjölnir in Sweden, and in Gróttasöngr 13 the maids recall fighting in battles there. Chapter 54 tells of Hrólfr kraki's visit to King Aðils at Uppsala. The prose of Völundarkviða makes Níðuðr a king in Sweden.

agnarr-geirrodsson.en:
Agnarr Geirröðarson is the ten-year-old son of King Geirröðr in the prose frame of Grímnismál, named after his father's brother. When Geirröðr has the disguised Óðinn, who calls himself Grímnir, set between two fires for eight nights, Agnarr alone brings him a full horn to drink. Grímnir greets him and foretells that he will rule the Goths (2-3); after Geirröðr falls on his own sword, Agnarr reigns long (closing prose).

The index also gathers here two other figures: the elder Agnarr, son of Hrauðungr and Frigg's fosterling, whom his brother Geirröðr pushes out to sea (opening prose of Grímnismál), and Agnarr, brother of Auða, whom Brynhildr helped against Hjálmgunnarr and so earned Óðinn's anger (Sigrdrífumál; Helreið Brynhildar 7).

elivagar.en:
Élivágar (ice waves) are the primeval rivers that flowed from the spring Hvergelmir in Niflheimr into Ginnungagap. In Gylfaginning chapter 5 their venomous foam hardened into ice and rime. When the rime met the heat from Múspell, the drops quickened into the first giant, Ymir; Vafþrúðnismál 31 says the same, which is why the giants are so fierce.

Élivágar also marks the boundary of the giants' world. Hymiskviða 5 places Hymir's home east of Élivágar, and in Skáldskaparmál chapter 25 Þórr tells how he carried Aurvandill in a basket from the north across Élivágar, one of whose toes froze and became a star. Forspjallsljóð (Hrafnagaldr Óðins) 13 also names it.

hodr.en:
Höðr is a blind god, son of Óðinn, the unwitting slayer of his brother Baldr. Snorri says he is strong but that the gods would rather his name were never spoken, for his deed will long be remembered (Gylfaginning chapter 28).

In Gylfaginning chapter 49, when the gods amuse themselves by throwing weapons at Baldr, who cannot be harmed, Loki gives Höðr the mistletoe, the one thing that had not sworn to spare Baldr, and guides his aim; the shaft kills Baldr. The deed is foretold in Völuspá 32 and Baldrs draumar 9, where the seeress says that Höðr will bear the fatal branch. Váli, a son of Óðinn born for the purpose, avenges Baldr by killing Höðr (Völuspá 32; Skáldskaparmál chapters 19-20). After Ragnarök Höðr and Baldr return from Hel and live together in peace (Völuspá 62; Gylfaginning chapter 53). Saxo Grammaticus tells a very different version in which Hotherus is a human hero and Baldr's rival for Nanna.

ran.en:
Rán is a sea goddess, wife of Ægir, with whom she has nine daughters, the waves (Skáldskaparmál chapters 33 and 76). The drowned are thought to go to her: in Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar (18) Atli says the giantess would have given Helgi's men to Rán.

In the prose of Reginsmál Loki borrows Rán's net to catch the dwarf Andvari, who lives as a pike. Skáldskaparmál uses her chiefly for kennings: the sea is "husband of Rán", her "road" or "mouth" is the sea, and gold is the fire of Ægir and Rán, from the tale of Ægir's hall lit by gold (chapter 41).

The "Rani" of Grógaldr (6), who taught a charm to Rindr, is a different figure (often taken as a name of Óðinn) and is probably a false match.

rindr.en:
Rindr is the mother, by Óðinn, of Váli, the god born to avenge Baldr. Gylfaginning counts her among the Ásynjur (chapter 36) and names her as Váli's mother (chapter 30); Skáldskaparmál names her among Óðinn's partners, calling Frigg and Jörð her "co-wives" (chapters 27, 32), and Váli is "son of Óðinn and Rindr" (chapter 19).

In Baldrs draumar 11 the seeress foretells that Rindr will bear Váli in Vestrsalir and that he will kill Baldr's slayer at one night old. A skaldic half-stanza quoted in Skáldskaparmál chapter 9 says "Óðinn worked seiðr on Rindr", alluding to a story of winning her by magic that is told fully only by Saxo Grammaticus (as Rinda). Grógaldr 6 refers to a charm "Rani taught Rindr".

voluspa.en:
Völuspá ("the prophecy of the seeress") is the opening poem of the Codex Regius collection of eddic poetry: a seeress, addressing Óðinn, tells of the world's creation, the early history of the gods, Baldr's death, Ragnarök and the rise of a new world.

The index entry records the places where Snorri names the poem in Gylfaginning, his most important source there. He quotes it on Ginnungagap and the beginning of things (chapters 4-5), the stars and the moon-hound (chapters 8 and 12), the dwarves (chapter 14), Mímir's well (chapter 15), Gimlé (chapter 17), Sleipnir's birth (chapter 42) and, at length, on Ragnarök (chapter 51). His wording sometimes differs from the Codex Regius and Hauksbók texts of the poem.

andvari.en:
Andvari is a dwarf, son of Óinn, who lives in a waterfall in the shape of a pike and owns a great hoard of gold (Reginsmál 2 and prose). When Óðinn, Hœnir and Loki must pay Hreiðmarr compensation for killing Otr, Loki catches Andvari and forces him to give up all his gold. Andvari tries to keep back one ring, but Loki takes that too, and the dwarf curses the ring and the gold to be the death of whoever owns them (Reginsmál; Skáldskaparmál chapter 46). The curse drives the rest of the Völsung and Niflung story.

The sources differ on the capture: Snorri says Loki caught him with his hands, while the prose of Reginsmál has Loki borrow the net of the sea goddess Rán. Andvari is also named in the dwarf lists of Völuspá (15) and Gylfaginning (chapter 14).

baugi.en:
Baugi is a giant, the brother of Suttungr, who appears in Snorri's account of how Óðinn won the mead of poetry (Skáldskaparmál chapter 6).

Óðinn, calling himself Bölverkr, first causes Baugi's nine thralls to kill one another while mowing. He then takes their place for the summer, asking as his wage one drink of Suttungr's mead. When Suttungr refuses, Baugi helps Óðinn bore through the mountain Hnitbjörg with the auger Rati. When he tries to cheat by leaving the hole unfinished, Óðinn notices. Once the hole is through, Óðinn slips in as a snake; Baugi stabs after him with the auger but misses. Óðinn then reaches Gunnlöð and the mead. Baugi is not named in Hávamál's version of the story.

draupnir.en:
Draupnir ("dripper") is Óðinn's gold ring, from which eight rings of equal weight drip every ninth night. In Skáldskaparmál chapter 43 it is one of the treasures forged by the dwarf Brokkr and his brother in a wager with Loki.

Óðinn laid it on Baldr's funeral pyre (Gylfaginning chapter 49), and when Hermóðr rode to Hel to ask for Baldr's return, Baldr sent the ring back to Óðinn as a keepsake. Skáldskaparmál chapter 12 accordingly calls Baldr its possessor, and gold can be called "Draupnir's drop" or "rain of Draupnir" (chapter 40). The ring offered to Gerðr in Skírnismál 22, "burned with Óðinn's son", is generally taken to be Draupnir, though the poem does not name it. Draupnir is also the name of a dwarf in Völuspá 15 and the dwarf list of Gylfaginning chapter 14; the index mixes the two.

gefjon.en:
Gefjun (Gefjon) is a goddess of the Æsir. Gylfaginning opens (chapter 1) with her taking from King Gylfi of Sweden as much land as four oxen could plough in a day and a night; she yoked her four sons by a giant, in ox shape, and dragged the land out to sea to become Zealand, leaving the lake now called Mälaren, as Bragi's verse quoted there tells. In Gylfaginning 35 Snorri calls her a virgin, attended by women who die unmarried.

In Lokasenna (19-21) she tries to calm the quarrel; Loki retorts that she gave herself to a fair youth for a necklace, and Óðinn warns him that she knows the fates as well as he does. She is among the goddesses at Ægir's feast in Skáldskaparmál (chapters 1 and 41).

glumr.en:
Glúmr Geirason is a tenth-century Icelandic skald who composed for the Norwegian kings of the line of Eiríkr blóðøx, especially Haraldr gráfeldr.

Snorri quotes his verses in Skáldskaparmál as examples of poetic diction: in chapter 9 and 10 for kennings of Óðinn and of poetry, in chapter 61 for "fire of the byrnie" as a kenning for a sword, and in chapters 66 and 80 for terms for kings and rulers. Only brief citations of his work survive, chiefly in Snorri's Edda and the kings' sagas.

gnitaheidi.en:
Gnitaheiðr (Gnita heath) is where Fáfnir lies in serpent form on the gold taken from Hreiðmarr, wearing the helm of terror (Skáldskaparmál chapter 47; prose of Reginsmál).

Reginn leads Sigurðr there; Sigurðr digs a pit in the track Fáfnir follows to water and stabs him from below (Skáldskaparmál chapter 47; prose of Fáfnismál). Grípir foretells this in Grípisspá 11. Hence gold may be called "metal of Gnitaheiðr" (Skáldskaparmál chapter 47; Háttatal). In Atlakviða 5-6 Atli's messenger offers Gunnarr "the field of wide Gnitaheiðr", and Gunnarr replies that no gold there equals his own.

gudmundr.en:
Guðmundr is a son of King Granmarr and brother of Höðbroddr, Sigrún's unwanted suitor, in the poems of Helgi Hundingsbani. When Helgi's fleet arrives, Guðmundr challenges it from the shore and is answered by Helgi's half-brother Sinfjötli. Their exchange of insults (Helgakviða Hundingsbana I 36-49; Helgakviða Hundingsbana II, prose) is the best-known flyting of the heroic poems, each charging the other with monstrous or unmanly deeds. Guðmundr then rides home with news of the fleet, and Granmarr's sons gather the army that is defeated at Frekasteinn, where all of them fall.

The index header identifies him with Guðmundr of Glæsisvellir, a king of a marvellous northern land in later sagas; the Eddic poems give him no such role.

hakon.en:
Hákon is the name of several Norwegian rulers who appear in Snorri's Edda. The most important for the Edda is King Hákon Hákonarson (reigned 1217-1263). Snorri composed Háttatal, his "list of verse-forms", in praise of the young Hákon and of Earl Skúli Bárðarson, and the opening stanzas of Háttatal (chapter 1) name and praise him.

In Skáldskaparmál other Hákons appear in the quoted verses. Eyvindr skáldaspillir's stanzas on gold as "Fulla's snood" and "seed of Fýrisvellir" (chapters 44 and 54) recall the generosity of King Hákon the Good (tenth century). Chapter 66 cites a poet calling Earl Hákon "son of Earl Sigurðr", that is, Hákon of Hlaðir. In Guðrúnarkviða II (stanza 14) Guðrún stays for seven half-years with Þóra, Hákon's daughter, in Denmark. The index mixes these figures.

hallfredr.en:
Hallfreðr vandræðaskáld ("troublesome skald") was an Icelandic poet of the late tenth century, court skald of King Óláfr Tryggvason, who gave him his nickname and stood sponsor at his baptism; he had earlier composed for Earl Hákon Sigurðarson. His life is told in Hallfreðar saga.

Snorri quotes him often in Skáldskaparmál as an authority on poetic diction, among other places in the sections on poetry and Óðinn (chapter 9), on the earth (chapter 32), on armour (chapter 61), and on terms for earls and the king's counsellors (chapter 66). His verse for Earl Hákon, which pictures the conquest of Norway as Hákon's wooing of the earth, Óðinn's bride, is a well-known example of an extended kenning. One mention in chapter 70 is actually introduced as Hallvarðr's verse and has been matched to Hallfreðr by mistake.

hlokk.en:
Hlökk is a valkyrie whose name means "noise" or "battle". She is named in the list of valkyries who bear ale to the einherjar in Grímnismál, which Snorri quotes in Gylfaginning.

All the indexed mentions are in skaldic kennings, where "Hlökk" stands for battle or a valkyrie as a base word: shields are "tents of Hlökk" and battle the "sleet" or "showers of Hlökk" (Skáldskaparmál chapters 60-61), and in Snorri's own Háttatal swords are "Hlökk's fires" and a warrior "sharpener of Hlökk".

hogni-hildar.en:
Högni is a legendary king, father of Hildr, whose story is the battle of the Hjaðningar told in Skáldskaparmál chapter 62. While he is away, Heðinn raids his realm and carries off his daughter.

Högni pursues Heðinn north along Norway and west over the sea to Hoy in Orkney. Hildr offers him a necklace for peace on Heðinn's behalf, and Heðinn himself offers gold, but Högni answers that it is too late: he has drawn the sword Dáinsleif, made by dwarves, which kills a man each time it is bared and whose wounds never heal. The two hosts fight all day; each night Hildr wakes the fallen, and the battle is to continue until Ragnarök. Snorri supports the story with stanzas from Bragi's Ragnarsdrápa. The Hyndluljóð mention in this index belongs to Högni, son of Gjúki.

odr.en:
Óðr is Freyja's husband. Gylfaginning chapter 35 says their daughter is Hnoss; Óðr went away on long journeys, and Freyja weeps tears of red gold for him and took many names while searching for him among strange peoples. He is otherwise almost unknown, and his name has long been compared with Óðinn's.

Most mentions are kennings for Freyja as "Óðr's wife" or "bedfellow", and for gold as her tears (Skáldskaparmál chapters 28, 44 and 61, including Einarr's verse in chapter 44). In Völuspá 25, quoted in Gylfaginning chapter 42, the gods ask who had given "Óðr's maid" to the giants, referring to the bargain with the master builder of Ásgarðr. Hyndluljóð also alludes to Freyja running after Óðr.

q1534414.en: Góinn and Móinn are two serpents, sons of Grafvitnir, named among the snakes that gnaw the roots of Yggdrasill in Grímnismál (34) and in Snorri's quotation of the same stanza in Gylfaginning (chapter 16). Nothing else is told of them. Their names, and Grafvitnir's, recur in the þula of names for serpents in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 73), and Grafvitnir also appears in a kenning for gold quoted in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 56).

sigrlinn.en:
Sigrlinn is the daughter of King Sváfnir, wife of King Hjörvarðr and mother of the hero Helgi Hjörvarðsson. She is known only from Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar.

Hjörvarðr has vowed to marry the fairest woman alive, and a talking bird tells his man Atli, son of Earl Iðmundr, about Sigrlinn (stanzas 1-4). Her hand is at first refused. When the wooers return, they find that a rival suitor, King Hróðmarr, has killed her father and burned his land. Atli kills the great bird guarding a house and finds Sigrlinn there with Álof, daughter of Earl Franmarr. Hjörvarðr marries Sigrlinn and Atli marries Álof (prose after stanza 5). Helgi is later called "Sigrlinn's son" (stanza 35), and a troll-woman's ride on a wolf foretells his death.

skogul.en:
Skögul is a valkyrie, one of the battle-maidens who choose the slain for Óðinn. Völuspá 30 names her among the valkyries the seeress sees riding out, and in Grímnismál 36 (quoted in Gylfaginning chapter 36) she is among those who bring ale to the einherjar in Valhöll.

In Eyvindr skáldaspillir's Hákonarmál, quoted in Skáldskaparmál chapter 9, Óðinn sends Göndul and Skögul to choose which king of Yngvi's kin should come to Valhöll, the dead King Hákon the Good. Her name is a common element in skaldic kennings: "Skögul's weather" or "Skögul's din" for battle and "Skögul's shirt" for a mail-coat (Skáldskaparmál chapters 60 and 79; Háttatal). The late poem Forspjallsljóð (Hrafnagaldr Óðins 19) has her pour mead at the gods' table.

beli.en:
Beli is a giant killed by Freyr. Snorri (Gylfaginning chapter 37) explains that Freyr, having given his sword to Skírnir, fought Beli without it and killed him with a hart's antler; he adds that Freyr will miss the sword far more at Ragnarök.

The deed gives Freyr the poetic name "Beli's slayer", used in Völuspá 53 (quoted in Gylfaginning 51) for Freyr's going against Surtr, and in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 14), with a verse by Eyvindr skáldaspillir, and in a þula of horses where the "slayer of Beli" rides Blóðughófi (72). No poem tells the fight itself.

bifrost.en:
Bifröst is the bridge the gods built from earth to heaven, which men call the rainbow. Gylfaginning (chapter 13) says it has three colours and is stronger and more skilfully made than other works, yet will break when the sons of Múspell ride over it.

The gods ride over it every day to their court at the well of Urðr (chapter 15); the red in the bow is burning fire, which keeps the giants from crossing. Heimdallr guards it from his dwelling Himinbjörg at heaven's end, where the bridge meets heaven (chapters 17, 27). It is named the best of bridges in the verse quoted in chapter 41, and its breaking under Surtr and the sons of Múspell is retold in the Ragnarök narrative of chapter 51. Grímnismál calls the bridge Bilröst.

danes.en:
The Danir (Danes) appear in the Eddas mainly in names of kings and peoples. In Guðrúnarkviða II 19 Valdarr king of the Danes is among the princes who come to Guðrún, and Hlöðskviða 1 likewise lists Valdarr as ruler of the Danes beside the rulers of the Huns, Goths and others. In Helreið Brynhildar 12 Sigurðr is "prince of the Danes", and in Heiðreks gátur 26 the riddle of the beast that protects the Danes is a shield.

In Skáldskaparmál the name appears in skaldic praise of Danish kings, quoted in the lists of heiti for rulers (chapters 79-80). Rígsþula 48 names Danr and Danpr, legendary kings of the Danes in other tradition.

eilifr.en:
Eilífr Goðrúnarson was an Icelandic skald of the late tenth century who composed for Hákon jarl Sigurðarson. His Þórsdrápa, a dense mythological poem on Þórr's journey to the giant Geirröðr, is quoted at length by Snorri after his prose version of the story (Skáldskaparmál chapter 26), and Snorri also draws on Eilífr for kennings of poetry and of Þórr (chapters 10-11).

The quotations in chapter 65, giving kennings for Christ such as 'Son of Mary' and 'King of Angels', belong to a different poet, Eilífr kúlnasveinn, a Christian skald known only from these fragments; the index groups both under one name.

eylimi.en:
Eylimi is a legendary king in the Völsung and Helgi poems. In the prose of Grípisspá (Frá dauða Sinfjötla) and in Skáldskaparmál chapter 47 he is the father of Hjördís, Sigmundr's last wife and Sigurðr's mother. He falls with Sigmundr fighting the sons of Hundingr, and Sigurðr must avenge both (Grípisspá 9; Reginsmál 15).

In Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar a King Eylimi is the father of the valkyrie Sváva, who names Helgi Hjörvarðsson and later becomes his betrothed. Skáldskaparmál chapter 80 traces Eylimi's line back to Lofði, son of Hálfdan the Old. The two Eylimis may be distinct figures; the index joins them.

gunnlod.en:
Gunnlöð is a giantess, daughter of Suttungr, set by her father to guard the mead of poetry inside the mountain Hnitbjörg (Skáldskaparmál chapter 5).

Óðinn, calling himself Bölverkr, bored his way into the mountain, lay with her for three nights and was allowed three draughts of the mead, with which he emptied the vessels Óðrerir, Boðn and Són and flew off in eagle shape (Skáldskaparmál chapter 6). Hávamál tells the episode from Óðinn's side: he speaks of being held in Gunnlöð's house (13), of the drill Rati that made way through the rock (105), and admits that he would hardly have escaped without her help, yet left her in grief and broke his oath (108, 110). Skáldskaparmál counts her among Óðinn's partners, so that Frigg and Jörð are both called her co-wife (chapters 27 and 32), and poetry is called the liquor of "Gunnlöð's arm-clasp" in a verse in chapter 9.

halfr.en:
Hálfr is a legendary sea-king of Hörðaland in Norway, hero of Hálfs saga ok Hálfsrekka. His warriors, the Hálfsrekkar, were so devoted that in a storm each offered to go overboard for his comrade. Returning home, Hálfr accepts a feast from his kinsman King Ásmundr against Innsteinn's warnings; Ásmundr burns the hall, and Hálfr breaks out but falls fighting (Hálfsrekkaljóð, especially 17-24).

Snorri knew the story: fire is "Hálfr's bane" in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 36), and he derives the word rekkar ("warriors") from Hálfr's men (chapter 81).

A different Hálfr appears in Guðrúnarkviða II, where Guðrún goes to "Hálfr's hall" in Denmark; the index may mix them.

haraldr.en:
Haraldr is a common royal name, and this index entry gathers several different bearers rather than a single figure; all its mentions are flagged as uncertain.

The best defined is King Haraldr Sigurðarson (harðráði), king of Norway from 1046 until he fell in England in 1066, who was himself a poet: Snorri quotes verses he composed in Skáldskaparmál chapters 64 and 66, and other verses in chapter 66 refer to a Haraldr as the king's kinsman or friend. Legendary bearers include Haraldr hilditönn ("War-tooth"), son of Auðr, in the genealogy of Hyndluljóð 28; Haraldr the Red-Bearded of the Hildingar, maternal grandfather of Hálfdan the Black (Skáldskaparmál chapter 80); and the Haraldr who rode the horse Fölkvir in the horse-name lists (Skáldskaparmál chapter 72 and the Eddubrot).

huginn.en:
Huginn ("thought") is one of Óðinn's two ravens, with Muninn ("memory"). According to Gylfaginning chapter 38 they sit on Óðinn's shoulders and tell him all they see and hear; he sends them out at daybreak to fly over the world and they return by breakfast time, so Óðinn is called the raven-god.

Snorri quotes Grímnismál 20, where Óðinn says he fears Huginn may not come back, but fears more for Muninn. Huginn is listed among the names of the raven in Skáldskaparmál chapter 75, and in skaldic verse "Huginn's" food or drink means the corpses and blood of battle.

laufey.en:
Laufey, also called Nál ('needle'), is the mother of Loki by the giant Fárbauti (Gylfaginning chapter 33; Skáldskaparmál chapter 23). Loki is regularly named after her rather than his father, as Laufey's son, in Þrymskviða (18, 20) and Lokasenna (52), and as son of Nál in Forspjallsljóð (16). Nothing else is told of her.

The dwarf Náli in the Völuspá list of dwarves (13) is a different being, linked here only by the name form.

muspelheim.en:
Múspell, or Múspellsheimr, is the bright, burning world in the south, the source of fire and the home of the fire-giant Surtr, who guards its border with a flaming sword (Gylfaginning chapter 4). It is also personified: "Múspell's sons" or "Múspell's people" are its fire-folk, who come against the gods at Ragnarök.

In Snorri's creation account (Gylfaginning chapters 4-5) the heat of Múspellsheimr meets the rime of Niflheimr in Ginnungagap and life quickens. The gods make the stars, sun and moon from sparks flying out of Múspellsheimr (chapters 8 and 11). At Ragnarök Múspell's sons ride out behind Surtr and break the bridge Bifröst (chapter 51). Gylfaginning chapter 43 says Múspell owns the ship Naglfar. Völuspá 51 instead has Múspell's people sailing over the sea with Loki at the helm, and Lokasenna 42 has them riding through Myrkviðr.

nanna.en:
Nanna is a goddess, daughter of Nepr, wife of Baldr and mother of Forseti (Gylfaginning chapter 32; Skáldskaparmál chapter 12).

At Baldr's funeral (Gylfaginning chapter 49) she died of grief when his body was carried out to the ship and was burned with him on his pyre. When Hermóðr visited the dead Baldr in Hel, Nanna sent gifts back with him: a linen robe for Frigg and a gold finger-ring for Fulla. Skáldskaparmál lists her among the Ásynjur at Ægir's feast (chapter 1) and calls Frigg her mother-in-law (chapter 27). In Saxo Grammaticus Nanna is the woman for whom Hotherus and Balderus compete. Hyndluljóð 20 names a "Nanna, daughter of Nökkvi" in Óttarr's ancestry, who may be a different figure.

nidhoggr.en:
Níðhöggr ("malice-striker") is the dragon or serpent that gnaws Yggdrasill from below. Grímnismál 35 and Gylfaginning (chapters 15-16) place it at the root over Niflheimr by the spring Hvergelmir, where it lives with many snakes; the squirrel Ratatoskr carries insults between it and the eagle at the top of the tree.

In Völuspá 39 it sucks the corpses of the dead, murderers, oath-breakers and adulterers, at Náströnd, and Snorri echoes this (Gylfaginning 52). The poem's last stanza (66) shows the dark dragon flying up from Niðafjöll bearing corpses on its wings, an image whose meaning after the renewal of the world is much debated. Níðhöggr also appears among the names for serpents in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 73).

noatun.en:
Nóatún ("ship-enclosure") is the dwelling of the god Njörðr. Gylfaginning (chapter 23) says Njörðr lives in heaven in the place called Nóatún, and Grímnismál 16 lists it as the eleventh of the gods' halls, where Njörðr rules in his high-timbered temple.

The name stands for Njörðr's sea-bound nature. In Gylfaginning chapter 23 his wife Skaði, who prefers her father's mountain home Þrymheimr, cannot bear the noise of the sea birds at Nóatún, and the two separate. Njörðr is "Njörðr of Nóatún" in Skáldskaparmál chapter 3, Freyr and Freyja are born to him there (Gylfaginning chapter 24), and in Þrymskviða 22 the giant Þrymr rejoices that Freyja, "Njörðr's daughter from Nóatún", is being brought to him as bride.

norway.en:
Nóregr (Norway) appears in the Eddas mostly in passing. In the Prologue (chapter 5) Óðinn sets his son Sæmingr over Norway, from whom its kings and jarls trace their descent, as Háleygjatal says, and the language of the Æsir is said to have spread over these lands.

In Skáldskaparmál chapter 62, the tale of the Hjaðningavíg, Högni pursues Heðinn to Norway and then west to Orkney. Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar includes Norway in the story of Heðinn (31, with the prose), and in Hervararkviða 25 Hervör values the sword from the mound above all of Norway. Snorri also uses Norwegian ranks and court terms in the chapter on men's titles (chapter 66).

tyrfing.en:
Tyrfingr is the cursed sword of the Hervarar saga tradition, forged by dwarves for King Svafrlami (Hervararkviða 8). It passes to the berserk Angantýr, who is buried with it. In Hervararkviða his daughter Hervör wakes him in his grave mound and demands the sword; he warns her that it will destroy her whole kin, and foretells that her son Heiðrekr will carry it (13-26).

Heiðrekr later draws it against Gestumblindi (Óðinn in disguise), who escapes as a falcon with his tail cut short (Heiðreks gátur), and it is the heirloom his sons Angantýr and Hlöðr quarrel over before the battle of Goths and Huns (Hlöðskviða 11). In Hyndluljóð (22) Tyrfingr is instead the name of a man, one of the berserk sons of Arngrímr.

urdarbrunnr.en:
Urðarbrunnr (the Well of Urðr) is a sacred spring beneath the root of the ash Yggdrasill that, in Snorri's account, reaches into heaven. Gylfaginning chapter 15 says the gods ride there every day over Bifröst to hold their court.

The norns, Urðr, Verðandi and Skuld, live by the well. They take water and clay from it each day and pour them over the ash so that its branches do not rot; the dew that falls from the tree is "honey-dew", and two swans feed in the well (Gylfaginning chapter 16). Völuspá 19 describes the tree standing ever green over Urðr's well, and in Hávamál 111 the speaker says he was at Urðr's well and heard the speech of Hár. A Christian verse quoted in Skáldskaparmál chapter 65, by Eilífr Goðrúnarson, places Christ seated "south at the Well of Urðr".

ylfingar.en:
The Ylfingar are a legendary royal kin, in the Eddas closely bound up with Helgi Hundingsbani; the prose of Helgakviða Hundingsbana II says that Sigmundr and his kin were called both Völsungar and Ylfingar. They are usually compared with the Wylfingas of Old English Beowulf.

In Helgakviða Hundingsbana I Helgi is "the Ylfings' son" at his birth (stanza 5), and his host coming to battle is called the Ylfings (34, 49); in Helgakviða Hundingsbana II Helgi again calls himself the Ylfings' son (8) and Sigrún addresses the dead Helgi as "kin of the Ylfings" (47). Hyndluljóð 11 names them among the great dynasties whose lineage Freyja wants to hear, and Skáldskaparmál chapter 80 lists them among famous royal houses.

dainn.en:
Dáinn ("dead one") is the name of one of the four harts that gnaw the branches of Yggdrasill, with Dvalinn, Duneyrr and Duraþrór (Grímnismál 33; Gylfaginning chapter 16); it is also listed among names for a hart in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 71).

The same name is borne by other figures, and the index mixes them: a dwarf in the list of Völuspá 11 (quoted in Gylfaginning 14) and in Hyndluljóð 7, where Dáinn and Nabbi made Freyja's boar Hildisvíni; the one who carved runes for the elves in Hávamál 143; and an obscure figure in Forspjallsljóð (13).

fenja.en:
Fenja is one of two giantess slave-women, with Menja, who turn the magic mill Grótti for the Danish king Fróði. Skáldskaparmál chapter 52 and the prose of Gróttasöngr say Fróði bought them from King Fjölnir in Sweden because they were huge and strong enough to turn the mill, which ground out whatever was asked of it.

Fróði allowed them no rest, so they sang Gróttasöngr and ground out an army against him: the sea-king Mýsingr came that night, killed Fróði and ended "Fróði's peace". Mýsingr took the mill and the women and had them grind salt until his ship sank, which, the story says, is why the sea is salt. In the poem (stanza 1) they describe themselves as "foreknowing" and, in stanza 9, as kin of giants such as Hrungnir and Þjazi. Gold is called "Fenja's labour" (Skáldskaparmál chapter 56, Háttatal).

geitir.en:
Geitir is the servant of King Grípir in Grípisspá: when the young Sigurðr arrives at Grípir's hall, Geitir is the man he speaks to at the gate, who names his master, announces the stranger, and is told to take charge of Sigurðr's horse Grani (stanzas 1-5).

The same name belongs to a sea-king: in Skáldskaparmál chapter 64 a ship is "Geitir's steed", in a verse of Erringar-Steinn, and Háttatal also uses the kenning. The index may mix these two figures.

h-nir.en:
Hœnir is one of the Æsir, often a companion of Óðinn and Loki. In Völuspá (18) he is one of the three gods who give life to the first humans, granting them sense, while Óðinn gives breath and Lóðurr warmth and colour; Snorri's Gylfaginning gives this act to the sons of Borr instead. After the war of the Æsir and Vanir he is given to the Vanir as a hostage in exchange for Njörðr (Gylfaginning chapter 23), and after Ragnarök he chooses the lots in the renewed world (Völuspá 63).

He travels with Óðinn and Loki on the journey when Þjazi seizes Loki (Skáldskaparmál chapter 2) and when Loki kills Otr (Skáldskaparmál chapter 46; Reginsmál prose). Skáldskaparmál (chapter 22) calls him Óðinn's bench-mate and friend, the swift god, the long-footed and king of clay. Ynglinga saga adds that the Vanir found him indecisive.

haki.en:
Haki is a legendary sea-king. Skáldskaparmál chapter 77 quotes a verse saying that "Haki was burned" on a pyre where the sea's wake rolled, alluding to the tradition (told in Ynglinga saga) of a sea-king who, mortally wounded, was laid on a burning ship and sent out to sea.

Haki's name is used chiefly in kennings: a ship is "Haki's steed" or similar in several stanzas of Háttatal (chapters 2 and 3), and Háttatal chapter 3 recalls "we have heard that Haki waged battle" among famous kings. In the verse list of riders and horses (Kálfsvísa) in Skáldskaparmál chapter 72, "Haki rode Fákr". Völuspá in skamma also has a Haki in its list of names. These may not all be the same figure.

jonakr.en:
Jónakr is a king, Guðrún's third husband. After killing Atli she tried to drown herself, but the waves carried her to his land and he married her (Guðrúnarhvöt prose; Skáldskaparmál chapter 50). Their sons were Hamðir and Sörli, and Guðrún's daughter by Sigurðr, Svanhildr, was brought up at his court.

Brynhildr foretells this marriage before her death in Sigurðarkviða in skamma 62-63. In Guðrúnarhvöt 14 Guðrún recalls coming to a king's bed for the third time and bearing sons to be his heirs. When Svanhildr was put to death by Jörmunrekkr, Guðrún sent the "sons of Jónakr" to avenge her; in Hamðismál 25 the Gothic king has them stoned, since iron will not bite them. Snorri tells the same story in Skáldskaparmál chapters 50-51.

magni.en:
Magni ("might") is a son of Þórr; Snorri (Skáldskaparmál chapter 24) names his mother as the giantess Járnsaxa. When Þórr is pinned under the dead Hrungnir's leg, the three-night-old Magni lifts it off him and boasts he would have killed the giant with his fist; Þórr rewards him with Hrungnir's horse Gullfaxi.

Magni is one of the survivors of Ragnarök: with his brother Móði he will possess Mjöllnir in the renewed world (Vafþrúðnismál 51, quoted in Gylfaginning chapter 53). In Hárbarðsljóð (9, 53) Þórr names himself "Magni's father", and "father of Magni" is a kenning for Þórr (Skáldskaparmál chapter 11).

mani.en:
Máni ("Moon") is the moon personified, son of Mundilfari and brother of Sól, the sun. Gylfaginning (chapter 11) tells how Mundilfari named his two beautiful children after the moon and sun, and the gods, angered at his pride, set them in the sky: Máni steers the moon's course and governs its waxing and waning. Snorri adds that Máni took two children, Bil and Hjúki, up from the earth to follow him.

Skáldskaparmál chapter 34 lists "sister of Máni" among kennings for the sun and quotes a verse speaking of "grey-sarked Máni", and Reginsmál 23 calls the sun "the moon's bright sister". Some mentions gathered under this name are unrelated: in Háttatal and Skáldskaparmál chapter 76 the form Manar refers to the Isle of Man, and in Skáldskaparmál chapter 64 a verse is quoted from a skald named Máni; the index may mix them.

markus.en:
Markús Skeggjason was lawspeaker of Iceland in the late eleventh and early twelfth centuries and a skald, author of a poem on the Danish king Eiríkr the Good (Eiríksdrápa). Snorri quotes him several times in Skáldskaparmál.

His verses illustrate kennings for the sea and for ships ("Gylfi's land", "steed of the gunwale", chapter 64), poetic names for Christ as "King of the Heavens" (chapter 65, a verse on God's creation of earth and sky), and names for the sea, for generous rulers and for kings such as Yngvi in the heiti lists of chapters 76, 79 and 80.

menja.en:
Menja is a giantess who, with Fenja, is bought as a slave by the Danish king Fróði at the court of King Fjölnir in Sweden, and set to turn the magic mill Grotti, which grinds whatever its owner asks (Skáldskaparmál chapter 52; prose before Grottasöngr). Fróði allows them no rest, so they grind out an army against him: the sea-king Mýsingr kills Fróði, takes the mill and the women, and has them grind salt until his ship sinks, which is why the sea is salt.

Their work song is Grottasöngr, in which they recall their giant kin and warlike past (1, 4). Gold is therefore called Fróði's meal, and Menja's treasure appears as a gold kenning in Sigurðarkviða in skamma (52).

munin.en:
Muninn (memory, or mind) is one of the two ravens of Óðinn, with Huginn (thought). Gylfaginning chapter 38 says the ravens sit on Óðinn's shoulders and tell him all they see and hear; he sends them out at daybreak to fly over the world, and they come back at breakfast, which is why he is called the raven-god.

Grímnismál 20, quoted by Snorri, has Óðinn say that both fly each day over Miðgarðr, and that he fears for Huginn lest he not return, but fears more for Muninn. In Skáldskaparmál chapter 75 Muninn is among the names of the raven, and a verse speaks of "dark Muninn" drinking blood from wounds on the battlefield.

odrerir.en:
Óðrerir is, in Snorri's account, the kettle into which the dwarves Fjalarr and Galarr drained the blood of the wise Kvasir; mixed with honey in it and in the two vats Són and Boðn, the blood became the mead of poetry (Skáldskaparmál chapter 5).

The mead passed to the giant Suttungr, and Óðinn won it by sleeping three nights with Suttungr's daughter Gunnlöð, emptying Óðrerir with his first draught (Skáldskaparmál chapter 6). Hence poetry can be called "Óðrerir's sea" or the liquid of Óðrerir (chapter 10). In Hávamál the name seems rather to refer to the mead itself: Óðinn says that "Óðrerir" has now been brought up to the dwellings of men (107), and that he drank of the precious mead poured from Óðrerir after learning nine mighty songs (140). Snorri's identification of Óðrerir as the vessel may be his own interpretation.

ormarr.en:
Ormarr is the foster-father of Hervör, sister of King Angantýr, in Hlöðskviða (the battle of the Goths and Huns in Hervarar saga). The two hold a fortress on the border of Gotland when the Huns under Hlöðr and Humli come through Myrkviðr. Ormarr rides out to challenge the invaders to battle before the gate.

When Hervör falls in the fighting, Ormarr flees and rides day and night to Angantýr at Árheimar to bring the news in verse: Myrkviðr scorched, Goðþjóð drenched in blood, and Heiðrekr's daughter slain by the Huns (Hlöðskviða 19-21).

sigar.en:
Sigarr is a name borne by several legendary figures, gathered together in this index.

In Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar a Sigarr is Helgi's companion, who rides to fetch Sváfa to the dying Helgi and reports that he fell at Frekasteinn (stanzas 37 and 39). In Helgakviða Hundingsbana II 4 Hagall claims that the disguised Helgi is a king's daughter, "sister of Sigarr and Högni". Skáldskaparmál chapter 80 names a Sigarr as ancestor of the Siklingar, including the house of Siggeirr, Völsungr's son-in-law, and the Sigarr who hanged Hagbarðr. The Prologue (chapter 4) has a Sigarr as father of Svebdeg (Svipdagr) in Óðinn's Saxon line of descent. Guðrúnarkviða II 16 mentions Sigarr and Siggeirr among the figures Guðrún wove in tapestry, and a verse in Háttatal calls shields "Sigarr's walls".

thordr.en: Þórðr is the name of several skalds quoted in Skáldskaparmál, and this index entry gathers them. Þórðr Sjáreksson, an eleventh-century Icelandic poet, is quoted for kennings of Njörðr (chapter 13) and for the sea and ships (chapter 64). Þórðr Kolbeinsson, an Icelandic skald of the early eleventh century who praised Eiríkr jarl, is quoted in the heiti lists (chapters 67 and 70). Þórðr Mæraskáld appears in chapter 56 with a kenning for gold and silver, and a Þórðr without by-name in chapter 71. The entry should probably be split.

thrymheimr.en:
Þrymheimr ('home of din') is the mountain dwelling of the giant Þjazi and, after his death, of his daughter Skaði; Grímnismál (11) counts it as the sixth of the divine homes. Þjazi carries the captured Iðunn there (Skáldskaparmál chapter 2).

In Gylfaginning (chapter 23) Snorri tells that Skaði, married to Njörðr, wanted to live in her father's home, while Njörðr preferred his home by the sea, Nóatún. They agreed to spend nine nights in each in turn, but neither could bear the other's home, and Skaði went back to the mountains of Þrymheimr, where she travels on skis and hunts with a bow.

vali.en:
Váli, also called Áli, is a son of Óðinn and the giantess Rindr. Gylfaginning chapter 30 calls him bold in battle and a fine marksman. Well-known traditions (Völuspá, Baldrs draumar, Hyndluljóð 29) say he was born to avenge Baldr and killed Höðr when only one night old, and Snorri lists him among the survivors of Ragnarök who will live in the renewed world (Gylfaginning chapter 53).

The mentions grouped here are mostly of other men called Áli. Skáldskaparmál chapter 54 tells of King Áli of the Uppland, who fell fighting Aðils on the ice of Lake Vænir, and Kálfsvísa lists "Áli rode Hrafn" (Skáldskaparmál chapter 72). A kenning in chapter 45 uses "Áli of the rock" for a giant. Loki's son Áli or Váli, named in Skáldskaparmál chapter 23, is a separate figure. The index mixes these.

borghild.en:
Borghildr of Brálundr is the first wife of Sigmundr, son of Völsungr, and the mother of Helgi Hundingsbani (Helgakviða Hundingsbana I 1; prose of Helgakviða Hundingsbana II); the prose places her kingdom in Denmark.

In the short prose piece Frá dauða Sinfjötla, which precedes Grípisspá, she takes revenge on her stepson Sinfjötli, who had killed her brother in a rivalry over a woman: Sigmundr pays her compensation, but at the funeral feast she offers Sinfjötli a horn of poison three times until he drinks and dies. Sigmundr carries the body to a fjord, where a mysterious ferryman takes it and vanishes. Völsunga saga tells the story more fully and adds that Sigmundr then drove Borghildr away and she died soon after.

christ.en:
Christ (Kristr) appears in the Edda only in learned or Christian frames. In Skáldskaparmál (chapter 65) Snorri lists the ways skalds may periphrase him: maker of heaven and earth, of angels and of the sun, ruler of the world, of Jerusalem and the Greeks' land, king of monks and of the apostles; he quotes Christian skaldic verses as examples, including one by Einarr Skúlason, and in chapter 66 compares titles such as "King of Jerusalem".

In the prose before Gróttasöngr (Skáldskaparmál chapter 52), the peace of the legendary Danish king Fróði is dated to the time when Augustus established peace throughout the world and Christ was born.

egill.en:
Egill is the name of two minor figures in the Poetic Edda, sometimes thought to be the same. In Völundarkviða he is one of three brothers, sons of a king of the Finns, with Slagfiðr and Völundr. The opening prose tells how they lived in Úlfdalir and took three swan-maiden valkyries as wives, Egill marrying Ölrún; when the women flew away after seven years, Egill went east to look for her and Slagfiðr south, while Völundr stayed at home (stanzas 4-5).

In Hymiskviða 7 Þórr and Týr travel from Ásgarðr to "Egill's home" and leave Þórr's goats there before going on to Hymir; the poem says no more about him. Háttatal also names a verse-form "Egill's metre" (Egils háttr), which refers to a poet rather than either of these figures.

eldir.en:
Eldir ("fire-kindler") is a servant of the sea-giant Ægir. In the prose of Lokasenna and in Skáldskaparmál chapter 41, Ægir's two servants at his feast for the gods are Fimafengr and Eldir; Loki kills Fimafengr and is driven out.

Lokasenna opens with Loki returning and meeting Eldir outside the hall (stanzas 1-5). Eldir tells him that the gods talk of their weapons and prowess and that none of them is his friend, and warns him that slander may be turned back on him; Loki threatens him and goes in.

fjolnir.en:
Fjölnir is a legendary king of the Swedes at whose court the Danish king Fróði buys the giant slave women Fenja and Menja (Skáldskaparmál chapter 52; prose before Grottasöngr). In Ynglinga saga and Ynglingatal he is a son of Yngvi-Freyr who drowns in a vat of mead while visiting Fróði.

Fjölnir is also one of Óðinn's names: Óðinn lists it in Grímnismál (47), Snorri repeats it in Gylfaginning (chapters 3 and 20), and in Reginsmál (18) Óðinn, as the man on the mountain, calls himself Hnikarr, Fengr or Fjölnir. The index groups both uses here.

fridleifr.en:
Friðleifr is a legendary Danish king of the Skjöldung line, son of Skjöldr son of Óðinn and father of Fróði, in whose days the peace of Fróði prevailed. Snorri gives this genealogy in Skáldskaparmál chapter 52, at the start of the tale of the mill Grótti, and it is repeated in the prose introduction to Gróttasöngr. In the poem itself Fenja and Menja are held at the court of "Fróði, son of Friðleifr" (quoted in Skáldskaparmál chapter 52).

In the Prologue (chapter 3) Friðleifr (Fríallaf) appears in a different position, in the Trojan-derived pedigree as the father of Vóden, that is, Óðinn. Chapter 4 also mentions him in connection with Skjöldr's rule in Reiðgotaland. The index joins these two genealogical uses.

garmr.en:
Garmr is a monstrous hound bound at Gnipahellir, whose breaking loose signals the beginning of Ragnarök.

In Völuspá the refrain "Garmr howls loud before Gnipahellir, the fetters will burst and the wolf run free" recurs as the end of the world approaches (stanzas 44, 49 and 58 in Bellows' numbering). Grímnismál 44, quoted in Gylfaginning chapter 41, calls him the best of hounds, as Yggdrasill is best of trees and Sleipnir of horses. In Gylfaginning chapter 51 Snorri describes him as loosed from his bonds before Gnipahellir and as the worst of monsters; in the last battle he fights the god Týr, and each kills the other. Some scholars identify him with the wolf Fenrir, whom the Völuspá refrain may also refer to.

gjallarhorn.en:
Gjallarhorn ("resounding horn") is the horn of Heimdallr, watchman of the gods. Snorri says its blast is heard in all worlds (Gylfaginning chapter 27), and at the onset of Ragnarök Heimdallr blows it to wake the gods (Völuspá 46; Gylfaginning 51). Snorri also says (Gylfaginning 15) that Mímir drinks from his well out of the Gjallarhorn.

Some indexed mentions are only forms of Gjöll: the river and bridge on the road to Hel (Gylfaginning 49) and kennings in Forspjallsljóð (9, 16); the index may mix them.

gjukungar.en:
The Gjúkungar are the sons of King Gjúki: Gunnarr and Högni, with Gutthormr as their (step)brother. Snorri says they were also called Niflungar, so that gold can be called "the Niflungs' treasure" (Skáldskaparmál chapter 50).

In Skáldskaparmál chapter 48 Sigurðr rides with "the sons of Gjúki" to woo Brynhildr for Gunnarr, and in Sigurðarkviða in skamma 35 Brynhildr recalls that three kings came riding to her land. The prose of Dráp Niflunga tells how, after Sigurðr's and Brynhildr's deaths, Atli held the Gjúkungar responsible for his sister's death, and how the quarrel was settled by marrying Guðrún to Atli, which led to his invitation and the brothers' deaths.

glaumvor.en:
Glaumvör is Gunnarr's wife in Atlamál in grænlenzku. The prose of Dráp Niflunga says he married her after being refused Oddrún, Atli's sister.

When Atli's messengers come with their invitation, she welcomes the guests with Kostbera, Högni's wife (Atlamál 6). That night she tells Gunnarr her ominous dreams, of a gallows prepared for him, a sword drawn bloody from his garments, a river sweeping the hall, and dead women summoning him (21-28), but he explains them away. She also reproaches the messenger Vingi with the evil that may follow his visit (32).

gramr.en:
Gramr is Sigurðr's sword. In Skáldskaparmál (chapter 47) Reginn forges it so keen that it cuts through a tuft of wool drifting downstream onto its edge, and Sigurðr cleaves Reginn's anvil with it; with it he kills Fáfnir and then Reginn (Reginsmál prose; Fáfnismál 25). When Sigurðr rides through the flames in Gunnarr's shape, he lays Gramr between himself and Brynhildr in bed (Skáldskaparmál chapter 48), and when Gotthormr stabs him in his sleep, the dying Sigurðr hurls Gramr after him and cuts him in two (chapter 49).

Völsunga saga adds that Reginn made it from the pieces of Sigmundr's broken sword. The word gramr also means 'king', and the index may have caught that sense in the þula of chapter 80.

grotti.en:
Grótti is the magic hand-mill of the Danish king Fróði, which ground out whatever its turner asked for. Its two huge millstones were too heavy for anyone in Denmark to turn, so Fróði bought the giant maidens Fenja and Menja to work it (Skáldskaparmál chapter 52; prose of Gróttasöngr).

Fróði had them grind gold, peace and prosperity without rest. In Gróttasöngr the slave-women sing as they grind, recalling their giant origin and that the stone itself came out of the mountain because of them (stanza 10), and then grind out an army. The sea-king Mýsingr comes that night, kills Fróði and carries off the mill, which is how the peace of Fróði ended. Snorri adds that Mýsingr had them grind salt until the ship sank, which is why the sea is salt. Gold is therefore called "Fróði's meal". A verse quoted in Skáldskaparmál chapter 33 pictures the nine daughters of the sea turning a "Grótti of the skerries" that once ground Amlóði's meal; Háttatal (chapter 2) also uses Grótti in a gold-kenning.

gulltoppr.en:
Gulltoppr ("golden forelock") is the horse of the god Heimdallr (Gylfaginning chapter 27; Skáldskaparmál chapter 15).

It is named among the horses the Æsir ride each day over Bifröst to their court at the well of Urðr (Grímnismál 30; Gylfaginning chapter 15), and Heimdallr rides it to Baldr's funeral (Gylfaginning chapter 49). It also appears in the þulur (verse lists of names) of horses, such as the Þorgrímsþula quoted in Skáldskaparmál chapter 72.

halfsrekkar.en:
The Hálfsrekkar ("Hálfr's champions") are the warrior band of the legendary King Hálfr, heroes of Hálfs saga ok Hálfsrekka. In the prose of Hálfsrekkaljóð they show their loyalty in a storm, each offering to go overboard for his comrade.

At King Ásmundr's feast they fall asleep from the strong drink and Ásmundr sets fire to the hall; one after another they wake and speak verses (16-18), saying their journey "will ever be remembered while mankind lives". They break out through the wall, but Hálfr falls, and the part of the band left with the ships joins the battle, which lasts until nightfall, when Innsteinn falls as well. Snorri derives the poetic word rekkar ("warriors") from the name of Hálfr's men (Skáldskaparmál chapter 81).

jord.en:
Jörð ("Earth") is a giantess and goddess, the earth personified, mother of Þórr by Óðinn. Gylfaginning (chapter 36) counts her among the Ásynjur, and Skáldskaparmál chapter 32 gives kennings for the earth that make her daughter of Ónarr and of Nótt (Night), Óðinn's bride and co-wife of Frigg, Rindr and Gunnlöð.

Þórr is regularly called "Jörð's son" (Skáldskaparmál chapter 11; Þrymskviða 1). Poetry also knows her as Hlóðyn and Fjörgyn: in Völuspá 56, quoted in Gylfaginning chapter 51, "Hlóðyn's son" and "Fjörgyn's son" go out to fight the serpent at Ragnarök. Correspondingly, Skáldskaparmál chapter 27 calls Frigg the co-wife of Jörð.

kormakr.en:
Kormákr Ögmundarson is a tenth-century Icelandic skald, hero of Kormáks saga, who composed a poem in honour of Sigurðr jarl of Hlaðir (Sigurðardrápa). Snorri quotes him several times in Skáldskaparmál.

In chapter 9 his verses supply kennings and allusions for Óðinn: "Óðinn wrought charms on Rindr" and Hroptr (Óðinn) bearing Gungnir. Elsewhere he is cited for poetic words for trees and beams (chapter 59), a sword as "Óðinn's fire" (chapter 61), kennings for men by their kindred (chapter 66), and in the heiti lists (chapters 67-68).

kvasir.en:
Kvasir is a being of surpassing wisdom whom the gods make from the spittle that the Æsir and Vanir spat into a vat to seal their peace (Skáldskaparmál chapter 5). He travels the world teaching, until the dwarves Fjalar and Galarr kill him and mix his blood with honey, making the mead that turns whoever drinks it into a poet or a scholar. The mead passes to the giant Suttungr and is won by Óðinn, and poetry is therefore called Kvasir's blood (chapter 10).

In Gylfaginning (chapter 50), however, Kvasir is alive and called the wisest: he recognises in the ashes of a burnt net how Loki, hiding in the river as a salmon, may be caught. Ynglinga saga gives yet another account, in which Kvasir is the wisest of the Vanir, sent to the Æsir as a hostage.

svipdagr.en:
Svipdagr is the hero of Fjölsvinnsmál and, by general agreement, of Grógaldr. In Fjölsvinnsmál he comes to the walled hall of Menglöð under a false name and questions the giant watchman Fjölsviðr about the hall, its gate and its guard-dogs. He learns that no one but Svipdagr may sleep in Menglöð's arms (stanza 42), reveals himself as "Svipdagr, Sólbjartr's son" (stanza 47), and the gates open to him. In Grógaldr a young man raises his dead mother Gróa for protective spells before setting out to woo Menglöð; he is not named there, but the two poems are usually read together as one story.

The name is also borne by other figures. Svipdagr is one of the berserks Hrólfr kraki sends to King Aðils (Skáldskaparmál chapter 54), and the Prologue (chapter 4) has a Svebdeg or Svipdagr in the Saxon royal genealogy descended from Óðinn. The index joins these.

vimur.en:
Vimur is a river in giant-land, the greatest of all rivers according to Snorri, which Þórr wades on his way to the giant Geirröðr (Skáldskaparmál chapter 26).

Girded with his belt of strength and leaning on the staff he had from the giantess Gríðr, with Loki clinging behind, Þórr struggles through the current as the river rises up to his shoulders. He speaks a verse commanding Vimur not to rise, for his divine strength will rise as high as heaven, and then sees Geirröðr's daughter Gjálp standing astride the river and making it swell; he hits her with a stone and pulls himself out. Þórr is therefore called "the wader of Vimur" in skaldic kennings (Skáldskaparmál chapter 11).

borr.en:
Borr (Burr) is the son of Búri, the first being licked out of the ice by the cow Auðhumla. He marries Bestla, daughter of the giant Bölþorn, and their sons are Óðinn, Vili and Vé (Gylfaginning chapter 6).

He is known almost only through his sons. "The sons of Borr" kill the giant Ymir, drowning the frost-giants in his blood, and make the world from his body (Gylfaginning 7-8); in Völuspá 4 "Burr's sons" raise the land and make Miðgarðr. Óðinn is accordingly "Burr's heir" in Völuspá in skamma (2) and "son of Borr" in a skaldic verse quoted in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 9). Though tagged as a giant here, the sources do not call him one: he is the ancestor of the gods, although his wife is a giantess.

brisingamen.en:
Brísingamen ("necklace of the Brísingar") is Freyja's necklace. Gylfaginning (chapter 35) simply states that she owns it.

In Þrymskviða, when Loki asks Freyja to marry the giant Þrymr so that Þórr can get his hammer back, she snorts so angrily that the necklace bursts (stanza 13); Heimdallr then proposes that Þórr be dressed as the bride and wear the necklace (15, 19). Skáldskaparmál refers to another myth: Heimdallr fought Loki at Vágasker and Singasteinn for the necklace, both in the form of seals, as told in Úlfr Uggason's Húsdrápa (chapter 15), and Loki is called "thief of Brísingamen" (chapter 23). A later prose tale, Sörla þáttr, tells how Freyja obtained it from four dwarves and how Loki stole it.

dagr.en:
Dagr ("day") is the personified day. In Gylfaginning chapter 10 he is the son of Nótt (Night) and Dellingr, of the race of the Æsir, bright and fair like his father. Óðinn gives Nótt and Dagr each a horse and chariot to ride around the earth; Dagr's horse is Skinfaxi (Sheen-mane), whose mane lights air and earth.

Vafþrúðnismál 25 also names Dellingr as the father of Day, and Skáldskaparmál chapter 32 gives the earth as "sister of Auðr and Dagr". The name is also borne by Dagr, son of Hálfdan the Old and ancestor of the Döglingar (Skáldskaparmál chapter 80); the index may mix them.

dagr-hognason.en:
Dagr is the son of King Högni and brother of Sigrún and Bragi in Helgakviða Hundingsbana II. At the battle of Frekasteinn, where Helgi Hundingsbani defeats the sons of Granmarr and their allies, Högni and Bragi fall, but Dagr is given quarter and swears oaths to the Völsungar (prose).

Seeking vengeance for his father, he later sacrifices to Óðinn, who lends him his spear. With it Dagr kills Helgi, his brother-in-law, at Fjöturlundr and rides to Sevafjöll to tell Sigrún, who curses him for breaking his oaths (prose and following stanzas).

fjalar.en:
Fjalarr is the name of several figures. The dwarf Fjalarr and his brother Galarr murdered the wise Kvasir and brewed the mead of poetry from his blood; they then drowned the giant Gillingr and killed his wife, so that Suttungr took the mead from them as compensation (Skáldskaparmál chapter 5). A dwarf Fjalarr also stands in the dwarf list of Völuspá 16.

Other bearers of the name: in Völuspá 42 Fjalarr is the red cock that crows over the giants' warden Eggþér before Ragnarök. In Hávamál 14 the speaker (Óðinn) recalls being drunk "with Fjalarr wise", usually taken to refer to Suttungr. In Hárbarðsljóð 26 Hárbarðr mocks Þórr for hiding in a glove, which points to the giant Skrýmir, so the name there is used for him. All mentions are flagged uncertain, and the index mixes these figures.

fjorgyn.en:
Fjörgyn is a name for the earth personified, the mother of Þórr, otherwise called Jörð. Völuspá 56 calls Þórr "Fjörgyn's son" at his last fight with the serpent, and in Hárbarðsljóð 56 the ferryman tells Þórr that his mother Fjörgyn will find him on the road home. Skáldskaparmál chapter 70 lists Fjörgyn among the poetic words for the earth.

A masculine form, Fjörgynn, is the name of Frigg's father: Skáldskaparmál chapter 27 calls Frigg "daughter of Fjörgynn", and Loki addresses her as "Fjörgynn's maid" in Lokasenna 26 (Bellows translates "Fjorgyn's wife").
