The two figures are distinct, though their names are related; the index mixes them.

frekasteinn.en:
Frekasteinn ("wolf's rock") is a battle site in the Helgi poems. In Helgakviða Hundingsbana I and II it is where Helgi Hundingsbani fights the sons of Granmarr, Höðbroddr's kin, to win Sigrún: Guðmundr threatens to feed the ravens there (Helgakviða Hundingsbana I 44), and Helgi is foremost in the battle (53). In Helgakviða Hundingsbana II Sigrún's father Högni and her brother Bragi fall there (prose and 20-21).

In Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar (39) the same name marks the place where the other Helgi, Hjörvarðr's son, falls in battle against Álfr. The name may be a conventional heroic battlefield rather than a real place.

fulla.en:
Fulla is a goddess, the servant and confidante of Frigg. Gylfaginning (chapter 35) describes her as a maiden with loose hair and a gold band about her head who carries Frigg's casket, looks after her shoes and shares her secrets; Frigg is accordingly called "mistress of Fulla" (Skáldskaparmál chapter 27). She is counted among the goddesses at Ægir's feast (Skáldskaparmál chapter 1).

In the prose of Grímnismál Frigg sends Fulla to warn King Geirröðr against a wizard, which leads him to torture the disguised Óðinn. In Gylfaginning's story of Baldr's death Nanna sends a gold ring from Hel to Fulla. Gold is called "Fulla's snood" or headband (Skáldskaparmál chapters 40, 44, the latter quoting Eyvindr skáldaspillir).

ginnungagap.en:
Ginnungagap (the "yawning void") is the primeval emptiness that existed before the world. In Gylfaginning chapters 4-5 it lies between icy Niflheimr in the north and burning Múspellsheimr in the south. The rivers Élivágar freeze into rime in its northern part, while its southern part is lit by sparks; where heat meets rime the drops quicken into life, and the giant Ymir is formed. Its middle is mild as windless air.

After killing Ymir, the sons of Borr carry him into the middle of Ginnungagap and make the earth, sea and mountains from his body (chapter 8). One root of Yggdrasill stands among the frost giants where Ginnungagap once was (chapter 15). Snorri's account rests on Völuspá, which says "there was a yawning void" before the world.

gjalp.en:
Gjálp is a giantess, daughter of Geirröðr and sister of Greip. In Snorri's account of Þórr's journey to Geirröðr (Skáldskaparmál chapter 26) she stands astride a river with one foot on each side and makes it swell to drown Þórr, who stops her with a stone. At Geirröðr's house she and Greip lift Þórr's chair toward the roof to crush him, but he pushes against the rafters with Gríðr's staff and breaks both their backs. The episode is also told in Eddubrot, and a skaldic verse praises Þórr for standing on lifeless Gjálp (Skáldskaparmál chapter 11).

A Gjálp is also named among the nine giantess mothers of Heimdallr in Völuspá in skamma (8); whether she is the same figure is unclear.

glasir.en:
Glasir is a grove (or tree) of golden leaves standing before the doors of Valhöll in Ásgarðr. Skáldskaparmál chapter 42 explains that its foliage is all of red gold and quotes the lines "Glasir stands with golden leafage before the High God's halls" (also preserved among the Eddic fragments).

Its main use is in poetry: because of this tree, gold can be called "Glasir's needles" or "leaves" (Skáldskaparmál chapter 40). A verse in Skáldskaparmál chapter 56 piles up gold-kennings, among them "Glasir's bright needles", "Fenja's labour" and "Grani's burden".

groa.en:
Gróa is a wise woman (völva) who appears in two unrelated contexts. In Skáldskaparmál chapter 25 she is the wife of Aurvandill the Bold; after Þórr's duel with Hrungnir she sings spells over him to loosen the piece of whetstone lodged in his head. When Þórr, to reward her, tells how he carried Aurvandill out of giant-land in a basket and made a star of his frozen toe, she forgets her spells for joy, so that the stone stays in his head.

In Grógaldr ("Gróa's spell"), the dead Gróa is the mother of Svipdagr, who wakes her at her grave to ask for help on a dangerous quest; she sings him a series of protective charms, the first of which "Rani taught to Rind" (stanza 6). Whether the two Gróas were thought of as the same figure is uncertain.

gungnir.en:
Gungnir is Óðinn's spear. Snorri (Skáldskaparmál chapter 43) tells that it was made by the dwarfs called Ívaldi's sons, together with Sif's golden hair and the ship Skíðblaðnir, after Loki had cut off Sif's hair; Loki presents it to Óðinn, saying the spear never stops in its thrust.

At Ragnarök Óðinn rides out with his golden helmet and Gungnir against Fenrir (Gylfaginning chapter 51). Sigrdrífumál (17) lists "Gungnir's point" among the places where runes were cut. A skaldic verse quoted in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 9) says that "Hroptr [Óðinn] bore Gungnir", and in Snorri's Háttatal battle is "the clash of Gungnir".

hagall.en:
Hagall is the foster-father of Helgi Hundingsbani in the prose and verse of Helgakviða Hundingsbana II; his son is Hámall.

The opening prose tells how Helgi went in disguise to spy at King Hundingr's court. When Hundingr's men came to Hagall's house looking for him, Helgi put on a bondmaid's clothes and worked at the quern. The evil-minded Blindr remarks on the bright eyes of "Hagall's bondmaid" and the splintering millstones (stanza 2), but Hagall explains that she is a captive king's daughter who once rode through the clouds and fought like a warrior, "sister of Sigarr and Högni" (4), and Helgi escapes. Hámall is named again in stanza 6, where Helgi says the ship by the shore is Hámall's.

heimir.en:
Heimir is Brynhildr's foster-father, living at Hlymdalir. In Grípisspá Grípir tells Sigurðr of the beautiful maid in Heimir's home, Buðli's daughter Brynhildr, whom Heimir fosters, and foretells the grief she will bring him (27-29, 39); Grípisspá 31 calls her "Heimir's fosterling".

According to Skáldskaparmál chapter 51, Áslaug, Sigurðr's daughter, was brought up with Heimir in Hlymdalir. His story is told more fully in the Völsunga saga, where he is married to Brynhildr's sister Bekkhildr and later raises Áslaug.

hjordis.en: Hjördís is the daughter of King Eylimi, the last wife of Sigmundr and the mother of Sigurðr. According to the prose Frá dauða Sinfjötla, Sigmundr marries her in the land of the Franks; after he falls fighting the sons of Hundingr she marries Álfr, son of King Hjálprekr, at whose court Sigurðr grows up. Her brother is the wise seer Grípir, to whom Sigurðr names his parents (Grípisspá prose and 3). Snorri also names her as Sigurðr's mother (Skáldskaparmál chapter 47). Hyndluljóð (26) lists her among Óttarr's ancestors but makes her of Hrauðungr's line.

hornklofi.en:
Þorbjörn hornklofi was a Norwegian skald of the late ninth and early tenth centuries and a court poet of King Haraldr hárfagri. His chief works are Glymdrápa, on Haraldr's battles, and Haraldskvæði (also called Hrafnsmál), partly a dialogue between a valkyrie and a raven about the king and his warriors.

Snorri quotes him in Skáldskaparmál for kennings of battle (chapter 60) and of ships as horses of the sea (chapter 64), and for names of the sea (chapter 76). The two verses ascribed to "Þorbjörn dísarskáld" in chapter 11, on Þórr's killing of giants and giantesses, belong to a different poet; the index wrongly joins them to Hornklofi.

humli.en:
Humli is a legendary king of the Huns in Hervarar saga and the poem embedded in it, Hlöðskviða ("The Battle of the Goths and Huns"). Hlöðskviða 1 lists him among ancient rulers: Humli over the Huns, Angantýr over the Goths, and so on.

He is the mother's father of Hlöðr, half-brother of King Angantýr. When Hlöðr comes to him angry at being offered only a bastard's share of their father Heiðrekr's inheritance and called a slave-woman's son, Humli takes up his cause, and the two raise so great an army that Húnaland is emptied of fighting men. They invade the land of the Goths, defeating and killing Hervör, Angantýr's sister, at her fortress. When the Gothic messenger Gizurr insults them, Humli forbids Hlöðr to seize him, saying that messengers who travel alone must not be harmed (Hlöðskviða 29).

hvergelmir.en:
Hvergelmir ("roaring cauldron") is the spring from which all rivers flow. Snorri places it in the middle of Niflheimr before the earth was shaped, the source of the rivers listed there, with Gjöll next to Hel's gate (Gylfaginning chapter 4).

It lies under the root of Yggdrasill that stands over Niflheimr, where Níðhöggr gnaws the root (Gylfaginning 15-16). In Grímnismál 26 the hart Eikþyrnir, standing on Valhöll, drips moisture from his horns into Hvergelmir, and from there the rivers run; Snorri repeats this with a long list of river names (Gylfaginning 39). In his account of the afterlife (Gylfaginning 52) Snorri says it is "worst in Hvergelmir", where Níðhöggr torments the dead.

hyndla.en:
Hyndla ("little dog") is the giantess of Hyndluljóð, who lives in a cave and rides a wolf. Freyja wakes her, calls her "sister" and asks her to ride with her to Valhöll (stanza 1), letting one of her wolves run beside Freyja's boar (5).

Hyndla mocks Freyja for travelling with her lover Óttarr in boar form (Freyja denies it, stanza 7), but then recites Óttarr's ancestry at length (12 onwards), passing through the great legendary families and on to the gods and giants (30, 33, the section often called Völuspá in skamma). At the end she is unwilling to give Óttarr the memory-ale and insults Freyja; when Freyja threatens to ring her with fire, she hands it over, but with a curse.

kostbera.en:
Kostbera is Högni's wife in Atlamál in grænlenzku. She welcomes Atli's messengers with Glaumvör, Gunnarr's wife (Atlamál 6). Skilled in runes, she reads the warning runes Guðrún sent by firelight but finds them garbled, since the messenger Vingi had altered them (9).

That night she warns Högni that they will meet no friendly welcome, and tells him her dreams of a bear breaking into the hall and an eagle spattering them with blood, which she takes for Atli's spirit (14, 17, 19); Högni dismisses them. The prose of Dráp Niflunga names her among the Gjúkungs' kin.

menglodr.en:
Menglöð is the maiden whom the hero Svipdagr seeks in Grógaldr and Fjölsvinnsmál, two poems often read together as Svipdagsmál. In Grógaldr (3) his stepmother sends him on the seemingly hopeless quest to win her, and he calls up his dead mother Gróa for protective spells.

In Fjölsvinnsmál she rules a rich hall guarded by the watchman Fjölsviðr, who names her as the daughter of the son of Svafrþorinn (8) and says that only Svipdagr may enter. When Svipdagr reveals his name, the gates open and the watchman announces him (43-44); Menglöð first threatens him if he lies, then welcomes him as the lover she has long awaited (45-48).

mist.en:
Mist is a valkyrie, named in Grímnismál 36 among the valkyries who bring the horn of drink to Óðinn and serve ale to the einherjar in Valhöll ("Hrist and Mist bring the horn at my will"). Snorri quotes the same list in Gylfaginning chapter 36.

Beyond this list Mist appears only in poetic diction, where a valkyrie's name stands for battle or the warrior's world. In Háttatal (chapters 2 and 3) a sword is "Mist's frost" or one of "Mist's leeks", and Helgakviða Hundingsbana I 47 speaks of "Mist's horse".

modi.en:
Móði ("wrath") is a son of Þórr and brother of Magni (Skáldskaparmál chapter 11, where Þórr is called "father of Magni and Móði and Þrúðr").

He is one of the gods who will survive Ragnarök: with Magni he will inherit his father's hammer Mjöllnir (Vafþrúðnismál 51, quoted in Gylfaginning chapter 53). Hymiskviða 34 calls Þórr "the father of Móði". Little else is told of him. Other matches under this name are unrelated: Móda in the euhemeristic genealogy of the Prologue (chapter 3), the horse Móðnir in the þulur, and a word in Háttatal.

myrkvidr.en:
Myrkviðr ("dark wood", Mirkwood) is a great forest of heroic legend, imagined as a frontier between peoples. In Hlöðskviða it divides the lands of the Huns and the Goths; Hlöðr demands half of it as part of his inheritance (10), the Hunnish army rides through it, and Ormarr reports its heath scorched by battle (19).

It also appears in the mythological poems: in Lokasenna (42) Loki tells Freyr he will be weaponless "when Muspell's sons ride through Myrkviðr", and the swan-maidens of Völundarkviða fly in through it from the south. In Atlakviða (5) it is among the treasures and lands Atli's messenger offers Gunnarr, and in Helgakviða Hundingsbana I (51) Höðbroddr sends riders there to gather his forces.

naglfar.en:
Naglfar is the ship that sails at Ragnarök. Gylfaginning (chapter 43) calls it the largest of ships and says it belongs to Múspell.

In the Ragnarök narrative of chapter 51 Snorri explains that it is made of dead men's nails, so a man who dies with uncut nails adds material to it, which gods and men wish to be finished as late as possible; when the sea floods the land the ship is set loose and floats, steered by the giant Hrymr. Snorri quotes Völuspá 50, where Hrymr comes from the east and "Naglfar is loosed". Völuspá itself does not say Hrymr steers Naglfar; in the next stanza another ship comes, with the people of Múspell (or of Hel, in some editions) and Loki at the helm, so Snorri's arrangement may combine the two.

niflheim.en:
Niflheimr ("mist world") is the cold, dark world of the north in Snorri's cosmology. Gylfaginning chapter 4 says it was made many ages before the earth, and in its midst is the spring Hvergelmir, from which flow many rivers. In chapter 5 cold and all terrible things come out of Niflheimr, meeting the heat of Múspellsheimr in Ginnungagap.

One root of Yggdrasill stands over Niflheimr, above Hvergelmir, where Níðhöggr gnaws it (chapter 15). Óðinn casts Hel into Niflheimr and gives her power over the dead who die of sickness and old age (chapter 34), and in chapter 42 Þórr sends the giant builder of Ásgarðr's wall down under Niflhel. The older poems do not use Niflheimr as a primeval world; there the related Niflhel is a place of the dead. The late Hrafnagaldr Óðins (26) names Niflheimr in the north.

sigyn.en: Sigyn is the wife of Loki and is counted among the goddesses (Skáldskaparmál chapter 1); their son is Nari or Narfi (Gylfaginning chapter 33). She is remembered for her faithfulness during Loki's punishment: when the gods have bound him and Skaði has fastened a venomous snake above his face, Sigyn stands beside him holding a bowl to catch the poison, and when she goes to empty it the drops fall on Loki, whose writhing shakes the earth (Gylfaginning chapter 50; prose at the end of Lokasenna). Völuspá (35) shows her sitting, joyless, beside her bound husband, and kennings call Loki Sigyn's husband (Skáldskaparmál chapter 23).

svafnir.en:
Sváfnir is a legendary king, father of Sigrlinn, the mother of Helgi Hjörvarðsson. In the opening prose and first stanza of Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar King Hjörvarðr learns that Sváfnir's daughter is the fairest woman. Sváfnir is later killed and his land, Sváfaland, burned by Hróðmarr, a rival suitor.

The same name is borne by quite different beings: Sváfnir is one of the serpents gnawing at the roots of Yggdrasill (Grímnismál 34; Gylfaginning chapter 16; the serpent-names in Skáldskaparmál chapter 73), and one of Óðinn's names (Grímnismál 54). All mentions are flagged uncertain, and the index mixes these figures.

thjodrekr.en:
Þjóðrekr is the legendary form of Theoderic the Great, king of the Ostrogoths, who is known in German tradition as Dietrich von Bern; in the Eddic poems he appears as a guest at the court of Atli. Guðrúnarkviða III 3 calls him "Þjóðmarr's son".

The prose before Guðrúnarkviða II says that Þjóðrekr, having lost most of his men, was staying with Atli, and that he and Guðrún told each other their griefs; the poem is her account of her sorrows. In Guðrúnarkviða III Atli's former concubine Herkja accuses Guðrún of lying with Þjóðrekr. Guðrún swears her innocence, pointing out that he came with thirty warriors and none of them survive (stanza 5), and clears herself by the ordeal of the boiling kettle, from which she brings up the stones unharmed; Herkja, made to do the same, is scalded and drowned in a bog.

thrudr.en:
Þrúðr ("strength") is the daughter of Þórr and Sif. Snorri lists "father of Þrúðr" among the kennings for Þórr and "mother of Þrúðr" for Sif (Skáldskaparmál chapters 11 and 29), and a skaldic verse on Þórr's fishing calls him "Þrúðr's father" (chapter 11). Bragi's Ragnarsdrápa, quoted in chapter 61, calls the giant Hrungnir "Þrúðr's thief", alluding to a lost story in which he carried her off.

Þrúðr is also the name of a valkyrie in the list in Grímnismál 36 (quoted in Gylfaginning chapter 36); whether this is the same figure is unclear, and the index includes both.

vingi.en:
Vingi is King Atli's messenger in Atlamál, sent to invite Gunnarr and Högni to his court. Guðrún, suspecting treachery, carves runes to warn her brothers, but Vingi alters them before delivering the message (stanza 4).

At the Gjúkungar's home Gunnarr's wife Glaumvör voices her distrust (32), and Vingi swears that giants may take him and the gallows have him if he is lying (33). When they reach Atli's court he reveals the plot and threatens to hang them (39), and the brothers kill him with their axes (41). The prose of Dráp Niflunga names the messenger as "Vingi or Knéfröðr"; in Atlakviða he is called Knéfröðr.

annar.en:
Annarr or Ónarr is the second husband of Nótt (Night) in Gylfaginning chapter 10, after Naglfari and before Dellingr; their daughter is Jörð (Earth), Þórr's mother.

He appears mainly through his daughter: in Skáldskaparmál chapter 32 the earth is called "daughter of Ónarr", and a skaldic verse by Hallfreðr vandræðaskáld there (repeated in chapter 66) says the ruler was to wed "the land, sole daughter of Ónarr". The dwarf named Ónarr in the dwarf list of Völuspá 11 is a different figure; the index may mix them.

bil.en:
Bil is one of two children, with Hjúki, whom Máni (the Moon) took up from the earth as they came from the well Byrgir carrying the pail Sægr on the pole Simul; their father is Viðfinnr, and they follow the Moon, as can be seen from the earth (Gylfaginning chapter 11). Snorri later counts Bil, with Sól, among the goddesses (Gylfaginning chapter 35).

Otherwise her name serves mainly as a base word in kennings for a woman, as in Oddrúnargrátr (33) and skaldic verse quoted in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 58).

bodn.en:
Boðn is one of the three vessels that hold the mead of poetry, the others being the kettle Óðrerir and the vat Són. In Skáldskaparmál chapter 5 the dwarfs Fjalarr and Galarr kill Kvasir and let his blood run into the three vessels; mixed with honey, it becomes the mead that makes whoever drinks it a poet or scholar.

In chapter 6 Óðinn, lying three nights with Gunnlöð, is allowed three draughts and empties one vessel with each, Boðn with the second. Because of this, poetry can be called the liquid or "wave" of Boðn, a kenning listed in chapter 10 and illustrated there by a verse beginning "Now that which Boðn's billow bodes forth will straight be uttered".

borgny.en:
Borgný is the daughter of King Heiðrekr, known only from Oddrúnargrátr ("Oddrún's lament").

According to the prose and opening stanzas, she had a secret lover, Vilmundr, and could not give birth to her child until Oddrún, Atli's sister, came to her and chanted powerful charms at her knees (stanzas 4-7); she then bore twins, a boy and a girl. When Borgný reproaches her helper as harsh and witless in her words (11), Oddrún replies by telling the story of her own unhappy love for Gunnarr and of the Gjúkungs' death at Atli's court, which forms the bulk of the poem.

byleistr.en:
Býleistr is a brother of Loki, sons of the giant Fárbauti and Laufey; their third brother is Helblindi (Gylfaginning chapter 33; Skáldskaparmál chapter 23). Nothing is told of him apart from this relationship.

He survives mainly in the phrase "brother of Býleistr" for Loki: in Völuspá 51 (quoted in Gylfaginning 51), where Loki's brother sails with the hosts of destruction at Ragnarök, and in Völuspá in skamma (11), on Loki as father of monsters.

forseti.en:
Forseti is a god, son of Baldr and Nanna. Gylfaginning (chapter 32) says he owns the hall Glitnir in heaven, and all who bring disputes to him go away reconciled, so that his is the best court of judgment among gods and men; Snorri supports this with Grímnismál 15, which describes Glitnir's golden pillars and silver roof.

Skáldskaparmál names him among the twelve Æsir sitting as judges at the feast (chapter 1) and calls Baldr "father of Forseti" (chapter 12). No myths about him survive. A god Fosite worshipped by the Frisians, known from early medieval sources, is often compared with him.

frankland.en:
Frakkland is the land of the Franks, in the Eddas chiefly the homeland of the Völsungar. In the Prologue (chapter 4) Óðinn's son Sigi, ancestor of the Völsungar, rules there, and Skáldskaparmál chapter 80 says the Völsungar descend from Völsungr in the land of the Franks.

The prose introduction to Grípisspá (in the Frá dauða Sinfjötla section) calls Sigmundr a king in Frankland, and in the prose of Sigrdrífumál Sigurðr rides up onto Hindarfjall and turns south towards Frankland before finding the sleeping valkyrie.

gilling.en: Gillingr is a giant, father of Suttungr, in Snorri's account of the origin of the mead of poetry. After killing Kvasir, the dwarves Fjalar and Galarr invite Gillingr and his wife to visit them; they take him out rowing and capsize the boat so that he drowns, and then kill his wife by dropping a millstone on her head because her weeping annoys them (Skáldskaparmál chapter 5). Suttungr avenges his father by setting the dwarves on a skerry covered at high tide until they give him the mead in compensation. Poetry is therefore called Gillingr's compensation in skaldic verse (chapter 10).

gimle.en:
Gimlé is the hall or place of the righteous after the end of the world, fairer than the sun and roofed with gold. Völuspá 64 tells how, after Ragnarök, the seeress sees a gold-roofed hall standing on Gimlé, where worthy lords will dwell in lasting happiness.

Snorri uses it three times in Gylfaginning. In chapter 3 the righteous go after death to Gimlé (or Vingólf), and the wicked to Hel and Niflhel. In chapter 17 Gimlé is the fairest hall, at the southern end of heaven, which will stand when heaven and earth have passed away. In chapter 52, after Ragnarök, it will be best to be in Gimlé. Snorri's placing of Gimlé in heaven goes beyond what Völuspá says.

gleipnir.en:
Gleipnir is the fetter with which the gods finally bound the wolf Fenrir (Gylfaginning chapter 34). When Fenrir had broken the iron fetters Læðingr and Drómi, Óðinn sent Skírnir to dwarves in the land of the dark elves, who made Gleipnir out of six things: the sound of a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish and the spittle of a bird. Snorri has Hárr point out that none of these things is to be found in the world. The fetter was smooth and soft as a silk ribbon, yet very strong.

Suspicious of so slight a band, Fenrir agreed to be bound only if one of the gods put a hand in his mouth as a pledge; Týr did so, and when the wolf could not break free he bit off Týr's hand (Gylfaginning chapters 25 and 34). A verse version of the list, in the Eddubrot section, has "milk of birds" in place of the spittle.

gnipahellir.en:
Gnipahellir ("overhanging cave") is the cave before which the hound Garmr is bound. In the refrain of Völuspá (44, 49, 54, 58) Garmr "howls loud before Gnipahellir", the fetter breaks and the wolf runs free, a sign that Ragnarök has come.

Snorri (Gylfaginning chapter 51) says that the dog Garmr, bound before Gnipahellir, will break loose at Ragnarök, fight Týr, and that each will kill the other. The cave is often thought of as an entrance to the underworld, but the sources say no more about it.

gondul.en:
Göndul is a valkyrie. She appears in the list of valkyries in Völuspá 30 and, with Skögul, in the opening of Eyvindr skáldaspillir's Hákonarmál, quoted in Skáldskaparmál chapter 9, where Óðinn sends the two to choose which king of Yngvi's kin should come to Valhöll.

Like other valkyrie names, hers is used in battle kennings: Skáldskaparmál chapter 60 quotes "the clash of Göndul" and "Göndul's storm-wind" for battle, and Háttatal speaks of "Göndul's gale".

gridarvolr.en:
Gríðarvölr ("Gríðr's staff") is the staff that the giantess Gríðr, mother of Víðarr, lends to Þórr, along with a girdle of strength and iron gloves, before his visit to the giant Geirrøðr (Skáldskaparmál chapter 26).

Þórr braces himself with it against the current while wading the river Vimur, which Geirrøðr's daughter Gjálp makes swell. At Geirrøðr's court, when the chair he sits on rises towards the roof, he thrusts the staff against the rafters and pushes down, breaking the backs of Geirrøðr's daughters Gjálp and Greip (chapter 26; the same story in the Eddubrot fragments).

gullinbursti.en:
Gullinbursti ('golden bristles') is the boar of Freyr. Snorri tells that the dwarf Brokkr's brother made it in the smithing wager with Loki, along with Óðinn's ring Draupnir and Þórr's hammer Mjöllnir: it runs through air and sea better than any horse, and its bristles shine so that it is never dark where it goes (Skáldskaparmál chapter 43). Freyr drives in a chariot drawn by it to Baldr's funeral (Gylfaginning chapter 49), and it is also called Slíðrugtanni, 'fearful tusk' (Skáldskaparmál chapter 14).

In Hyndluljóð (7) the shining boar with golden bristles that Freyja rides is called Hildisvíni and is said to have been made by other dwarves; Hyndla takes it to be Óttarr in disguise. The index links that stanza here, but it concerns a different animal.

halfdan.en:
Hálfdan is a name borne by several legendary kings. Skáldskaparmál chapter 80 tells of Hálfdan the Old, the most famous of kings. At a midwinter sacrifice he asked to live three hundred years, and was told instead that for three hundred years there would be no one in his line who was not renowned. He killed King Sigtryggr in single combat and married Alvig the Wise.

He had eighteen sons, born in two sets of nine. The names of the first nine became poetic words for king, and the second nine founded the great royal families: Hildir of the Hildings, Nefir of the Niflungs, Auði of the Ödlungs, Yngvi of the Ynglings, Dagr of the Döglings, Bragi of the Bragnings, Buðli of the Buðlungs, and Lofði of the Lofðungs. In Gróttasöngr 22 another Hálfdan, the Danish Skjöldung, is meant: "Yrsa's son, Hálfdan's kinsman" (Hrólfr kraki) will avenge Fróði. The index joins them.

hallvardr.en:
Hallvarðr háreksblesi was an Icelandic skald of the early eleventh century who composed a poem in praise of Knútr the Great (Cnut), king of Denmark and England.

Snorri quotes his verses several times in Skáldskaparmál as examples of kennings: in the section on the earth (chapter 31), for gold and rings (chapter 61), for ships, which he calls the reindeer and the deer of the sound (chapter 64), and in the list of terms for kings (chapter 79). These quotations are the main part of what survives of his poetry.

hjadningar.en:
The Hjaðningar are the followers of King Heðinn, son of Hjarrandi, who carried off Hildr, daughter of King Högni. Snorri tells the story in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 62): Högni pursues them, Hildr's offer of a necklace and attempts at peace fail, and the battle called Hjaðningavíg begins. Each night Hildr wakes the slain by magic, and they fight again the next day; so it will go on until Ragnarök. Snorri cites Bragi's Ragnarsdrápa as his source.

The tale explains kennings: battle is the storm or snow-shower of the Hjaðningar and weapons are their fire or wands (Skáldskaparmál 58, 62), and Snorri's own Háttatal plays on it. The story is also known from Sörla þáttr, Saxo Grammaticus and Old English allusions to Heoden.

hjalprekr.en:
Hjálprekr is the king at whose court Sigurðr grows up. After Sigmundr's death his widow Hjördís marries Hjálprekr's son Álfr (prose of Grípisspá, Frá dauða Sinfjötla).

Skáldskaparmál chapter 47 places him at Þjóð and says Reginn, after Fáfnir drove him away, came to him as his smith and took Sigurðr into fosterage. In the prose of Reginsmál Sigurðr chooses Grani from Hjálprekr's stud, and it is at Hjálprekr's house that Reginn urges him to fight Fáfnir.

hlidskjalf.en:
Hliðskjálf is the high seat in Ásgarðr from which the whole world can be seen. In Gylfaginning chapter 9 it is Óðinn's seat; sitting there he sees all lands and the doings of all men.

Others use it too. In Gylfaginning chapter 37 and the prose of Skírnismál, Freyr sits in Hliðskjálf, sees Gerðr in Jötunheimar and falls sick with love, which leads to Skírnir's journey. In the prose of Grímnismál Óðinn and Frigg sit there watching their foster-sons Geirrøðr and Agnarr. It is mentioned also in Hrafnagaldr Óðins 10.

hrist.en: Hrist ('shaker') is a valkyrie, named first in the list of valkyries who bring drink to the warriors in Valhöll in Grímnismál (36), a stanza Snorri quotes in Gylfaginning (chapter 36). Nothing is told of her as an individual. Like other valkyrie names, hers serves the skalds in kennings, such as Hrist's storm for battle in Snorri's own Háttatal (chapter 2), and in a kenning for a woman quoted in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 58).

hugi.en:
Hugi (thought) is the young man whom Útgarða-Loki sets to race against Þórr's servant Þjálfi in Gylfaginning chapter 46. Þjálfi, the fastest of Þórr's party, runs three heats against him and loses each one by a wider margin.

In chapter 47, as Þórr and his companions leave, Útgarða-Loki reveals his illusions: Hugi was his own thought, and no runner could keep pace with thought. The contest parallels Loki's eating match against Logi (wildfire) and Þórr's wrestling with Elli (old age).

laedingr.en: Læðingr is the first fetter the gods made to bind the wolf Fenrir (Gylfaginning chapter 34). Alarmed at how fast he grew and at prophecies that he would be their ruin, the Æsir made a very strong fetter and invited Fenrir to test his strength on it; he broke it at the first kick. The second, twice as strong, called Drómi, fared no better, and the wolf was finally held by Gleipnir. Snorri adds the proverbial phrases "to loose oneself from Læðingr" and "to dash out of Drómi" for something done with great effort.

lofdi.en:
Lofði is a legendary war-king listed in Skáldskaparmál (chapter 80) among the founders of famous royal houses. Snorri says the host that followed him were called Lofðar, and that his kin, the Lofðungar, include Eylimi, maternal grandfather of Sigurðr Fáfnisbani.

He is mentioned to explain poetic words: lofðar is a common poetic word for "men", and Snorri derives it from Lofði's followers (chapters 80-81), quoting a verse by Arnórr jarlaskáld. No story about Lofði himself survives in the Edda.

mysingr.en:
Mýsingr is a sea-king in the story of the mill Grótti. Told in Skáldskaparmál chapter 52 and the prose of Gróttasöngr, he is the leader of the army that the giantesses Fenja and Menja grind out against King Fróði.

He comes that same night, kills Fróði, takes great plunder and ends "Fróði's peace". He carries off the mill and the two women and has them grind salt on board his ship; when they ask at midnight whether he has had enough, he tells them to grind on, until the ship sinks. Since then there has been a whirlpool where the sea runs through the hole in the millstone, and the sea has been salt.

narfi.en:
Narfi or Nörfi is the giant of Jötunheimar who is father of Nótt (Night) in Gylfaginning chapter 10; Nótt is dark and swarthy like her kin, and her children are Auðr, Jörð and Dagr.

The same name is borne by a son of Loki and Sigyn, also called Nari (Gylfaginning chapter 33). After Baldr's death the gods turn Loki's son Váli into a wolf, which tears Narfi apart, and bind Loki with Narfi's entrails (chapter 50); the prose at the end of Lokasenna reverses the roles, with Loki bound by Váli's bowels and Narfi changed into a wolf. The index mixes these two figures.

olrun.en:
Ölrún is one of three swan-maidens in Völundarkviða, daughter of Kíarr of Valland. She and the two daughters of King Hlöðvér, Hlaðguðr and Hervör, are found spinning flax by a lake in Úlfdalir by three brothers, sons of a king of the Finns. Ölrún becomes the wife of Egill, while Slagfiðr takes Hlaðguðr and Völundr takes Hervör (prose introduction). The prose calls the three valkyries.

After seven winters the women fly away to seek battles and do not return; Egill goes east in search of Ölrún (4), and the poem then follows Völundr alone.

randver.en:
Randvér is the son of the Gothic king Jörmunrekkr. In Skáldskaparmál chapter 50 Jörmunrekkr sends him to woo Svanhildr, Sigurðr and Guðrún's daughter, as a bride for himself. Earl Bikki advises Randvér to take her for himself, since both are young and the king is old, and then reports this to Jörmunrekkr.

The king has his son hanged. Before he dies, Randvér plucks the feathers from his hawk and sends it to his father; seeing it, Jörmunrekkr understands that he is now as powerless as the plucked bird, being old and without a son. Svanhildr is trampled to death by horses, which leads to the vengeance of Hamðir and Sörli. The prose introduction to Guðrúnarhvöt gives the same account of Bikki's counsel and Randvér's death.

sefafjoll.en:
Sefafjöll ("sedge fells") is the home of the valkyrie Sigrún, daughter of Högni, in Helgakviða Hundingsbana II.

After Dagr Högnason kills Helgi with Óðinn's spear, he rides to Sefafjöll to tell his sister the news (prose). There Sigrún laments that she will sit joyless at Sefafjöll now that Helgi will not return (stanza 36), and her maid tells her to go out from Sefafjöll because Helgi's mound is open and he has come back (42). In his speeches from the mound Helgi addresses her as "Sigrún of Sefafjöll" (45, 48).

sigrdrifa.en:
Sigrdrífa ("victory-urger") is the valkyrie whom Sigurðr wakes after killing Fáfnir. In Fáfnismál (44) the birds tell him of a helmeted maiden sleeping on a mountain. The prose of Sigrdrífumál explains that she had given victory to Agnarr and killed the old king Hjálmgunnarr, whom Óðinn had promised victory; Óðinn pricked her with a sleep-thorn and decreed that she should marry, and she vowed to wed only a man who knew no fear. She then teaches Sigurðr lore about runes and gives him a series of counsels (Sigrdrífumál, for example 22).

Whether she is Brynhildr is a famous problem. The poem never says so, and "Sigrdrífa" may be a descriptive name; but Helreið Brynhildar tells the Hjálmgunnarr story of Brynhildr, Snorri (Skáldskaparmál chapter 48) calls the woman Sigurðr wakes Hildr or Brynhildr, and the Völsunga saga identifies the two outright.

skaevadr.en: Skævaðr is a horse known only from the lists of horse names. In the þula of horse names in Skáldskaparmál chapter 72 (also preserved among the Eddubrot) he appears in the line "Vigg and Stúfr were with Skævaðr", and another verse in the same chapter says Skævaðr was ridden by "the ruler of the Haddingjar". No story about him survives.

skjoldungs.en:
The Skjöldungar are the legendary royal house of Denmark, named after Skjöldr, a son of Óðinn. In the Prologue (chapter 4) Óðinn sets Skjöldr over Reiðgotaland and the line descends through his son Friðleifr; Skáldskaparmál chapter 52 and the prose of Gróttasöngr say Skjöldr ruled the land now called Denmark, then Gotland, and that his grandson was Fróði of Fróði's peace.

Skáldskaparmál chapter 80 lists them among the famous royal houses beside the Ynglingar and Völsungar, and Hyndluljóð 16 counts the Skjöldungar among Óttarr's illustrious kin. The same dynasty appears as the Scyldings in Beowulf.

skuld.en:
Skuld is the youngest of the three Norns, with Urðr and Verðandi, the maidens who come from the well beneath Yggdrasill and shape the lives of men (Völuspá 20; Gylfaginning chapter 15). Her name is usually connected with skulu, 'shall', and is the ordinary word for a debt.

She is also a valkyrie: in Völuspá (30) Skuld carries a shield among the valkyries, and Snorri says that the youngest Norn, Skuld, rides with Guðr and Róta to choose the slain (Gylfaginning chapter 36). Her name also occurs in Grógaldr (4).

slagfidr.en:
Slagfiðr is one of three brothers, with Egill and Völundr, sons of a king of the Finns, in the prose introduction to Völundarkviða. The brothers hunt on snowshoes and settle in Úlfdalir. There they find three swan-maidens spinning flax by a lake and take them as wives; Slagfiðr marries Svanhvít.

After seven years the women fly off to battle and do not return. Egill goes east in search of Ölrún, and Slagfiðr goes south after Svanhvít, while Völundr stays behind. The poem names him only once more, when the brothers come back from hunting to find the hall empty (stanza 4); his further fate is not told.

son.en:
Són is one of the two vats, with Boðn, which together with the kettle Óðrerir received the blood of the wise Kvasir when the dwarves Fjalarr and Galarr killed him; mixed with honey, the blood became the mead of poetry (Skáldskaparmál chapter 5).

Óðinn emptied all three vessels in three draughts when Gunnlöð let him drink in the mountain Hnitbjörg (Skáldskaparmál chapter 6). Hence poetry can be called the liquid of Són or of Boðn, and skaldic verse speaks of "the seed of Són" growing in the poet's mouth (chapter 10).

stufr.en:
Stúfr ("stump") is a horse name in the þulur of poetic names. In Skáldskaparmál (chapter 72) it occurs in the list of famous horses, and in a verse naming riders and their mounts in which "Vífill rode Stúfr"; the same lists appear in the Eddubrot material (Þorgrímsþula).

The index also catches the eleventh-century skald Stúfr inn blindi, quoted in Skáldskaparmál chapter 80 ("As Stúfr sang"), who is a different figure.

ulfdalir.en:
Úlfdalir ("Wolf-dales") is the place where Völundr and his brothers Slagfiðr and Egill live in Völundarkviða. The opening prose says the three came there on skis while hunting, built a house beside the lake Úlfsjár, and there found three swan-maidens spinning flax on the shore, whom they took as wives.

After the women fly away, Völundr stays alone in Úlfdalir forging gold rings while waiting for his wife (stanza 5). King Níðuðr learns that he is there alone, sends his men by night (6), and has him bound; when Völundr wakes, Níðuðr accuses him of having taken "our treasures" in Úlfdalir (13).

vanir.en:
The Vanir are the second family of gods beside the Æsir, associated with wealth and fertility; Njörðr, Freyr and Freyja belong to them.

Snorri tells that the Æsir and the Vanir were at war and made peace by exchanging hostages: Njörðr was given to the Æsir, and Hœnir went to the Vanir (Gylfaginning chapter 23). In Skáldskaparmál chapter 5 both sides spit into a vat to seal the peace, and from that spittle the gods make Kvasir, whose blood becomes the mead of poetry. Freyr is called "god of the Vanir" and Freyja "lady of the Vanir" in kennings, and in one Eddubrot passage some Vanir see the goddess Gná riding through the air. Völuspá alludes to the war, and Snorri's Ynglinga saga tells it differently.

voggr.en:
Vöggr is the poor boy in Snorri's anecdote of how Hrólfr kraki got his nickname (Skáldskaparmál, chapters 53-54 in this edition). Seeing the slender young king in the high seat, Vöggr says he looks like a mere pole (kraki). Hrólfr accepts the name, gives Vöggr a gold ring as a name-gift, and Vöggr vows to kill whoever kills the king; Hrólfr laughs that Vöggr is pleased with a small thing. Snorri tells the story to show Hrólfr's generosity, as part of the explanation of the gold kenning Kraki's seed.

In other sources, such as Hrólfs saga kraka and Saxo Grammaticus (where he is Wiggo), he fulfils his vow after Hrólfr's fall.

yrsa.en:
Yrsa is the mother of the legendary Danish king Hrólfr kraki and wife of the Swedish king Aðils of Uppsala. Gróttasöngr 22 alludes to her story: Hrólfr, "Yrsa's son", will be called "her own son and brother", because, as other sources tell, he was born of her union with her own father, Helgi.

In Skáldskaparmál chapter 54 Snorri tells how Hrólfr rode to Uppsala to claim payment from Aðils. Yrsa welcomed her son, and after Aðils' men tried to scorch Hrólfr's company with great fires, she gave Hrólfr a horn filled with gold, including the ring Svíagríss, and sent them away. On the plain of Fýrisvellir Hrólfr scattered the gold to delay his pursuers, which is why gold is called "Kraki's seed" or "seed of Fýrisvellir". A verse there speaks of gold as "the crop of Yrsa's offspring".

alsvidr.en: Alsviðr ('all-swift') is one of the two horses that draw the chariot of the sun, the other being Árvakr ('early-waking'). Snorri tells that the gods set Sól, daughter of Mundilfari, to drive them, and placed bellows under their shoulders to cool them (Gylfaginning chapter 11); Grímnismál 37 names the pair, and Skáldskaparmál chapter 72 repeats the list of horses of the sun, night and day. In Forspjallsljóð (Hrafnagaldr Óðins) 4 the name Alsviðr appears in an obscure stanza about worlds sinking and being gathered again; what it refers to there is uncertain.

andvaranaut.en: Andvaranautr ('Andvari's gift') is the gold ring that Loki takes from the dwarf Andvari with the rest of his hoard. In the prose of Reginsmál Óðinn uses it to cover the last whisker showing on the gold-filled otter-skin paid to Hreiðmarr. Snorri has Sigurðr give it to Brynhildr as her bride-gift while in Gunnarr's shape; in the queens' quarrel Guðrún names the ring on Brynhildr's hand and says it was not Gunnarr who won it on Gnitaheiðr, and after Sigurðr's death Gunnarr and Högni take it with Fáfnir's hoard (Skáldskaparmál chapter 49). In Dráp Niflunga, by contrast, Guðrún holds it and sends it to Högni with a wolf's hair tied round it, as a warning against Atli's invitation.

arvakr.en: Árvakr ("early-awake") is one of the two horses that draw the chariot of the sun, the other being Alsviðr. Gylfaginning chapter 11 says the gods set Sól, daughter of Mundilfari, to drive them, with bellows under their shoulders to cool them; Grímnismál 37 gives the same picture in verse. In Sigrdrífumál 15 runes are said to be written on Árvakr's ear, and the horse is named again in the list of horses in Skáldskaparmál chapter 72.

bergelmir.en: Bergelmir is the frost giant who survives the flood of Ymir's blood. Vafþrúðnismál makes him the son of Þrúðgelmir and grandson of Aurgelmir (Ymir), born countless winters before the earth was shaped, and the earliest thing the giant Vafþrúðnir remembers is Bergelmir being laid in a lúðr (Vafþrúðnismál 29, 35). Snorri explains in Gylfaginning chapter 7 that when the sons of Borr killed Ymir, all the frost giants drowned in his blood except Bergelmir, who escaped with his wife in a boat; the later race of frost giants descends from them. The meaning of lúðr in the poem is uncertain (possibly a cradle or a mill-frame), and Snorri's boat may be his own interpretation.

bikki.en: Bikki is the evil counsellor of King Jörmunrekkr in the Gothic part of the Völsung cycle. In Skáldskaparmál chapter 50 and the prose introduction to Guðrúnarhvöt, Jörmunrekkr sends his son Randvér to bring home Svanhildr, Sigurðr's daughter, as his bride; Bikki advises Randvér that the young pair are better matched than the old king, then reports the affair to Jörmunrekkr. The king has Randvér hanged and Svanhildr trampled to death by horses, which leads to the vengeance of Guðrún's sons.

bilskirnir.en: Bilskirnir is the hall of Þórr, which Snorri places in Þrúðvangar and Grímnismál in Þrúðheimr. Its size is its fame: Óðinn says in Grímnismál 24 that it has five hundred rooms and forty, the greatest of all roofed houses he knows, a stanza Snorri quotes in Gylfaginning chapter 21. In Skáldskaparmál chapter 11 Þórr may be called owner of Bilskirnir, and a stanza by Gamli there names him "Lord of high Bilskirnir" as he strikes at the Miðgarðr serpent.

blakkr.en: Blakkr ('the dark one') is a horse name in the verse lists of horses. In Þorgrímsþula, quoted in Skáldskaparmál chapter 72 and among the Eddubrot, 'Blakkr could carry a thane'; in Kálfsvísa, in the same chapter, Blakkr is the horse ridden by Björn ('Björn rode Blakkr'). Nothing more is told of either. The word blakkr is also a common poetic word for a horse.

breidablik.en: Breiðablik ('broad-gleaming') is Baldr's hall in heaven. Grímnismál 12 counts it the seventh of the gods' dwellings, in a land that lies most free of baleful runes. Snorri lists it among the heavenly abodes, saying there is none fairer (Gylfaginning chapter 17), and in his account of Baldr says that nothing unclean may be there, quoting the Grímnismál stanza (Gylfaginning chapter 22).

brimir.en: Brimir is a giant whose name is bound up with the halls of the world after Ragnarök. Völuspá 37 speaks of the beer-hall of the giant Brimir in Ókólnir, and Snorri, following it, makes Brimir the name of the hall itself, where good drink awaits the righteous (Gylfaginning chapter 52). Völuspá 9 has the gods shape the dwarfs out of "Brimir's blood", which Snorri understands as Ymir's, and Sigrdrífumál 14 mentions "Brimir's sword", where the name stands in a sword-kenning.

brokkr.en: Brokkr is a dwarf, brother of the smith who in this text is called Sindri (other manuscripts name him Eitri). In Skáldskaparmál chapter 43 Loki wagers his head with Brokkr that his brother cannot make three treasures as good as those made by the sons of Ívaldi. Brokkr works the bellows while a fly, Loki in disguise, stings him, and the smith produces the golden boar, the ring Draupnir and the hammer Mjöllnir, whose handle comes out short when Brokkr falters. Brokkr presents the gifts to Óðinn, Freyr and Þórr, and the gods judge the hammer best, so the dwarf wins the wager; denied Loki's head, he sews up his lips instead.

droma.en: Drómi is the second fetter the Æsir made for the wolf Fenrir, twice as strong as the first, Læðingr. In Gylfaginning chapter 34 the Æsir urge the Wolf to test himself against it for the sake of fame; he does so and breaks it, as he had broken Læðingr, so that the dwarf-made Gleipnir has to be fetched. The Eddubrot prose likewise names Drómi and Læðingr as the two fetters that failed to hold him.

durinn.en: Durinn is a dwarf, named second after Mótsognir at the creation of the dwarves in Völuspá 10, which also says the dwarves made figures in human likeness "as Durinn said". Snorri retells this in Gylfaginning chapter 14, explaining that the dwarves first quickened as maggots in Ymir's flesh before the gods gave them human shape and wit. In Hervarar saga a dwarf Durinn (in some versions Dulinn) forges the sword Tyrfingr together with Dvalinn.

eyjolfr.en: Eyjólfr dáðaskáld ('valiant skald') was an Icelandic poet of the early eleventh century who served Earl Eiríkr Hákonarson; his poem on the earl is known as Bandadrápa. Snorri quotes him twice: for 'ski' as a word for ship (Skáldskaparmál chapter 64) and for bönd, 'bonds', as a name of the gods, in a half-stanza on Eiríkr (Skáldskaparmál chapter 68). The Eyjólfr son of Hundingr whom Helgi kills in Helgakviða Hundingsbana I 14 and the prose of Helgakviða Hundingsbana II is a different figure.

fakr.en: Fákr is a horse name that occurs only in verse lists of horses. Þorgrímsþula, quoted in the list of horse names in Skáldskaparmál chapter 72, names it among other horses, and Kálfsvísa, quoted in the same chapter, says that Haki rode Fákr; both verses recur among the Eddubrot fragments. Fákr is also an ordinary poetic word for a horse.

falhofnir.en: Falhófnir is one of the horses of the Æsir on which the gods ride each day to their court of judgement at the ash Yggdrasill. It appears in the list of the gods' horses in Grímnismál 30 and in Gylfaginning chapter 15, where it is named ninth after Sleipnir, and again among the horse names of Skáldskaparmál chapter 72 and the corresponding þula among the Eddubrot. Nothing is told of it beyond its name.

freki.en: Freki (roughly "the greedy one") is one of Óðinn's two wolves, the other being Geri. Gylfaginning chapter 38 explains that Óðinn gives the food on his table to the wolves, since he needs none himself and lives on wine alone, and quotes the stanza that appears as Grímnismál 19. The wolves suit Óðinn as god of battle, wolves being the beasts that feed on the slain.

geirrodargardar.en: Geirröðargarðar, "Geirröðr's courts", is the dwelling of the giant Geirröðr. Skáldskaparmál chapter 11 recalls the river Vimur that Þórr waded on his way there, and in chapter 26 Bragi tells the full tale: Loki, flying into the courts in Frigg's hawk-plumage, is caught and starved by Geirröðr until he promises to bring Þórr there without his hammer and girdle of might. Þórr, helped by the giantess Gríðr, goes nonetheless and kills Geirröðr and his daughters.

glenr.en: Glenr is the husband of Sól, the sun. In Gylfaginning chapter 11 Mundilfari, proud of his beautiful children, names them Máni and Sól and marries his daughter to Glenr; the angered gods set brother and sister in the sky to drive the chariots of moon and sun. In Skáldskaparmál chapter 34 the sun may accordingly be called Glenr's wife, illustrated by a stanza of Skúli Þorsteinsson about "Glenr's god-blithe Bed-Mate". The same name is given to one of the Æsir's horses in Gylfaginning chapter 15.

glitnir.en: Glitnir ('the shining one') is the hall of Forseti, son of Baldr and Nanna, in heaven. Its pillars and posts are of red gold and its roof of silver (Gylfaginning chapter 17). Snorri calls it the best seat of judgement among gods and men: all who come there with disputes go away reconciled (Gylfaginning chapter 32, quoting the stanza that is Grímnismál 15, where it is the tenth of the divine dwellings).

gnipalundr.en: Gnipalundr is a coastal place in Helgakviða Hundingsbana I where Helgi Hundingsbani's fleet comes to land before his battle with the sons of Granmarr. Sigrún shields the ships as they come in off Gnipalundr (30). In the flyting that follows, Sinfjötli tells Guðmundr that the Ylfings have come there from the east (34), and Guðmundr retorts that giantesses once gelded Sinfjötli at Gnipalundr (40). Guðmundr then reports Helgi's ships lying at anchor off it (50).

gotland.en: Gotland, the land of the Goths, is in Snorri's account the old name of the realm later called Denmark, where Óðinn's son Skjöldr ruled, followed by Friðleifr and Fróði (Skáldskaparmál chapter 52, repeated in the prose before Gróttasöngr). In Skáldskaparmál chapter 81 Snorri derives the name from a king Goti, himself named after Óðinn's name Gautr, and says that Gautland or Gotland was so called after Óðinn. It is not the Baltic island of the same name.

greip.en: Greip is a giantess, one of the two daughters of the giant Geirröðr. In Skáldskaparmál chapter 26 she and her sister Gjálp are under the chair on which Þórr sits in Geirröðr's goat-shed; the chair rises to crush him against the roof, but he pushes back with the staff Gríðarvölr and breaks both their backs. The same episode, with a stanza in which Þórr boasts of the deed, is given in the Eddubrot section. Gjálp and Greip are also named among the nine giantess mothers of Heimdallr in Völuspá in skamma 8; whether these are the same figures is unclear.

gullfaxi.en: Gullfaxi, "Gold-mane", is the horse of the giant Hrungnir. In Skáldskaparmál chapter 24 Óðinn wagers that no horse in Jötunheimar is as good as Sleipnir, and Hrungnir races after him on Gullfaxi as far as Ásgarðr. After Þórr has killed Hrungnir, he gives Gullfaxi to his three-night-old son Magni, who had lifted the giant's leg off him; Óðinn objects that the horse should have gone to him rather than to the son of a giantess. The name also appears among the horses of Þorgrímsþula in Skáldskaparmál chapter 72 and the Eddubrot.

guthormr.en: Gotþormr (Guthormr) is the younger brother of Gunnarr and Högni (Snorri makes him Gjúki's stepson) and the killer of Sigurðr. Because he had not sworn blood-brotherhood with Sigurðr, the brothers rouse him to the deed, as Gunnarr urges in Sigurðarkviða in skamma 20; Brot af Sigurðarkviðu 8 says they fed him wolf and serpent flesh to make him fierce. He stabs Sigurðr in bed, and the dying hero hurls his sword Gramr after him and cuts him in two (Sigurðarkviða in skamma 22; Skáldskaparmál chapter 49). The Brot and Guðrúnarkviða II instead place Sigurðr's death out of doors.

gyllir.en: Gyllir ('golden') is one of the horses on which the Æsir ride each day to their court of judgement at the well of Urðr under Yggdrasill. Snorri counts it the third of their steeds after Sleipnir and Glaðr (Gylfaginning chapter 15), following the list in Grímnismál 30. It is named again in Þorgrímsþula, quoted in Skáldskaparmál chapter 72 and among the Eddubrot. Nothing is said of who rides it.

haddingjar.en: The Haddingjar are a legendary people or royal line, usually connected with the Hasdingi, a ruling house of the Vandals. The name appears only in verse. It forms part of a kenning in a stanza about the death of a Sigurðr at Ögló (Skáldskaparmál chapter 9), and the 'land of the Haddingjar' is among the signs carved on the drinking-horn Grímhildr gives Guðrún (Guðrúnarkviða II 22). Kálfsvísa, quoted in the list of horses in Skáldskaparmál chapter 72 and again among the Eddubrot fragments, says that the lord of the Haddingjar rode Skævaðr.

heidrun.en: Heiðrún is the she-goat who stands at Valhöll and browses the branches of the tree Læraðr; from her udders flows mead enough to fill a great vat each day, so that all the einherjar can drink their fill (Gylfaginning chapter 39; Grímnismál 25). In Hyndluljóð 30 and 31 the giantess Hyndla insults Freyja with the refrain that she runs about at night like Heiðrún among the he-goats.

herkja.en: Herkja is Atli's serving-woman and former concubine in Guðrúnarkviða in þriðja. In the prose introduction she tells Atli that she has seen Guðrún together with Þjóðrekr, and Atli confronts Guðrún with the charge (stanza 2). Guðrún clears herself by the ordeal of taking stones from the bottom of a boiling cauldron unharmed. Atli then makes Herkja undergo the same test (stanza 10); her hands are scalded, and she is thrown into a foul bog (stanza 11).

hervardr.en: Hervarðr is one of the twelve berserk sons of Arngrímr and Eyfura, who in the legendary tradition fell together on Sámsey. Hyndluljóð 22 names him among them as kinsmen of Óttarr. In Hervararkviða 9 and 11 Angantýr's daughter Hervör, at the burial mounds, calls on Hervarðr, Hjörvarðr, Hrani and Angantýr by name, cursing them to rot unless they give up the sword Tyrfingr. A different Hervarðr, a son of Hundingr killed by Helgi, is named in the prose of Helgakviða Hundingsbana II.

himinbjorg.en: Himinbjörg (roughly 'heaven-cliffs') is the dwelling of Heimdallr, standing at heaven's end where the bridge Bifröst reaches the sky. Grímnismál 13 counts it the eighth of the gods' homes, where the watchman of the gods gladly drinks good mead. Snorri lists it among the heavenly abodes in Gylfaginning chapter 17 and in chapter 27 places Heimdallr there to guard the bridge against the hill-giants, quoting the Grímnismál stanza.

hlesey.en: Hlésey ('Hlér's island', probably the Danish island of Læsø in the Kattegat) is the home of the sea-giant Ægir, also called Hlér, according to the opening of Skáldskaparmál (chapter 1). In Hárbarðsljóð 37 Þórr boasts that he killed the 'brides of berserks' on Hlésey. Helgi names it as his home when Sigrún questions him in Helgakviða Hundingsbana II 6, and in Oddrúnarkviða 30 Oddrún hears from Hlésey the sound of Gunnarr's harp as he lies in the snake pit.

hlodver.en: Hlöðvér is a king whose name corresponds to Frankish Chlodowech (Louis). In Völundarkviða he is the father of the swan-maidens Hlaðguðr and Hervör, who with Ölrún become the wives of Völundr and his brothers (opening prose; 15); when Völundr counts his rings and finds one missing, he hopes that Hlöðvér's daughter has come back (10). In Guðrúnarkviða II 25 Grímhildr offers the widowed Guðrún 'Hlöðvér's halls' among other treasures; whether the same king is meant there is not clear.

hofvarpnir.en: Hófvarpnir ("hoof-tosser") is the horse of the goddess Gná, Frigg's messenger, which runs through the air and over the sea. Gylfaginning chapter 35 tells how some of the Vanir saw her riding in the sky and asked what flew there; she answered in verse that she did not fly but rode on Hófvarpnir, whom Hamskerpir begot on Garðrofa. The same passage is repeated among the Eddubrot.

holgi.en: Hölgi is a legendary king from whom Hálogaland in northern Norway takes its name, and the father of Þorgerðr Hölgabrúðr. Skáldskaparmál chapter 55 tells that both were worshipped with sacrifices and that Hölgi's burial mound was raised with alternate layers of gold or silver offerings and of earth and stones. Hence gold may be called the roof of Hölgi's mound (Skáldskaparmál chapter 40), as in the stanza by Skúli Þorsteinsson about the battle of Svöldr quoted in chapter 55.

hrimfaxi.en: Hrímfaxi, "Rime-mane", is the horse that draws Nótt (Night) across the sky. In Gylfaginning chapter 10 Alföðr gives Nótt and her son Dagr each a horse and chariot; Nótt rides first behind Hrímfaxi, who every morning bedews the earth with the foam from his bit. Vafþrúðnismál 14 says the same, deriving the dew in the valleys from it. Skáldskaparmál chapter 72 gives Fjörsvartnir as an alternative name for Night's horse, and Forspjallsljóð (Hrafnagaldr Óðins) 23 refers to it in its account of nightfall.

hrym.en: Hrymr is a giant who leads the forces of chaos at Ragnarök. Völuspá 50 has him come from the east holding his shield before him, as the serpent writhes and Naglfar is loosed. Snorri, quoting the stanza in Gylfaginning chapter 51, makes Hrymr the helmsman of Naglfar, the ship built from dead men's nails; Völuspá itself says that Loki steers a ship from the east, so the two accounts differ on who commands which vessel.

hunaland.en: Húnaland, the land of the Huns, is the kingdom of King Humli in the poem and prose of the Battle of the Goths and Huns (Hlöðskviða). Hlöðr, Heiðrekr's son by Humli's daughter, is born there (Hlöðskviða 2) and returns there angry when his half-brother Angantýr refuses him an equal share of the inheritance. Humli then raises so great a host that Húnaland is left empty of fighting men, and leads it through the forest Myrkviðr, which divides Húnaland from the land of the Goths, to war on Angantýr (prose of Hlöðskviða).

idavollr.en: Iðavöllr is the plain where the gods meet. In Völuspá 7 they gather there at the beginning of time to build shrines and temples and set up forges; after Ragnarök they meet there again on the renewed earth and recall the past (Völuspá 60). Snorri places it in the middle of Ásgarðr and makes it the site of the gods' first works, the court Glaðsheimr and the goddesses' hall (Gylfaginning chapter 14), and says that Víðarr and Váli will live there after the end, where Ásgarðr once stood (Gylfaginning chapter 53).

jarnsaxa.en: Járnsaxa is a giantess, the mother of Þórr's son Magni. Skáldskaparmál chapter 24 tells how the three-night-old Magni lifted Hrungnir's leg off his father, and chapter 29 lists "co-wife of Járnsaxa" among the kennings for Sif. In a verse in Skáldskaparmál chapter 75 the wolf is called Járnsaxa's steed, as giantesses ride wolves. Völuspá in skamma 8 names a Járnsaxa among the nine giantess mothers of Heimdallr, possibly a different figure of the same name.

konr.en: Konr ungr ("Konr the young") is the youngest son of Jarl in Rígsþula (stanza 41). He learns runes that protect warriors, blunt blades and calm the sea (stanza 43), and wins the name Rígr for himself. Hunting birds in the forest, he is told by a crow that he would do better to ride out and fight armies (stanzas 46-47), and is pointed to the rich halls of Danr and Danpr; there the poem breaks off. His name is usually read as a play on konungr, "king", so that the poem ends with the origin of kingship.

lettfeti.en: Léttfeti, "Light-foot", is one of the horses of the Æsir. It appears only in lists: Grímnismál 30 names it among the steeds the gods ride each day to judgement at Yggdrasill, and Gylfaginning chapter 15 counts it as the eleventh of the Æsir's horses. It is also among the horse names of Þorgrímsþula in Skáldskaparmál chapter 72 and the Eddubrot.

logi.en: Logi ('flame') is one of Útgarða-Loki's household in the story of Þórr's visit to Útgarðr. In Gylfaginning chapter 46 he is set against Loki in an eating contest: both reach the middle of a meat-filled trough at the same moment, but Logi has eaten the bones and the trough as well. In chapter 47 Útgarða-Loki reveals the deception: Logi was wildfire itself, which consumes wood as fast as meat.

mead-of-poetry.en: The mead of poetry makes whoever drinks it a poet or a scholar. Snorri tells its story in Skáldskaparmál chapters 5 and 6: the dwarves Fjalarr and Galarr brew it from the blood of the wise Kvasir mixed with honey, and give it to the giant Suttungr as ransom for their lives; he hides it in Hnitbjörg in the keeping of his daughter Gunnlöð. Óðinn, calling himself Bölverkr, works for Suttungr's brother Baugi wins three draughts from Gunnlöð, drinks it all and flies back to Ásgarðr as an eagle and spits it into vats; some escapes behind him, the share of bad poets. Hence poetry is called Suttungr's mead, Kvasir's blood and Óðinn's drink. Hávamál gives Óðinn's own account.

muspell-sons.en: The sons of Múspell (Múspells synir) are the fiery host that comes out of the burning southern realm Múspell at Ragnarök, led by Surtr. Snorri mentions them three times in Gylfaginning: when they go harrying not even Bifröst will hold (chapter 13); Freyr will miss the sword he gave away when they come (chapter 37); and in the account of the last battle they ride over Bifröst, which breaks under them, and make for the field Vígríðr, where they form a bright company of their own (chapter 51).

nordri.en: Norðri ("northern one") is one of the four dwarfs set under the four corners of the sky, made from Ymir's skull, together with Austri, Suðri and Vestri (Gylfaginning chapter 8). Hence the sky can be called the helmet of Norðri and the others (Skáldskaparmál chapter 31). He is also named in the catalogue of dwarfs in Völuspá 11, which Snorri quotes in Gylfaginning chapter 14.

nott.en: Nótt (Night) is the personified night. In Gylfaginning chapter 10 she is the dark daughter of the giant Nörfi or Narfi; she is married first to Naglfari, by whom she has Auðr, then to Ánarr, by whom she has Jörð, and last to Dellingr of the race of the Æsir, by whom she has Dagr (Day). Óðinn sets Nótt and Dagr in the sky with horses and chariots to ride around the earth; Nótt's horse Hrímfaxi bedews the earth each morning with the foam from its bit. Vafþrúðnismál 25 likewise says that Nótt was born of Nörr.

oku-thor.en: Öku-Þórr, "Driving Þórr", is a byname of Þórr. In Gylfaginning chapter 21 Hárr names it alongside Ása-Þórr and explains it by Þórr's chariot drawn by his two goats, Tanngnjóstr and Tanngrisnir. The name opens the tale of Þórr's journey to Útgarða-Loki, where Öku-Þórr drives out with Loki and lodges with the farmer whose children become his servants (chapter 44), and Útgarða-Loki uses it mockingly when he greets the travellers, wondering whether this little fellow can really be Öku-Þórr (chapter 46).

ori.en: Óri is a dwarf, named in the dwarf list of Völuspá 15 alongside Dóri, Dúfr and Andvari, and in the same lists as quoted by Snorri in Gylfaginning chapter 14. A Dóri and Óri also appear together in Fjölsvinnsmál 34, among those named as builders in Fjölsviðr's answers to Svipdagr; the pairing suggests the poet drew on the same traditional list.

reidgotaland.en: Reiðgotaland is a land of the Goths in legendary geography. In Snorri's Prologue (chapter 4) Óðinn, travelling north, takes it and sets his son Skjöldr over it, adding that it is now called Jutland; in Skáldskaparmál chapter 81 the mainland ruled by Óðinn was called Reiðgotaland and the islands Eygotaland. In Heiðreksgátur it is where the powerful Gestumblindi lives, out of favour with King Heiðrekr, before the riddle contest. Its location differs between sources.

saehrimnir.en: Sæhrímnir is the boar whose flesh feeds the einherjar in Valhöll. Snorri says it is boiled every day and is whole again by evening, however great the host, and that the cook is Andhrímnir and the kettle Eldhrímnir (Gylfaginning chapter 38), quoting the stanza of Grímnismál (18) that names all three. In Forspjallsljóð 19 the gods themselves are sated with Sæhrímnir at a feast.

saxony.en: Saxland (Saxony) is, in Snorri's Prologue, the first land Óðinn and his followers settled on their way north from Asia: Óðinn ruled there long and set three of his sons over it, Vegdeg ruling East Saxland (Prologue chapter 4). From there the Æsir and their language spread through the northern lands (Prologue chapter 5). Skáldskaparmál chapter 66 mentions it in passing, saying that the governors called lendir menn in the Danish tongue are called counts in Saxland.

sighvatr.en: Sighvatr Þórðarson was an Icelandic skald of the early eleventh century, court poet and close companion of King Óláfr Haraldsson (Saint Óláfr). Snorri quotes him in Skáldskaparmál for a heiti of Christ as king of the Jordan (chapter 65), for terms for a ruler's household men (chapter 66), and for the loanword sinjór or senjór, "lord", among the words for rulers (chapters 79 and 80).

sinir.en: Sinir is one of the horses of the Æsir; the name means roughly "sinewy". It appears only in lists: Grímnismál 30 names it among the steeds the gods ride each day to judgement at Yggdrasill, and Gylfaginning chapter 15 counts it as the seventh of the Æsir's horses. It is also among the horse names of Þorgrímsþula in Skáldskaparmál chapter 72 and the Eddubrot.

skeidbrimir.en: Skeiðbrimir is one of the horses the Æsir ride each day to their court at Yggdrasill. Snorri names him fifth in his list of the gods' steeds in Gylfaginning chapter 15, drawing on Grímnismál 30, and he recurs in the horse names of Þorgrímsþula cited in Skáldskaparmál chapter 72 and in the Eddubrot. Nothing is told of him beyond the name.

sudri.en: Suðri ('southern') is one of the four dwarves set under the corners of the sky, which the sons of Borr made from Ymir's skull; the others are Austri, Vestri and Norðri (Gylfaginning chapter 8). Hence the sky can be called 'helm of Austri, Vestri, Suðri and Norðri' (Skáldskaparmál chapter 31). The name also stands in the list of dwarves in Völuspá 11, which Snorri quotes in Gylfaginning chapter 14.

svadilfari.en: Svaðilfari is the stallion of the giant builder who offers to build the gods a fortress. Snorri tells that the horse hauled stones by night and did twice the work of its master, so the walls were nearly finished in time; Loki, turned into a mare, lured it away into the woods, the work stopped, and later Loki gave birth to its foal, the grey eight-legged Sleipnir (Gylfaginning chapter 42). Völuspá in skamma 11 also says that Loki bore Sleipnir to Svaðilfari.

svanhvit.en: Svanhvít ("swan-white") is one of the three swan-maidens and valkyries of Völundarkviða. The opening prose calls her Hlaðguðr svanhvít, daughter of King Hlöðvér, and says she lived seven winters with Völundr's brother Slagfiðr before flying away to battle. Stanza 2 describes her wearing swan feathers, and in stanza 4 Slagfiðr goes south in search of her, while Egill goes east after Ölrún.

thokk.en: Þökk is the giantess who refuses to weep for Baldr. In Gylfaginning chapter 49 the messengers of the Æsir, having asked everything in the world to weep Baldr out of Hel, find her sitting in a cave; she answers in a stanza that she will weep "waterless tears" and that Hel should keep what she has. So Baldr does not return. Snorri adds that people believe she was Loki. The same prose and stanza are also given in the Eddubrot section of this edition.

thorgrimsthula.en: Þorgrímsþula, "Þorgrímr's þula", is a lost or fragmentary versified name list from which Snorri draws two sets of heiti. Skáldskaparmál chapter 72 introduces a list of horse names from it (Hrafn, Sleipnir, Léttfeti, Gullfaxi and others), and chapter 73 a short list of ox names. The same verses are given in the Eddubrot. Nothing is known of the Þorgrímr after whom it is named.

thrymr.en: Þrymr is the lord of the giants who steals Þórr's hammer Mjöllnir in Þrymskviða, hides it eight leagues underground and demands Freyja as the price of its return. When she refuses, Þórr goes to Jötunheimr disguised as the bride, with Loki as bridesmaid. Þrymr has the benches strewn for Njörðr's daughter (stanza 22), marvels at a bride who eats an ox and eight salmon and drinks three casks of mead (25), and has the hammer laid in her lap to hallow the marriage (30). Þórr seizes it and kills Þrymr first, then all his kin (31). The story is not told by Snorri.

tror.en: Trór is the name Snorri's Prologue gives to Þórr as a human prince of Troy: the son of King Múnón or Mennón and of Tróán, daughter of Priam. Fostered in Thrace by the duke Lóríkus, whom he kills, he grows to great strength, marries the prophetess Sibil, whom 'we call Sif', and becomes the ancestor of Óðinn's line (Prologue chapter 3). The account is a learned euhemerist construction linking the northern gods to Troy.

valgardr.en: Valgarðr á Velli was an eleventh-century Icelandic skald who composed for King Haraldr harðráði of Norway. Snorri quotes him only for single words: for a word for wave among the names of the sea (Skáldskaparmál chapter 76), for two names of fire (Skáldskaparmál chapter 77), and for the royal title Skilfingr, in a half-stanza about the king's host in the south and the laying waste of Sicily (Skáldskaparmál chapter 80).

vestri.en: Vestri ("western one") is one of the four dwarfs set under the four corners of the sky made from Ymir's skull, with Austri, Suðri and Norðri (Gylfaginning chapter 8). The sky may therefore be called the helmet of Vestri and the others (Skáldskaparmál chapter 31). He is also named in the catalogue of dwarfs in Völuspá 11, quoted by Snorri in Gylfaginning chapter 14.

vid.en: Víð ("the wide one") is one of the mythical rivers. In Gylfaginning chapter 4 it is among the rivers that spring from the well Hvergelmir, and in chapter 39 among the streams fed by the drops from the horns of the hart Eikþyrnir. It appears in the river lists of Grímnismál 27 and 28, the first group flowing through the gods' lands and the second among men and down to Hel.

viga-glumr.en: Víga-Glúmr Eyjólfsson was a tenth-century Icelandic chieftain of Eyjafjörður and the hero of Víga-Glúms saga. Snorri quotes his verses for kennings in Skáldskaparmál: in chapter 9 and again in chapter 61 a helmet is called the hood of Hangatýr, the Hanged God, a name of Óðinn; in chapter 63 battle is the storm of Óðinn and warriors the staves of that storm; and a further verse of his is quoted in chapter 75.

vingolf.en: Vingólf is a hall of the gods whose role differs from passage to passage. In Gylfaginning chapter 3 the righteous are to live with the All-father "in Gimlé or Vingólf"; in chapter 14 it is the sanctuary built by the gods for the goddesses, next to Glaðsheimr; in chapter 20 Óðinn assigns Valhöll and Vingólf to the warriors fallen in battle. In Forspjallsljóð 17 the gods' messengers come to Vingólf and greet the Æsir at Óðinn's feast.

ynglings.en: The Ynglingar are the royal house of the Swedes, said to descend from Yngvi. In the Prologue (chapter 5) Yngvi is Óðinn's son who rules in Sweden after him; in Skáldskaparmál chapter 80 Yngvi is one of the nine sons of Hálfdan the Old, and the Ynglings are among the royal houses whose names skalds use for princes. In Hyndluljóð 16 they are listed with the Skjöldungs, Skilfings and Öðlings among Óttarr's illustrious kin. The sources thus differ on who Yngvi was.

alof.en: Álof is the daughter of Jarl Fránmarr, foster-father of Sigrlinn, in the prose of Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar. When Atli comes to woo Sigrlinn for King Hjörvarðr he is refused. Returning with the king, he finds the two young women in a house guarded by Fránmarr in the shape of an eagle, and brings them away. Hjörvarðr marries Sigrlinn and Atli marries Álof.

amma.en: Amma ("grandmother") is the wife of Afi in Rígsþula, the couple of the middle household that the god Rígr visits on his journey. She sits spinning in their well-kept house and serves Rígr a meal of boiled veal (Rígsþula 16 and 17). Nine months after his visit she bears a son, sprinkled with water and named Karl, ancestor of the free farmers (Rígsþula 21).

arheimar.en: Árheimar is the seat of the Gothic king Angantýr in Hlöðskviða, the poem of the battle of the Goths and the Huns. His half-brother Hlöðr rides there to claim his share of their father Heiðrekr's inheritance while Angantýr is drinking Heiðrekr's funeral ale (stanza 3). When Hervör falls fighting the invading Huns, Ormarr rides to Angantýr in Árheimar with the news, and Hlöðr calls Angantýr's messenger Gizurr a man come from Árheimar (stanza 29). The saga places it at Danparstaðir, a name linked with the river Dnieper.

asia.en: Asía is one of the three parts of the world in the learned geography of the Prologue. In chapter 2 it is the region stretching from north through east to south, the richest and fairest part of the earth and the site of its centre. In chapter 5 the Æsir are explained as "men of Asia" who came north with Óðinn; when they settle in Sweden under King Gylfi and intermarry, their language, the tongue of the men of Asia, becomes the speech of all the northern lands.

aurboda.en: Aurboða is a giantess of the hill-giants, wife of Gymir and mother of Gerðr, whom Freyr sees from Hliðskjálf and marries (Gylfaginning chapter 37). Völuspá in skamma 2 likewise names her as Gerðr's mother. An Aurboða also appears in Fjölsvinnsmál 38 as one of the maidens who sit at the knees of Menglöð; whether the poet meant the same figure is unclear.

aurvandill.en: Aurvandill is the husband of the seeress Gróa. In Skáldskaparmál chapter 25, after the duel with Hrungnir, Gróa chants over the piece of whetstone lodged in Þórr's head; to please her, Þórr tells that he carried Aurvandill in a basket on his back out of Jötunheimar, across the icy river Élivágar. One toe stuck out and froze, so Þórr broke it off and threw it into the sky, where it became the star called Aurvandill's toe. Gróa, delighted, forgets her spells and the stone stays in Þórr's head.

austrvegr.en: Austrvegr ('the eastern way') is the Old Norse name for the lands east of Scandinavia across the Baltic. The prose opening of Hárbarðsljóð has Þórr returning from a journey there when he meets the ferryman. Snorri says that Hálfdan the Old raided widely in Austrvegr and killed King Sigtryggr there, and that the kindred of the Skilfingar lives there (Skáldskaparmál chapter 80).

bestla.en: Bestla is a giantess, daughter of Bölþorn, wife of Borr and mother of Óðinn, Vili and Vé (Gylfaginning chapter 6). In Hávamál 140 Óðinn says he learned nine mighty songs from the son of Bölþorn, Bestla's father, that is from his mother's brother. A skaldic verse in Skáldskaparmál chapter 9 calls Óðinn the son of Bestla.

beyla.en: Beyla is a servant of Freyr and wife of his servant Byggvir, present at Ægir's feast in Lokasenna (prose introduction). When she hears the mountains shake and announces that Þórr is coming to silence Loki (stanza 55), Loki turns on her too, calling her Byggvir's wife and abusing her as foul (stanza 56). Her name has been connected with words for bee, cow or bean, and Byggvir's with barley, but neither interpretation is certain.

blodughadda.en: Blóðughadda ('the one with bloody hair') is one of the nine daughters of Ægir and Rán, personifications of the waves. She appears only in Skáldskaparmál: among the daughters named in the kennings for the sea in chapter 33, and in the lists of their names in chapter 76.

brunavagar.en: Brunavágar is a stretch of coast where Helgi Hundingsbani lies with his fleet after killing King Hundingr, and where his men slaughter cattle on the shore and eat the meat raw (prose of Helgakviða Hundingsbana II). There Sigrún rides to his ship and asks why they wait in Brunavágar; Helgi answers that they wait for a fair wind to sail east (Helgakviða Hundingsbana II 5-6).

byggvir.en: Byggvir is a servant of Freyr, present with his wife Beyla at Ægir's feast in Lokasenna (opening prose). When he speaks up for Freyr, Loki mocks him as one who could never share out food among men and who hid in the straw when warriors went to fight (46), and later abuses Beyla as Byggvir's wife (56). His name seems to be related to bygg, 'barley'.

bylgja.en: Bylgja ("billow") is one of the nine daughters of Ægir and Rán, who personify the waves of the sea. She is named in the list of Ægir's daughters among the kennings for the sea in Skáldskaparmál chapter 33 and again in chapter 76, where her name is also illustrated, as a word for a wave, by a verse of Óttarr svarti.

danpr.en: Danpr is a legendary name linked with the river Dnieper. In Rígsþula 48 the crow tells Konr ungr that Danr and Danpr have nobler halls and greater wealth than he; Danpr appears to be an early king, and the poem breaks off soon after. In Atlakviða 5 "the steads of Danpr" are among the riches Atli offers Gunnarr and Högni, and in Hlöðskviða 10 a fair stone at Danparstaðir is part of the inheritance Hlöðr claims; in these heroic poems the name points to the old Gothic lands by the Dnieper.

dufa.en: Dúfa is one of the nine daughters of Ægir and Rán, whose names are poetic words for waves. She appears only in the lists of these daughters in Skáldskaparmál chapter 33, where the sea may be called the father of Ægir's daughters, and chapter 76, where the nine are named again among the heiti for sea and waves and her name is among the six used by Einarr Skúlason in one stanza.

duneyrr.en: Duneyrr is one of the four harts that run in the branches of Yggdrasill and gnaw its leaves, with Dáinn, Dvalinn and Duraþrór. Grímnismál 33 names them, and Snorri repeats the list in Gylfaginning chapter 16; the name also appears among words for hart in Skáldskaparmál chapter 71.

dunheidr.en: Dúnheiðr ('Dún heath') is a battle-site of the Goths in the Battle of the Goths and Huns. Angantýr names it with Dylgja and the Jassarfjöll as the place where Hlöðr and the Huns are to be challenged (Hlöðskviða 26 and 28), and in the prose Angantýr leads his host to Dúnheiðr, where the eight-day battle is fought in which Hlöðr and King Humli fall. Its location is unknown.

durathror.en: Duraþrór is one of the four harts that graze in the branches of the ash Yggdrasill, with Dáinn, Dvalinn and Duneyrr. They are named in Grímnismál 33 and in Snorri's description of the tree (Gylfaginning chapter 16), and the name appears again in the list of words for a hart in Skáldskaparmál chapter 71.

edda-rigsthula.en: Edda ("great-grandmother") is the wife of Ái in Rígsþula, the old couple of the poorest household, whom the god Rígr visits first. In stanza 2 the two sit by the hearth in old-fashioned dress; Edda serves him a heavy loaf full of husks and broth (Rígsþula 4), and nine months after his visit she bears a black-haired son named Þræll, ancestor of the thralls (Rígsþula 7).

eitill.en: Eitill is a son of Atli and Guðrún and brother of Erpr (prose of Dráp Niflunga).
